findings.status: FIXED — verified (NR-006 execution) — and its anchor Table is the single blocker for a shared MetaData (NR-078)
findings.title: Table national_facilities is mapped by two ORM classes on different bases
findings.description: app/models/clinical_scope.py::NationalFacility(Base) and app/national/domain/facility.py::Facility(AuditEntity) both map the physical table national_facilities. INTERACTION RECORDED (NR-078). The repair replaced the duplicate mapped class with a bare reference-only Table in NationalBase.metadata, so that seventeen app/national models can resolve ForeignKey('national_facilities.id') inside their own MetaData. That was correct for the problem it solved and is not reopened here. It does mean national_facilities is claimed by two registered metadata, which is exactly what Alembic's multi-metadata target refuses -- so this anchor is the one and only collision standing between the repository and a single shared MetaData. Both definitions are column-identical, so adopting Option A costs one deleted declaration, not an ownership decision.
findings.root_cause: Two domains modelled the same physical table independently; no ownership constitution enforced.
findings.evidence: AST scan of 828 mapped tables found exactly one table claimed by two app packages; both class definitions confirmed by reading. BATCH-2.5 settled which mapping is authoritative: app/models/clinical_scope.py::NationalFacility declares exactly the 6 columns created by migration 20260813_0004 (id, facility_code, name, status, created_at, updated_at) and is the target of the physical foreign key clinical_ehr_facility_bindings.national_facility_id. app/national/domain/facility.py::Facility declares 18 entirely different columns, has zero physical backing, and is marked extend_existing=True. clinical_scope.py states in-source that the national EHR facility is a separate resource from the operational facility and that no relationship may be inferred from identifier similarity. | NR-051: migration 20260813_0004_clinical_ehr_scope_bridge.py creates national_facilities with exactly NationalFacility's six columns (id, facility_code, name, status, created_at, updated_at). national.domain.facility.Facility maps eight columns that do not physically exist, including facility_type NOT NULL, so any query through it raises UndefinedColumn. This is not a choice between two designs - one cannot execute. Both are dormant (Facility only re-exported by national/domain/__init__.py), so the defect is latent. Canonical owner on the evidence: NationalFacility. | NR-006 EXECUTION: measured rather than estimated. national.domain.facility.Facility mapped 28 columns (its own 18 plus AuditEntity's audit, soft-delete, optimistic-lock and FHIR columns), 24 of which migration 20260813_0004_clinical_ehr_scope_bridge.py never creates -- the earlier counts of 18 and 8 were both undercounts -- and it omitted two columns that do exist (facility_code, status). Three of the phantom columns are NOT NULL (facility_type, is_deleted, version). Zero consumers: every `Facility` import in the repository resolves to app.models.organization.Facility, which maps the unrelated `facilities` table; the national one was named only by its own package __init__. What NationalBase.metadata genuinely required was the foreign-key target -- 14 tables in that metadata carry a foreign key to national_facilities.id -- which is a table, not an entity.
findings.affected_users: Anything reading or writing facility data
findings.clinical_impact: Facility scoping underpins clinical authorization; divergent writes can misroute or mis-scope records.
findings.security_impact: Facility scope is an authorization input; two writers with different invariants weaken scoping.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Different column/audit expectations against one table; no shared invariants.
findings.operational_impact: Schema migrations may satisfy one mapping and break the other.
findings.intersections: I-02 NR-023 (this is its single remaining blocker).
findings.recommended_fix: Keep app/models/clinical_scope.py::NationalFacility as the single mapping of the physical table. Rename or retire app/national/domain/facility.py::Facility and follow the rename through the nine sibling foreign keys inside the national domain. Not applied in BATCH-2.5: it is an ORM schema change, and it is the first item of BATCH-3.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED: the mapped class is replaced by a bare sqlalchemy.Table in NationalBase.metadata mirroring the physical table column for column. The 14 dependent foreign keys still resolve, create_all now builds the migration's shape instead of a 28-column table no deployment has, and app.models.clinical_scope.NationalFacility is the sole ORM owner. No migration, no schema change, no data movement: the table was already correct, only one of its two ORM views was not.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_canonical_table_ownership.py: AST scan asserting one ORM owner per physical table with an empty exception ledger, a named NR-006 assertion, and a behavioural test that builds NationalBase.metadata and compares the resulting national_facilities to NationalFacility column for column. Negative-proven both ways: reintroducing a second mapper fails two tests, drifting the anchor by one column fails the third.
findings.acceptance_criteria: MET — exactly one writable mapping per physical table, across all 828.
findings.regression_risk: Medium-High.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (physical migration source + both class definitions read)

findings.status: PARTIALLY RESOLVED — 4 collisions attributed; 28 synthetic keys BLOCKED
findings.title: Clinical state machine is entity-agnostic by construction
findings.description: transition(current, target, entity=...) uses 'entity' only for the error message; one flat dict governs blood units, orders, samples, crossmatches, transfusions and reactions. Any state name shared by two entity types collides.
findings.root_cause: No per-entity keying in the state machine design.
findings.evidence: Measured, not argued. Four state values are shared by more than one entity enum: 'completed' (DonationStatus, TransfusionStatus), 'in_progress' (DonationStatus, TransfusionStatus), 'expired' (ComponentStatus, DonorStatus), 'discarded' (ComponentStatus, DonationStatus). Three of the four are keys in the shared table, so one entity's rules silently govern another's — a donation in progress is validated against transfusion rules. Twenty-eight table keys are not any enum value at all: 'issued_order', 'received_sample', 'testing_crossmatch', 'ordered_transfusion' and others are synthetic names invented to dodge collisions, which is the workaround made visible. NR-004 and NR-020 are both instances of this. BATCH-2.5 measured the full registry: 39 table keys, 43 distinct vocabulary, 5 lifecycle enums, 4 colliding states (3 of them live keys), 28 synthetic keys, 18 enum values with no key at all, and — the sharpest number — exactly 2 distinct entity values are ever passed at a call site ('blood_unit', 'transfusion'), so the rows keyed for orders, samples, crossmatches and reactions govern nothing today and would govern the wrong thing once wired up. Four synthetic keys (issued_order, received_sample, testing_crossmatch, ordered_transfusion) are explicit <state>_<entity> compounds — (entity, state) keying already implemented by hand inside the string. BATCH-2.6 CORRECTION: the claim that 'a donation in progress is validated against transfusion rules' is wrong. Only two entity values are ever passed to transition(): blood_unit (11 call sites) and transfusion (2). crossmatch, donation and donor are never validated by the state machine at all, so no cross-entity mis-validation happens today. NR-007 is a latent trap that fires when a new entity is wired up — the mechanism of NR-004 and NR-020 — not an active defect. ATTRIBUTION: for each of the four colliding states exactly one claimant reaches the machine, so the live row provably belongs to it — completed and in_progress to transfusion, expired and discarded to blood_unit. No migration is required: no colliding value is a server_default on a Blood Bank table.
findings.affected_users: All Blood Bank clinical users
findings.clinical_impact: A future duplicate state name silently widens or blocks a clinical transition, as already happened once.
findings.security_impact: None directly.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Invalid transitions may be permitted across entity types.
findings.operational_impact: Fixes require union semantics that over-permit (current residual risk).
findings.recommended_fix: Key transitions by (entity, state) and fail closed on an unknown entity. The keying is mechanical; attributing the 28 synthetic keys and the 4 colliding states to entities is not, because the per-entity transition sets have never been written down.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None applied. See the decision required.
findings.verification_method: Property-based test over every entity/state pair.
findings.acceptance_criteria: No transition is reachable for an entity type that does not define it.
findings.regression_risk: Medium — requires auditing every call site.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (code read + realised defect)
findings.decision_required: Now narrowed to the 28 synthetic keys only. They describe order, sample, crossmatch and reaction lifecycles, and none of those entities is ever passed to transition(); order, sample and reaction have no lifecycle enum at all. Those 28 rows govern nothing today and would begin governing — and colliding — the moment the corresponding entity is wired up. The mechanical keying must land in the same change as the attribution.

findings.status: RESOLVED for the lock gaps; one dependency DECISION is reserved and ledgered
findings.title: requirements-lock.txt could not build a working environment: signxml, its transitive lxml, and two more
findings.description:
CORRECTED. This recorded one gap, signxml. Measured: TWO declared packages were unlocked, with different dispositions, and signxml's own runtime dependency was unlocked as well -- so pinning signxml alone would still have produced an environment that could not install.
  signxml  DECLARED, UNLOCKED, IMPORTED. app/security/saml_service.py imports signxml.algorithms, signxml.exceptions and signxml.verifier at module level, so a lock-only environment cannot import that module. POST /auth/saml/acs is one of the 21 endpoints NR-108 declared reachable without a credential, so the dead module is on the authentication surface.
  lxml     signxml requires lxml<7,>=5.2.1 and it was absent from the lock.
  psycopg  DECLARED, UNLOCKED, NEVER IMPORTED. Nothing in app/ imports psycopg and no configuration uses the postgresql+psycopg:// scheme; psycopg2-binary is the driver in use and is declared and locked.
  annotated-doc and typing-inspection -- runtime dependencies of fastapi, pydantic and pydantic-settings -- were also unlocked. Unrelated to signxml, and found only by the transitive check.
findings.root_cause: The lock was maintained by hand against the top-level declarations, so it drifted in two directions at once: a declaration with no pin, and pins whose own runtime closure was never followed. Nothing measured either.
findings.evidence: Parsed both files: 30 declarations, 70 pins. Set difference gave signxml and psycopg. Resolving each installed distribution's Requires-Dist WITH environment markers evaluated gave lxml, annotated-doc and typing-inspection; without marker evaluation the same scan reported six, four of which were Windows-only or old-Python conditionals -- a check that ignores markers over-reports and would have been dismissed.
findings.affected_users: Developers and any lock-based environment
findings.clinical_impact: None.
findings.security_impact: SAML service unavailable in lock-only environments.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None.
findings.operational_impact: Reproducible builds diverge from production image.
findings.recommended_fix: DONE for the three real gaps: signxml==5.1.0, lxml==6.1.3, annotated-doc==0.0.5 and typing-inspection==0.4.4 added to the lock, each inserted in alphabetical position (the file has two pre-existing out-of-order pairs that were left alone).\nNOT DONE for psycopg, deliberately. Locking a driver nothing imports adds a binary wheel to every image to satisfy a declaration that is more likely the mistake; removing a declared dependency is a call for a human. Declared in DECLARED_UNLOCKED with the evidence.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_requirements_lock_covers_declarations.py -- 6 tests in the unit job: top-level coverage, the runtime closure with markers evaluated, a shrink-only exemption ledger with a ceiling of 1 and a rot check in both directions, floors on both parsers so a parser that stops parsing cannot pass, and a direct import of app.security.saml_service, which is the consequence this finding actually had. Five negative proofs: removing signxml, removing lxml, removing typing-inspection, growing the ledger and keeping a stale exemption each fail with the intended message.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met for the lock; the psycopg declaration awaits a decision.
findings.regression_risk: Low.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (both files parsed, closure resolved with markers, 6 CI-gated tests, 5 negative proofs)

findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED
findings.title: The changed-files quality gate reported PASS when MyPy had failed to execute
findings.description: scripts/quality_changed_files_gate.py printed '0 diagnostics' and PASS while MyPy exited 2 without analysing anything. Two causes combined: run_mypy parsed diagnostics regardless of the exit code, so a failed run contributed an empty list that read as clean; and execution_error_regression only fired when the head's error DIFFERED from the baseline's, which is never the case when both sides run in the same environment. A tool that never ran was certifying the change.
findings.root_cause: Zero diagnostics was treated as evidence of cleanliness without first establishing that the tool actually ran. The gate shelled out to a bare 'mypy' on PATH, which can resolve to an interpreter lacking the project dependencies MyPy must import to load its SQLAlchemy and Pydantic plugins.
findings.evidence: Reproduced at d9fdd988: the pre-fix gate printed 'baseline.mypy_changed: 0 diagnostics ... QUALITY_CHANGED_FILES_GATE: PASS' while returncode was 2 with "No module named 'sqlalchemy'". Post-fix the same comparison reports real counts (mypy_changed 170 -> 135) and PASS.
findings.affected_users: Engineers, reviewers
findings.clinical_impact: None directly.
findings.security_impact: A green gate is evidence a reviewer relies on. Any type regression, including one weakening a security or tenant-isolation path, could pass unexamined.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None directly.
findings.operational_impact: False confidence in the merge gate.
findings.intersections: Generalises beyond MyPy: any executable check whose empty output is read as success without first proving it ran.

findings.title: The pharmacy warehouse is modelled in the schema but implemented nowhere
findings.description: pharmacy_warehouses is referenced by four columns (pharmacy_stores.warehouse_id, pharmacy_stock_levels.warehouse_id, pharmacy_inventory_transfers.from_warehouse_id and .to_warehouse_id) and the org model names warehouse_officer and warehouse_manager roles, yet no endpoint, service, seed, demo generator or migration ever creates a Warehouse or a Store. The columns are reachable from the API but unusable: any value fails the foreign key because no row can exist. receive_transfer moves stock by store only, ignoring the transfer table's own warehouse columns. A third, parallel location representation exists as a free-text 'location' VARCHAR on batches, stock, stores and warehouses.
findings.root_cause: The physical schema was drafted for a warehouse/store hierarchy that was never implemented, and no ADR ever decided whether it should be. P0-2 Phase 2A classified warehouse_id as RECONCILE (keep) rather than REMOVE_FROM_ORM, so M4 preserved it faithfully without resolving what it means.
findings.evidence: On a migrated database at 20260912_0001: pharmacy_warehouses and pharmacy_stores both have 0 rows; inserting a stock row with warehouse_id=42 raises a foreign-key violation. Warehouse and Store are imported nowhere outside backend/app/pharmacy/models.py. pharmacy_warehouses has exactly one outbound FK (lab_id -> labs) and no FK to national_facilities, so it is lab-scoped, not facility-scoped. pharmacy_stores.warehouse_id is nullable, so store does not determine warehouse. pharmacy_stock_levels carries no CHECK constraint, so nothing prevents a stock row whose store_id and warehouse_id disagree.
findings.affected_users: Pharmacy operations, inventory planners
findings.clinical_impact: None today: the feature is inert. If implemented incorrectly later, stock attributed to the wrong location can misdirect dispensing.
findings.security_impact: GET /inventory/stock-levels accepts warehouse_id and store_id as internal integer keys on the public API surface, which CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §3 forbids. Currently unreachable because no such row can exist.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The schema permits stock rows whose store_id and warehouse_id contradict each other. Unreachable today only because neither can be set to a valid value.
findings.operational_impact: Dead schema that reads as a supported feature. Two role names promise a subsystem that does not exist.
findings.dependencies: Depends on deciding whether pharmacy inventory locations are lab-scoped or facility-scoped, and on reconciling the free-text 'location' column.
findings.intersections: P0-2-M4-GAP-STOCK-WAREHOUSE; NR-016's stock uniqueness constraint uq_pharmacy_stock; CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §2 and §3.
findings.contradictions: The schema, the role catalogue and the transfer table all assume warehouses exist; every code path assumes they do not.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the question before writing any code. Either (a) warehouse is first-class: give it creation endpoints, a public identifier per CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §2, a decision on lab- versus facility-scoping, a rule tying stock.warehouse_id to stock.store_id, and a resolution of the free-text location column; or (b) it is not: retire the two tables and four columns deliberately through a migration. Do not implement either speculatively.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None available — the fix requires a domain decision. What was done instead: the analysis and its evidence are recorded in docs/pharmacy-platform/P0-2-M4-GAP-STOCK-WAREHOUSE.md, and two regression guards assert that warehouse_id stays out of the stock uniqueness key and that the premise behind that conclusion (no creation path exists) still holds.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_pharmacy_inventory_identity_postgres.py::test_warehouse_is_not_part_of_stock_identity and ::test_nothing_can_create_a_warehouse_or_a_store. findings.title: Transfusion state machine had no "verified" state, so a verified transfusion could never be started
findings.description: tests/test_icu_lab_workflow_p0.py::test_transfusion_requires_independent_crossmatch_and_bedside_verification fails with BloodBankWorkflowError: Invalid transfusion transition: verified -> in_progress. The test asserts that a transfusion verified at the bedside can then start; the state machine does not allow that edge.
findings.root_cause: The shared _TRANSITIONS table keys transfusion states on TransfusionStatus values ("in_progress" -> "completed" is present and correct), but "verified" was absent. transition() fails closed on an unknown current state, so start_transfusion_safely — which requires status == VERIFIED and targets IN_PROGRESS — could never succeed. The table also carries a parallel "verification"/"started"/"ordered_transfusion" chain that no code path ever writes. Same defect class as NR-004.
findings.evidence: TransfusionStatus (domain/enums.py:111) defines ordered/dispensed/verified/in_progress/completed/reacted/cancelled — no "verification" or "started". verify_transfusion_safely (service.py:529) is the only writer of "verified". start_transfusion_safely (service.py:543-545) requires VERIFIED then calls transition(status, IN_PROGRESS, entity="transfusion"). complete_transfusion_safely (service.py:586) validates in_progress -> completed and that key exists, proving the table keys on real status values for this entity. grep confirms nothing ever writes "verification", "started" or "ordered_transfusion". An existing test, test_state_machine_rejects_completion_without_start, already treated "verified" as a transfusion state and asserted only that verified -> completed is illegal.

findings.title: Blood bank inventory and component endpoints ignore lab_id
findings.description: GET /blood-bank/inventory calls BloodBankService.get_inventory(facility_id), which queries BloodInventoryModel filtered only by an optional facility_id. The table has a lab_id column and the method never filters it, so any authenticated user can read every laboratory's blood inventory. POST /blood-bank/components calls process_component(body), which mass-assigns a raw request dict onto BloodComponentModel — a model that also carries lab_id — so a caller can write a row attributed to another tenant. Both endpoints are registered and reachable. CORRECTION: the router does enforce require_permission('system:admin') globally, so the exposure was across laboratories for system:admin holders, not for every authenticated user as first recorded. The scope was also wider than first found: NINE route-reachable methods queried without a lab filter (register_donor, get_donor, find_donors, defer_donor, register_donation, complete_donation, get_inventory, get_critical_inventory, get_dashboard), and every blood_bank_* table carries lab_id.
findings.root_cause: Four legacy service methods (process_component, record_transfusion, start_transfusion, complete_transfusion) predate the *_safely variants and were never brought up to the same guards. The safe variants filter lab_id, take a row lock, increment version and validate through the state machine; these do none of it.
findings.evidence: AST scan of blood_bank/application/service.py: process_component (line 168), record_transfusion (255), start_transfusion (263), complete_transfusion (273) all have transition=N lab_id=N for_update=N version=N, against issue_units_safely / start_transfusion_safely / complete_transfusion_safely which are Y on all four. Reachability: process_component is called from blood_bank/api/routes.py:160 and get_inventory from routes.py:171. BloodComponentModel and BloodInventoryModel both have lab_id. BATCH-2.7 found one route-reachable method the original fix missed: create_blood_request mass-assigned the raw request body onto BloodRequestModel, a TenantEntity whose blood_bank_requests.lab_id is NOT NULL, so a caller could file a blood request against another laboratory by putting lab_id in the payload. Fixed with the same _owned() helper. Two regressions added, both proven to fail with the fix reverted. record_transfusion_safely also mass-assigns but its route injects the server lab_id after **body, so it was already safe.
findings.affected_users: Every laboratory on the platform
findings.recommended_fix: Filter lab_id in get_inventory as the *_safely methods do, and stop mass-assigning a raw dict in process_component. record_transfusion, start_transfusion and complete_transfusion are called from nowhere and are retirement candidates.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: BloodBankService now takes a server-supplied lab_id; _require_lab() fails closed when it is absent, _scoped() filters every query, and _owned() strips client lab_id and sets it from the authenticated context. The route dependency supplies it through the same _lab_id helper the row-locked routes already used — no new authorization mechanism.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/blood_bank/test_tenant_isolation_nr021.py, 7 tests: A cannot read B, B cannot read A, missing tenant context refuses rather than returning everything, client lab_id cannot override the server on components or donors, id lookup does not cross laboratories, dashboard counts only the caller's lab. findings.acceptance_criteria: Every reachable blood bank read and write filters lab_id.
findings.regression_risk: Adding the filter will change results for any caller relying on the unfiltered listing.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (AST scan plus route trace plus column check)

findings.title: Four of the five most-depended-on tables in the repository do not exist
findings.description: national_practitioners (58 inbound references), national_citizens (51), national_patients (51) and national_encounters (42) are mapped but have no physical table. national_facilities (44) is physical but is the one table mapped by two declarative bases. care_continuum, ehr, nursing and national_data all declare foreign keys into this national core, which is why 77 tables classify as CROSS_DOMAIN_OWNER: they cannot be created in isolation.
findings.root_cause: The national person/practitioner/encounter core was modelled and consumed but never built, and the one piece that was built acquired a second owner.
findings.evidence: Disposition matrix: 77 CROSS_DOMAIN_OWNER tables; cross-domain edges care_continuum->national 153, ehr->national 60, care_continuum->models 39, nursing->models 27. 16 of EHR's 18 tables depend on national_*. | NR-022 CORE MAP: FK references counted across app/, then every candidate checked against op.create_table in the migration chain by AST rather than by name appearance -- the latter matches foreign-key references inside migrations and gives false positives (it wrongly reported national_citizens and national_patients as built). 419 tables are physically created against 828 ORM-mapped. CORRECTION to this finding's headline: three of the five most-depended-on tables are unbuilt, not four. The sharper statement is that the four most-depended-on NATIONAL CORE concepts are all unbuilt -- national_practitioners (88 FK refs), national_citizens (77), national_patients (63), national_encounters (35) -- so 263 foreign-key references name tables no migration creates. Meanwhile a parallel BUILT core does exist and is what the platform runs on: labs (76), national_facilities (66), lab_users (56), niam_accounts (36), niam_organizations (35), niam_persons (28), patients (24). | NR-022 DECISION APPLIED: the binary patients-vs-national_citizens framing is REJECTED. Person/Identity is the canonical national subject; Patient and Citizen are contextual roles. All 263 references to the four unbuilt subject tables were extracted by AST (owner table, column, target) and classified by explicit per-column rules: CITIZEN 75 (portal/registry context), PATIENT 63 (clinical subject), PRACTITIONER 57 (licensure load-bearing), ENCOUNTER 35 (clinical episode, not a subject), PERSON_ACTOR 11 (who performed the action), ASSIGNMENT 11 (posting/coordination role), REVIEW 9 (undecidable from the column name, named individually), PERSON_KIN 2 (mother_id/father_id -- kinship is between persons). Zero unclassified. The load-bearing result: only 57 of the 88 practitioner references require practitioner semantics; 11 are actor identity and 11 are an assignment role. Pointing all 88 at a Practitioner table would be as wrong as pointing all 88 at Person.
findings.affected_users: Every clinical domain awaiting implementation
findings.recommended_fix: Per-class transitions, not one bulk re-point. PERSON_ACTOR and PERSON_KIN resolve to the canonical Person (niam_persons). PRACTITIONER resolves to the canonical Practitioner composition built in NR-061. ASSIGNMENT resolves to niam_assignments. PATIENT remains a clinical-domain concept and CITIZEN a citizen/portal context -- neither is replaced by Person. ENCOUNTER is not a subject question at all. Each transition uses add -> backfill -> validate -> shadow-read; no destructive mass rewrite. The nine REVIEW sites must be decided against their call sites before the practitioner transition lands.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_subject_reference_semantics.py holds the classification while the transition is in flight. Unit 5 APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_stable_core_invariants.py asserts every Core concept is still built, has exactly one ORM owner in the module the map names, and that nothing in the Core references a table outside the Core and outside the Identity Platform substrate -- domains reference Core, never the reverse. findings.title: alembic revision --autogenerate cannot run: foreign keys cross MetaData boundaries
findings.description: target_metadata is a list of 18 distinct MetaData objects and Alembic sorts each independently. SQLAlchemy resolves ForeignKey('table.col') only within the referrer's own MetaData, so 360 foreign-key references across 24 distinct targets are unresolvable and 6 of the 18 metadata objects fail their topological sort. The first failure reported is ehr_allergies.encounter_id -> national_encounters.
findings.root_cause: Cross-MetaData foreign keys. CORRECTION: the previously recorded root cause — 'the national core is mapped and consumed but never built' — is DISPROVEN. All 24 unresolvable targets ARE mapped; they are simply mapped by a different MetaData than the table referencing them. The earlier measurement was taken before import_all_models() was added to env.py.
findings.evidence: Reproduced with NO database connection — a pure metadata failure. Measured against the exact env.py import graph: 18 target_metadata entries / 18 distinct MetaData; 12 sort cleanly, 6 fail (EHRBase, TrustBase, CareContinuumBase, IdentityBase, NursingBase, DataPlatformBase); 360 unresolvable FK references across 24 targets; 0 targets mapped by no metadata; exactly 1 table name claimed by two metadata (national_facilities). Earlier figures (13 targets / ~130 refs / 'citizens' mapped nowhere) were measured on a partial import graph and are superseded. BATCH-2.6 evaluated the architectures against real behaviour. A single canonical MetaData assembled with Table.to_metadata() RESOLVES ALL 363 cross-MetaData FK references and sorts all 651 tables — but compare_metadata against a database at head then emits 5101 operations INCLUDING 76 DROP TABLE, a larger hazard than the 74 BATCH-2.5 closed. env.py now imports the 14 model modules no other import reached, cutting that to 12 (84% reduction). The residual blockers are exactly three: NR-006 (1 name collision), NR-030 (12 physical tables mapped by no ORM class), NR-029 (2 FK targets that exist nowhere). BATCH-2.7: NR-029 is closed, so two blockers remain. NR-030's twelve tables are now classified and named, but seven are permanent exclusions that a combined MetaData must be told about explicitly. | NR-006, recorded here as one of two blockers, is FIXED: national_facilities now has a single ORM owner and its foreign-key anchor stays inside NationalBase.metadata, so no new cross-MetaData reference was introduced. NR-030 remains.
findings.affected_users: Every engineer who needs a migration
findings.recommended_fix: Option C: one combined MetaData built at env.py time, with a named collision resolution, a named exclusion list for physical-only tables, and a fail-closed check that refuses to build when anything unlisted appears. Blocked until NR-006, NR-029 and NR-030 are resolved; none is infrastructure-only.

findings.status: OPEN — DESIGN DEFECT — count updated in BATCH-3: 12 truncated-UUID4 _ulid() definitions, was 13; app/nursing/base.py now uses the INTEGER key the schema creates
findings.title: One name, two incompatible identifier schemes: _ulid() is a ULID in 2 places and a truncated UUID4 in 13
findings.description: Fifteen functions in the tree are named _ulid(). Thirteen return str(uuid.uuid4()).replace('-', '').upper()[:26] — the first 26 hex characters of a random UUID4, with no timestamp prefix, no Crockford base32 and no monotonic ordering. Two are genuine ULIDs (48-bit millisecond timestamp plus 80 random bits, Crockford base32, time-sortable). Identifiers minted under one name are therefore not mutually ordered, and a call site does not reveal which scheme it gets. Every declarative base uses the fake one; the genuine implementation mints no primary keys.
findings.root_cause: A ULID was intended; a truncated UUID4 was written and copied. A correct implementation was later written twice, under the same name, without reconciling the copies.
findings.evidence: AST scan of every _ulid() definition under backend/: 13 truncated-UUID4 bodies (app/{care_continuum,citizen_platform,clinical,ehr,identity,national,nursing}/base.py, two national notification-platform modules, three staticmethods in app/identity/certificates/services.py, and one test helper) and 2 genuine ULIDs (app/services/consent_service.py:30, app/services/mpi/resolver.py:57), both using the standard Crockford alphabet '0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ'. An earlier draft of this finding claimed all fifteen were identical; that was wrong and is corrected here.
findings.affected_components: backend/app/*/base.py (15 modules) and every model keyed on String(26)
findings.affected_users: None directly — this is a performance and design defect, not a correctness one.
findings.clinical_impact: None.
findings.security_impact: None. 104 bits of randomness remains collision-safe; the truncation is undocumented rather than dangerous.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None. Keys remain unique.
findings.operational_impact: The 13 fake keys pay the full 26-byte cost of a string primary key while delivering none of ULID's only benefit — time-ordered index insertion. Random insertion order causes B-tree page splits a monotonic key would avoid. Separately, two identifier populations under one name cannot be ordered against each other.
findings.scalability_impact: Grows with row count. This is the measured basis for choosing INTEGER/BIGINT keys for the national core rather than copying the VARCHAR shape.
findings.intersections: NR-003 (pharmacy PK type divergence, same key shape).
findings.recommended_fix: Pick one implementation and give the other a different name. For new tables, follow the identity contract (INTEGER/BIGINT internal key, UUID4 public id). Do not retype live keys merely for consistency.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Rename the function and document the truncation. Not applied: fifteen call sites, and the name appears in no external contract, so the change is safe but out of this batch's scope.
findings.verification_method: An AST guard pinning the 13/2 split, plus an ordering test asserting that two identifiers generated a second apart sort in creation order — which the 13 fail and the 2 pass.
findings.acceptance_criteria: The generator's name matches its behaviour.
findings.regression_risk: Low.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (AST scan of all 15 definitions)

findings.status: RESOLVED — all mutating routes audited; proven by execution against PostgreSQL
findings.title: Six legacy Blood Bank routes wrote no audit record (the canonical paths did)
findings.description: SECOND CORRECTION, then RESOLVED. The count was 7; it is 6. Two items in the earlier list were wrong. POST /crossmatch/check was already noted as non-mutating. The 'sample transition' route, POST /samples/{sample_id}/transition at routes.py:671, is in fact guarded -- it calls guard.claim and guard.complete, so it was audited all along. The six genuinely unaudited mutating routes were POST /donors, POST /donors/{donor_id}/defer, POST /donations, POST /donations/{donation_id}/complete, POST /components and POST /requests. All six now write a hash-chained audit_logs row inside the same transaction as the clinical effect. A seventh write path, _update_donor, was reachable from POST /donors and also unaudited -- see NR-105.
findings.root_cause: Two causes, both fixed. (1) BloodBankService.__init__ took db, event_bus and lab_id but NO actor, so there was no user to attribute an audit row to; the six methods commit inside the service, so the route layer could not wrap them either. (2) The register's own recommended fix conflated two different changes -- 'bring them under ClinicalCommandGuard' (which needs an idempotency key and a precondition contract on each, a behavioural API change CLAUDE.md reserves) with 'write an audit record' (purely additive). The audit half was held hostage to the reserved half and so was never done.
findings.evidence: AST scan of blood_bank/api/routes.py: 21 mutating routes; 14 audited via ClinicalCommandGuard (which calls log_action at command_guard.py:200 and :247), 6 unaudited, 1 (/crossmatch/check) non-mutating. Execution proof against PostgreSQL at revision 20260916_0001: each of the six writes exactly one audit_logs row carrying user_id, lab_id, resource_type and chain_hash; a rolled-back mutation leaves zero audit rows, observed by counting the row inside the transaction (before+1) and again after the rollback (before); a service built without an actor records NULL rather than borrowing the last one. 12 tests pass, 5 of them integration; the fixture leaves zero rows, which matters because audit_logs denies DELETE by trigger. Five negative proofs: dropping the actor, restoring the mass-assign, removing deferred_from, removing one _audit call and un-normalising the resource key each make the intended test fail with the intended message; service.py restored byte-identical (md5 ab10d85169701ee08674f34b93bda63a).
findings.affected_users: All Blood Bank clinical users
findings.clinical_impact: Transfusion, issue, crossmatch, reservation, reaction, return, discard and sample transition were audited. Donor registration and deferral, donation registration and completion, component processing and blood requests were not: a component could be processed and released with no record of who did it.
findings.security_impact: Security Invariant #2 is now met on every mutating route in the domain.
findings.data_integrity_impact: CORRECTION to the earlier text: the hash-chained log was never empty for this domain -- 14 routes wrote to it. The chain was incomplete, not absent.
findings.operational_impact: An incident in the blood bank cannot be reconstructed from the audit trail.
findings.legal_impact: Transfusion traceability is a regulatory expectation; the record does not exist.
findings.intersections: NR-013 (narrow audit coverage), NR-021 (same service).
findings.recommended_fix: DONE, and deliberately narrower than the earlier recommendation. The actor is threaded from get_current_user into BloodBankService, and each of the six methods calls self._audit(...) BEFORE its own commit. log_action does db.add + db.flush and never commits, so the audit row cannot survive a rolled-back mutation and the mutation cannot commit without its audit. Bringing these routes under ClinicalCommandGuard remains a separate, reserved decision: it changes the request contract. Audit coverage did not need it.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied. audit_logs.resource_id is INTEGER while every blood bank primary key is varchar, so the key is normalised the way ClinicalCommandGuard normalises it and the full string is carried in details['resource_id']. Passing it straight through raises DataError from inside the audit writer and takes the clinical transaction down -- an audit attempt that breaks the endpoint is worse than the gap it closes. This was found by execution, not by reading.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_blood_bank_mutations_are_audited.py, gated in the iam-hardening unit job (structural, 7 tests) and the PostgreSQL migration job (all 12). Carries a shrink-only DECLARED_UNAUDITED ledger, a rot check, an exact-equality ratchet and a MINIMUM_MUTATING_ROUTES=21 floor so a scan that stops seeing routes cannot pass vacuously.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met: every mutating Blood Bank route appends an attributed, chained audit row.
findings.regression_risk: Low — adding audit writes does not change clinical behaviour.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (route AST scan + 12 tests, 5 against PostgreSQL + 5 negative proofs)
