findings.category: Authorization gate that could not evaluate
findings.title: The assurance-profile administrator gate filtered on a column that does not exist
findings.status: VERIFIED (NR-044.3)
findings.description: _require_assurance_administrator in app/identity/trust/routes.py is the gate that decides whether an actor may recompute an assurance profile for a different account. It filtered on Assignment.account_id, which is not a column on that model: an assignment belongs to a person, and an account reaches one through Account.identity_id -> IdentityRecord.person_id. The gate therefore raised AttributeError instead of deciding anything.
findings.root_cause: Written against the wrong side of the account/person split, and never executed. NR-044 meant the whole trust router could not run, so the error could not surface; AUTH-005 reviewed the predicate as source rather than as behaviour.
findings.evidence: `AttributeError: type object 'Assignment' has no attribute 'account_id'`, raised the first time the gate was called with a real session — which was the first time it had ever been called, in the NR-044.3 Part H proof. app/identity/models/assignment.py declares person_id, employment_id and organization_id; there is no account_id.
findings.security_impact: Fails closed, so nothing was ever wrongly allowed: the AttributeError propagates and the request is refused as a 500. The finding is that the control had never once been evaluated, so 'an active administrative assignment is required' was an untested claim, and the refusal was an availability failure wearing an authorization decision's clothes — the same confusion as NR-048.
findings.clinical_impact: None direct. Assurance profiles feed identity-linkage decisions, so a gate that cannot evaluate is a control gap in the chain that governs who may assert another person's identity assurance.
findings.recommended_fix: Join through the account's identity to the person, matching the chain ClinicalAuthorizationContextService already uses.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py::test_asserting_for_another_account_needs_an_administrative_assignment_nr038 calls the gate with a real account and session against migrated PostgreSQL and asserts HTTP 403. Negative proof: restoring `Assignment.account_id` fails that test.
findings.discovered_by: NR-044.3 Part H (proving NR-038 once the path became reachable)
findings.resolution: The gate joins Assignment to IdentityRecord on person_id and matches the actor's identity_id, keeping the identity's own active standing in the conjunction rather than trusting the account alone. The predicate is at least as strict as the one that was intended, and it now evaluates.

findings.title: The capability generator still emits all three defects that made nine packages unimportable
findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED (NR-053)
findings.description: app/engineering/generators/capability.py is the tool that produced app/capabilities/. It still emits: a bare top-level import at line 485 (`from {cap}.capability import ...`), which makes every generated package unimportable; `from backend.app...` at lines 8, 191 and 514, which resolves only because the repository root is on sys.path; and an entity template that places a defaulted `id` before the caller's non-default fields, raising TypeError at class creation.
findings.root_cause: The generator was written and used once, in bulk, and its output was never imported. Nothing tests the generated code, so three template bugs shipped 267 modules deep.
findings.evidence: Line 485 `from {cap}.capability import {cap_cap}Capability`; lines 8/191/514 `from backend.app...`; the entity template emits `id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid4()))` immediately before `{fields}`. All three reproduce exactly in the generated tree: nine ModuleNotFoundError, ten backend.app imports, four TypeError. PR #209 fixed the first of them by hand for one package.
findings.security_impact: None directly. The risk is that a future capability is generated broken and the breakage is only noticed when something tries to import it — which, on this evidence, may be never.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly; a clinical capability generated from this template would not run.
findings.recommended_fix: Three template edits: relative import, `app.` instead of `backend.app.`, and non-default fields before defaulted ones. Then generate one capability into a temporary directory in a test and assert it imports.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_generator.py — eight tests that RUN the generator into a temporary directory and import what comes out, rather than grepping its source. D1: the generated package imports through its own name. D2: no generated file names the backend.app root, and the package imports in a subprocess given only the application root (backend/) and not the repository root — the environment D2 broke. D3: an entity with two required and one optional field is imported and instantiated; the required fields are still required and `id` still defaults. Four negative proofs, one per defect, each failing the intended test and each restored.
findings.resolution: Six edits in app/engineering/generators/capability.py. D1: the __init__ template emits `from .capability import` instead of a bare top-level import. D2: `module_path` is `app.capabilities.<cap>` — one string that feeds the infrastructure repository's two imports, the unit test's import and the descriptor metadata — plus the two literal template imports (routes, capability) and the generator's own import of its base class. D3: the entity template puts required fields ahead of the defaulted `id`, and the field list is split by whether a field carries a default; no field is renamed, retyped, added or dropped. A fourth defect (NR-055) was found by generating rather than reading. The ten existing packages were NOT touched — their disposition remains NR-050's decision.

findings.title: Nine frontend routes call capability endpoints that are never registered
findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED (NR-054)
findings.description: frontend-v3 shipped nine lazy-loaded routes under /capabilities/*, nine pages and nine navigation entries gated on dashboard:read. Each issued api.get('/<capability>') against a router under app/capabilities/ that factory.py never includes, so every one answered 404 while the navigation presented it as a working feature.
findings.root_cause: scripts/zero_drift_engine.py generates pages from docs/api/backend_inventory.json, and that inventory catalogues backend ROUTE FILES rather than REGISTERED ROUTES. Defining an APIRouter was therefore enough to put a feature in front of a user, whether or not the application ever mounted it. A secondary mismatch came from the same generator: the pages read `name` and `created_at`, fields no capability returns.
findings.evidence: Live probe: GET /encounter-management -> 404; GET /national-data/encounters -> 200 with a JSON array. The canonical endpoint filters on current_user.lab_id and is gated on require_permission('patients:read'), so the nav gate moved from dashboard:read to patients:read to match what the server enforces. Of 207 literal frontend API calls, 39 resolve to nothing: these 9 and 30 others in unrelated domains (NR-057).
findings.security_impact: None — the endpoints do not exist, so nothing is exposed. Gating is dashboard:read, the broadest permission there is.
findings.clinical_impact: Nine clinical-section navigation entries lead to pages that cannot load data. No patient-safety consequence; a visible quality defect in the clinical navigation.
findings.recommended_fix: Dispositioned per route rather than as a block. encounter-management was BOUND to its existing canonical owner, GET /national-data/encounters. The other eight were DISABLED_UNTIL_BACKEND_READY: removed from the router and from NAV_ITEMS, components preserved and documented. Registering the existing capability routers was rejected outright — every list_* returns a literal {'items': [], 'total': 0} and every create_* returns {'success': true, 'id': ''} without writing, so registering them would replace a visible 404 with an invisible lie.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_frontend_backend_contract.py — 27 tests comparing every statically resolvable frontend call against the application's own OpenAPI schema. Negative proofs: restoring the orphan call failed 2 tests; re-routing a disabled capability failed its own test.
findings.next_batch: Blocked on the NR-050 disposition, but the defect is live today either way.
findings.resolution: 1 route bound to a canonical API, 8 disabled and documented, 0 deleted, 0 stub endpoints registered, 0 fabricated datasets introduced. NR-050's ten packages were not touched: their disposition remains that finding's decision.

findings.title: The routes template built Python function names from the hyphenated URL prefix
findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED (NR-053)
findings.description: _ROUTES_TPL used a single {prefix} placeholder for both the FastAPI path prefix and the five generated function names. The prefix is the capability name with underscores replaced by hyphens, so the template emitted `async def list_clinical-foundation(` — a SyntaxError. Every generated routes.py with a multi-word capability name was invalid Python.
findings.root_cause: One placeholder serving two purposes with incompatible character sets: a URL segment may contain hyphens and a Python identifier may not.
findings.evidence: Found by running the generator, not by reading it: the first Phase 3 generation produced `SyntaxError: expected '('` at routes.py line 13 for both test specs. It had been invisible because the on-disk routes.py in app/capabilities/ say `async def list_clinical_foundation` with underscores — those files were hand-corrected after generation and the template never was, so the shipped tree is not a faithful sample of what the generator produces today.
findings.security_impact: None. A module that does not parse cannot run.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly; a clinical capability generated from this template would not import.
findings.recommended_fix: Separate the two placeholders: {prefix} for the URL, {func} for the identifier.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_generator.py::test_a_minimal_capability_generates_compiles_and_imports and ::test_a_capability_with_entities_generates_every_layer compile every generated module with py_compile. Negative proof: restoring {prefix} in the function names fails both.
findings.resolution: The routes template takes {func} for the five function names, fed by the underscored capability name, while {prefix} continues to carry the hyphenated URL. Route paths and the generated API are unchanged.

findings.title: Seventeen generator modules and the engineering CLI resolved only from the repository root
findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED (NR-056)
findings.description: NR-053 removed the `backend.app.` root from the capability generator and from everything it emits. The same defect remained in seventeen sibling modules that build on BaseGenerator (cqrs, crud, dto, openapi, repository, rest; generators/microservice, module, plugin, project; deployment/github_actions; docs/adr, docs/mermaid; testing/factories, fixtures, performance, unit) and across all twenty-seven imports of app/engineering/productivity/cli.py, which loads them. The original NR-056 entry named ten of the seventeen; the other seven are reached through the CLI's deferred, in-handler imports and carry the identical line.
findings.root_cause: `backend/` is not a package — it has no `__init__.py` — and backend/pyproject.toml publishes `include = ["app*"]`. `backend.app.` therefore resolves only as an implicit namespace package when the repository root is on sys.path. tests/conftest.py puts it there for the unrelated `shared` package and CI exports it too, so the whole family sat broken behind a green suite.
findings.evidence: Before: a probe importing the nineteen modules with backend/ as the only root failed eighteen times with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'backend'`; only NR-053's capability.py passed. After: 19/19 import, `cd backend && python3 -c 'import app.engineering.productivity.cli'` prints CLI_IMPORT_OK, and `python3 -m app.engineering.productivity.cli capability summary` reads all 52 registry descriptors — exercising the deferred app.kernel imports end to end.
findings.security_impact: None. No authorization, tenancy or audit path runs through these modules.
findings.clinical_impact: None. Development tooling only; no clinical request touches it.
findings.recommended_fix: Rewrite the import root from `backend.app.` to `app.` in place. The imports were already absolute, so only the root prefix changed: no relative-import conversion, no sys.path or PYTHONPATH manipulation, no importlib indirection, no duplicated modules, no new dependency.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_engineering_tooling_imports.py — 24 tests. Every importability assertion runs in a subprocess rooted at backend/ with no PYTHONPATH, because the pytest process can import both roots and would mask a regression. Generator membership is discovered structurally from the AST (an import of BaseGenerator or a class subclassing it), so a generator added later is covered without editing the test. One architecture guard asserts that no module under app/engineering names `backend` as an import root.
findings.discovered_by: NR-053 (while verifying the repaired generator's own import root)
findings.resolution: 44 import statements across 18 files, plus the unused PACKAGE constant in cli.py which named the same dead root. Negative proof: reintroducing the defect in one module failed three tests — that module's import, the CLI deferred-load test, and the architecture guard.

findings.title: Thirty further frontend calls resolve to no registered backend route
findings.status: OPEN
findings.description: Beyond NR-054's nine capability routes, 30 more statically resolvable api.<method>('/literal') calls in frontend-v3 name endpoints the application never registers. They cluster: /niam/* (governance, trust, lifecycle, adaptive-auth, certificates, federation) 15, /citizen-platform/* 6, /certification/* 2, and 7 singletons across blood-bank, control-plane, health-data, lifecycle, national notifications and pilot-platform.
findings.root_cause: The same generator defect as NR-054 — pages built from a route-file inventory rather than from registered routes — applied to domains whose routers are likewise defined but not mounted, or whose paths drifted after generation.
findings.evidence: Measured against the app's own OpenAPI schema (1787 registered paths): of 207 literal calls, 39 do not resolve — 9 are NR-054's, 30 are these. A further 21 apparent misses are concatenated URLs whose literal prefix the scanner sees in isolation; they are excluded, not counted.
findings.security_impact: None directly. Unregistered paths return 404; no authorization is bypassed.
findings.clinical_impact: User-visible dishonesty rather than data risk: a clinician may be shown a navigable page that cannot load. Whether any of these sit on a clinical path has not been assessed.
findings.recommended_fix: Per-domain, as NR-054 was: bind to a canonical owner where one exists, otherwise disable the route until a real contract does. Not attempted here — each cluster belongs to a different domain owner and NR-054's scope was explicitly the nine.
findings.verification: Held by the DECLARED_UNREGISTERED_CALLS ledger in backend/tests/test_frontend_backend_contract.py. The guard fails on any NEW orphan, and a separate test fails if a ledger entry becomes registered but is left in the list, so the population can shrink but never silently grow.
findings.discovered_by: NR-054 (while building the frontend/backend contract guard)

findings.title: A real application start loads a second copy of the application through the backend.app root
findings.status: FIXED — verified inside app/; declared stateless residual in shared/
findings.description: A real create_app() loaded 36 backend.app.* modules — a second copy of the application inside the same process, including a second kernel, a second config, and a second database module with its own Base and its own Engine. NR-050 repaired the capability share (10 capability.py files), bringing it to 34 and removing the second kernel. The residual belongs to app/national/task_engine (13 modules) and app/national/workflow_runtime (14), plus services/governance, services/reference and integration/connectors/email.py.
findings.root_cause: Dockerfile:24-26 copies the application twice — `COPY backend ./backend` alongside `COPY backend/app ./app` — so from WORKDIR /app both `app.x` and `backend.app.x` resolve to the same file as two distinct module objects, each with its own module-level globals. Modules that name the backend.app root then bind to the shadow copy.
findings.evidence: `import app.kernel.integration as a; import backend.app.kernel.integration as b; a is b` → False with identical __file__. app/kernel/integration.py:15 holds `_kernel_instance` as a module-level global. Counted live: 36 shadow modules before the NR-050 repair, 34 after. The shadow Base carries 0 tables and the shadow engine is unused, so nothing has diverged yet. | NR-058 CLOSURE: the residual was 73 import statements across 25 files in five packages (national/task_engine 27, national/workflow_runtime 37, services/governance 5, services/reference 3, integration/connectors 1), plus one module path passed as a string -- engineering/performance/benchmark.py benchmarked the import time of 'backend.app.kernel', which an AST guard cannot see. After the rewrite a real create_app() loads 2 shadow modules, down from 34, and both are namespace packages on the way to backend.app._compat, imported by shared/ (which lives at the repository root, outside backend/). _compat holds constants: no engine, no session factory, no declarative base, no registry, so the duplicate cannot diverge. That exemption is itself tested.
findings.security_impact: None demonstrated. No authorization or tenancy path runs through the shadow tree today.
findings.clinical_impact: None today. The hazard is silent divergence: state written through one copy is invisible to the other, and a capability registering through the shadow kernel would succeed while reaching nobody.
findings.recommended_fix: Permanent fix is the container layout — stop copying the application twice. Correcting the task_engine and workflow_runtime import roots is a package-wide change with its own review. Neither was done under NR-050, whose brief forbade a repository-wide import migration.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_import_roots.py holds the repaired capability tree and carries the residual as DECLARED_SHADOW_ROOT_PACKAGES — a ledger that may shrink but never grow, with a per-entry test that fails if a listed package is repaired and left in the list.
findings.next_batch: unscheduled — DECISION REQUIRED on container layout
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED: `backend.app.` -> `app.` across the five packages. No behaviour change intended and none measured: 1787 OpenAPI paths before and after, the same 42 task/workflow endpoints registered. The container layout (Dockerfile:24-26 copying the application twice) is still the root cause and is unchanged; the repair removes every in-process consequence of it under app/.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_capability_import_roots.py, widened: the AST ledger is empty and no longer exempts engineering, and the behavioural test now asserts a real create_app() loads no second copy of any *stateful* module, not just the kernel -- the three that matter are the kernel (redirects registration), app.database (splits the connection pool) and any declarative base (hides tables from Alembic and conftest). Negative-proven: restoring one import in task_engine/infrastructure/models.py fails both the static and the behavioural test.

findings.status: DECISION-READY (all 42 classified; product-intent decision required)
findings.title: 42 registered endpoints are served by fifteen tables that no migration builds
findings.description: factory.py registers the task_engine (23 paths) and workflow_runtime (19 paths) routers. Their repositories read and write fifteen tables -- national_tasks, national_task_queues, national_task_assignments, national_task_escalations, national_task_sla_definitions, national_task_comments, national_task_audit_logs, national_workflow_definitions, national_workflow_executions, national_workflow_execution_steps, national_workflow_approvals, national_workflow_timers, national_workflow_compensations, national_workflow_templates, national_saga_logs -- and no migration in the chain creates any of them.
findings.root_cause: Same shape as NR-022: a domain was modelled and exposed before its schema was built. What is specific here is that NR-058's import defect hid it. Both packages registered their models on a second NationalBase reached through the backend.app root, so test_schema_fidelity's ORM surface -- the gate whose entire purpose is to inventory ORM tables with no migration -- never saw them and was under-counting by fifteen.
findings.evidence: grep of every file in backend/migrations/versions for each of the fifteen names: no match. create_app() OpenAPI schema: 1787 paths, of which 42 are under /national/tasks and /national/workflows. Importing one repository module loads a second app.database with its own Engine against the same URL, so these paths would also have run outside the documented pool budget (WEB_CONCURRENCY x (DB_POOL_SIZE + DB_MAX_OVERFLOW)). | NR-059 CLASSIFICATION: 51 handlers across the two route modules, 42 unique OpenAPI paths. Registration corrected: these are registered DIRECTLY at factory.py:695/698, not via national_router (which is unregistered — that is why the NR-060 consent stub is unreachable while these are live). Exactly 2 handlers touch no repository (/national/tasks/health, /national/workflows/health) and work today; the other ~40 each reach a service -> repository -> one of the 15 unbuilt tables. They are NOT placeholders: the packages contain domain entities, enums, domain events, repository interfaces, SQLAlchemy implementations, a workflow state machine and a saga engine — a complete implementation that was never given a schema. A CONSUMER EXISTS: frontend-v3 pages NationalWorkflowRuntimeApiPage.tsx and NationalTaskEngineApiPage.tsx issue ten queries against these endpoints, so on a migrated database those pages return server errors. Four of the ten are additionally malformed with a double slash where a path parameter belongs (/executions//steps, /executions//approvals, /tasks//comments, /tasks//history) — the NR-054 auto-generated-page signature. These pages are a different class from NR-057: they resolve to registered routes that cannot return data.
findings.affected_users: Any caller of /national/tasks/* or /national/workflows/*
findings.clinical_impact: Workflow and task routing are coordination surfaces, not clinical record surfaces; no patient record is at risk. A caller relying on a task being persisted would be wrong about it.
findings.security_impact: None identified — the endpoints authenticate before reaching persistence.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No data is written, so none can be corrupted; nothing is durable.
findings.operational_impact: 42 endpoints are advertised in the OpenAPI schema that cannot complete a persisted operation on a migrated database.
findings.dependencies: NR-022 (the National Core is unbuilt as a whole); NR-058 (which hid this).
findings.recommended_fix: Classification complete; the remaining question is product intent and is not derivable from the repository: is national task/workflow orchestration a feature GULA ships, or scaffolding that was generated and never removed? Shipping -> build the 15 tables in one migration and fix the four malformed frontend URLs; ownership (NR-051) and implementation already exist, making this the cheapest of the NR-022-family decisions. Not shipping -> retire both packages and both frontend pages, shrinking the National Core problem by 15 tables. What must NOT happen is building 15 tables so 42 endpoints stop erroring without deciding whether anyone wants the feature. Separately, under NR-054's rule the two frontend pages should be hidden until that resolves — recommended, not applied, because it is an API-surface change.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: NOT ATTEMPTED. What was done is to make the state visible and keep it visible: the fifteen tables are now declared in test_schema_fidelity's unbuilt ledger with the endpoint count stated, so the next model added to these packages is a review rather than a silent addition.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_schema_fidelity.py — the ledger entry fails if any of the fifteen acquires a migration and the entry is left behind, and the gate now sees the ORM surface it was always meant to.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Either the fifteen tables are migration-backed, or the 42 endpoints are not registered.
findings.regression_risk: Low for the declaration; the decision itself is Medium.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (migration chain searched by table name; endpoint count from a live OpenAPI schema)

findings.status: DECIDED — canonical owner established; dormant fail-open stand-in guarded, not executed
findings.title: Consent had eight implementations across six domains and no stated canonical owner
findings.description: Seven ORM classes map seven distinct *consent* tables (consents, niam_consents, niam_lifecycle_consents, trust_consent_records, dp_consent_directives, national_consents, rp_consent_records) and an eighth implementation, citizen_platform.privacy.ConsentEngine, is not an ORM model at all. No two share a table, so this was never NR-051's one-table-two-owners problem; it is eight concepts sharing a word.
findings.root_cause: Consent was modelled independently by each domain that needed it, with no constitution naming which store an authorization decision must consult.
findings.evidence: Cached 829-class ownership scan re-queried for 'consent': 7 ORM classes, 7 tables, 6 domains, zero duplicate table ownership. Migration search by table name: only 4 of 7 are built (consents 20260417_0001, niam_consents 20260814_0006, niam_lifecycle_consents 20260723_0002, trust_consent_records 20260716_0013); the other 3 are ORM-only and all three are already declared in test_schema_fidelity's unbuilt ledger. Live OpenAPI from create_app(): 16 of 1787 registered paths mention consent. Decisive evidence for ownership: exactly one implementation is wired into an authorization decision -- security/consent_dep.py::require_consent is a route dependency guarding services/mpi/api.py:316, and it queries `consents` via services/consent_service.py. It is also the only one that audits: log_access_decision writes an AuditLog row on all five decision branches (owner bypass, emergency denied, emergency allowed, no-consent deny, allow). Subject/tenancy columns measured per table: consents keys on gpid (citizen ULID) + grantee_id with no tenant column; trust_consent_records is the only one carrying lab_id.
findings.affected_components: app/models/consent.py, app/services/consent_service.py, app/security/consent_dep.py, app/identity/models/consent.py, app/identity/lifecycle/models.py, app/trust/models.py, app/citizen_platform/privacy.py, app/national/security/consent_enforcement.py
findings.affected_users: Any actor reading citizen data through a consent-gated path
findings.clinical_impact: Consent gates citizen data reads and carries doctor-only emergency break-glass. The canonical path is intact; no clinical path was found reading a non-canonical store.
findings.security_impact: Two dormant hazards, neither live. (1) ConsentEnforcementService returns granted=True for any input and its log_consent_check is `pass` -- fail-open with no audit. It is unreachable for two independent reasons: factory.py does not register national_router, and its only call site passes citizen_id= to a parameter named patient_id while omitting the required requestor_id, so it would raise TypeError. (2) ConsentEngine stores consent in a process-local dict, so a grant is lost on restart and invisible to other gunicorn workers; nothing authorizes on it, so it misinforms rather than mis-authorizes.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None found; the canonical store's invariants are the strongest of the eight.
findings.operational_impact: Eight consent surfaces mean a caller can grant consent somewhere that the enforcement path will never read.
findings.legal_impact: Consent is a legal artifact in this domain. A grant recorded in a non-enforced store is evidence of an intent the system does not honour.
findings.dependencies: NR-050 (this was its last blocked disposition), NR-051.
findings.recommended_fix: CANONICAL OWNER: app/models/consent.py::Consent over table `consents`, written through app/services/consent_service.py and enforced by app/security/consent_dep.py. Chosen on evidence -- it is the only store an authorization decision consults, the only one that audits every outcome, and the only one with break-glass semantics. Consolidating the other seven is NOT recommended as a single step: niam_consents (account-to-account grants), trust_consent_records (lab-scoped, the only tenant-scoped one) and niam_lifecycle_consents (person lifecycle) are different relations, not copies, and merging them would be an irreversible data decision.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_consent_canonical_ownership.py records the decision as an executable invariant. No consent code was changed. Specifically NOT done: correcting the ConsentEnforcementService call signature, because a correct call to a fail-open service is strictly worse than a broken call to one -- the guard ties the two facts together instead, so the service must fail closed before that router may be registered.
findings.verification_method: 5 tests: the consent-table ledger is exact both ways; each declared migration still builds its table; the enforced path resolves to `consents` and audits all five branches; a fail-open consent service must not be reachable; and no enforcement module consults the in-memory ConsentEngine. Negative-proven by registering national_router in factory.py -- the reachability test fails with the intended message and passes again on restore.
findings.acceptance_criteria: One consent store is named canonical and no permissive stand-in is reachable.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; it adds tests and alters no runtime code.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (live OpenAPI, migration chain by table name, enforcement call graph read end to end)

findings.status: DECIDED — canonical composition named; rival registries guarded, not built
findings.title: Practitioner is modelled seventeen times; the only built natural-person registry is the Identity Platform's
findings.description: 17 ORM classes model practitioner/provider/staff/employee/healthcare-worker/person. Only 4 are built, and 3 of those 4 are homonyms: fin_providers (financial service provider), pay_providers (payment processor), niam_fed_providers (OIDC/SAML identity provider). Exactly one built table represents a natural person: niam_persons. Every clinical variant is unbuilt, including national_practitioners -- at 88 foreign-key references the single most-depended-on table in the repository.
findings.root_cause: Each domain modelled its own practitioner rather than composing the Identity Platform's, and NR-022's framing ('the most-depended-on tables do not exist') invites closing the gap by building them.
findings.evidence: Cached 829-class ownership scan filtered for person-like concepts (17 classes), cross-referenced against an AST parse of every op.create_table in the migration chain (evidence-created-tables.json, 419 tables). Column-level comparison: national_practitioners flattens into one row what the Identity Platform models relationally and has BUILT -- niam_persons (full_name, date_of_birth, gender, nationality, phone, email, national_id_hash), niam_licenses/ProfessionalLicense (license_number, issuing_authority, expiry_date, board_certification), niam_employments/Employment (person_id -> organization_id, position, dates), niam_assignments (posting) and niam_role_assignments (permissions). The Identity Platform is 84 of 87 tables built. One genuine gap: specialty/sub_specialty has no equivalent in niam_licenses, which carries license_type and board_name only.
findings.affected_users: Every clinical path that names a practitioner
findings.clinical_impact: Practitioner identity underpins attribution of clinical acts and licence validity at the time of care.
findings.security_impact: Building a rival registry would copy name, date of birth, phone, email and national ID hash outside the proofing, assurance and verification governance that surrounds niam_persons, and would contradict CLAUDE.md's rule that the Identity Platform is the single trusted identity provider.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Two person registries cannot be reconciled without a matching strategy; none exists.
findings.operational_impact: 88 foreign keys name a table that does not exist.
findings.legal_impact: Duplicated personal data enlarges the custodianship surface.
findings.dependencies: NR-022 (Stable Core map), NR-047.
findings.recommended_fix: CANONICAL: a practitioner is not an entity. It is a Person (niam_persons) who holds a ProfessionalLicense (niam_licenses) and an Employment (niam_employments) / Assignment (niam_assignments), with permissions through niam_role_assignments. Do NOT build national_practitioners. Re-pointing its 88 references is an architectural change that depends on the NR-022 subject/identifier decision and is not attempted here. The one real additive gap -- clinical specialty -- belongs on niam_licenses, not in a new table.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_practitioner_canonical_identity.py asserts the canonical composition is still built and that no rival person registry has acquired a migration. Retiring the rivals stays allowed; building one fails the gate. No code changed.
findings.verification_method: 4 tests: the created-table evidence is present and plausible (>=400 tables); the canonical composition is migration-backed; no rival person registry is built; the rival ledger still names real ORM tables. Negative-proven by marking national_practitioners as built in the evidence file -- the guard fails with its intended message and passes again on restore.
findings.acceptance_criteria: One registry of natural persons, and it is the Identity Platform's.
findings.regression_risk: None; tests only.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (column-level comparison against a migration-derived built-table set)

findings.status: MEASURED — corrected and double-ratcheted (package + module). Stage 1 rollout applied
findings.title: CLAUDE.md requires every mutation to be audited; 328 mutating endpoints are in packages with no audit call at all, and 1065 are in modules with none
findings.description: The audit architecture itself is sound and needs no redesign: services/audit_service.py chains each entry as SHA-256(previous_chain_hash + record), anchors it off-database under an HMAC (AUDIT_ANCHOR_KEY) and can re-verify the chain (verify_audit_chain). That is tamper-evident. Coverage is the gap. Of 1222 mutating endpoints (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) across 42 packages, 271 (22%) are in 25 packages containing no audit call anywhere. Corrected in Unit 4: the original 271/25 figure was produced by a detector matching its tokens as plain substrings, which counted `query_audit_log(`, `access_audit_log(`, `get_audit_log(` (app/control_plane -- three read helpers) and `_write_audit` (app/governance) as canonical audit calls. Word-boundary matching restores both packages: 27 packages, 328 endpoints. Measured per module instead of per package, 130 of the 160 modules containing a mutating endpoint contain no audit call, covering 1065 of 1222 endpoints -- the upper bound, now ratcheted alongside the lower one.
findings.root_cause: The rule is stated in CLAUDE.md but enforced nowhere mechanically: auditing is a call each author must remember to make, at the layer furthest from the mutation.
findings.evidence: AST scan of app/ counting POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE route decorators per package, against a broad token search for audit participation. 271 unaudited mutating endpoints across 25 packages is the LOWER bound -- 'the package audits somewhere' does not prove a given endpoint audits. A module-level pass gives the upper bound: 435 of 527 route-module endpoints (83%) are in modules that never name an audit call. Both are proxies and are reported as such. Highest-count unaudited packages: payments 34, capabilities 29, document_intelligence 25, ai_fabric 23, blood_bank 21, research_platform 16, devices 15, critical_care 14. 21 audit-like tables exist in the ORM, 12 built, but only audit_logs carries the chain.
findings.affected_components: app/ (25 packages); canonical chain in app/services/audit_service.py
findings.affected_users: Anyone relying on the audit trail to reconstruct who changed what
findings.clinical_impact: blood_bank (21 unaudited mutating endpoints) and critical_care (14) are traceability domains: blood product lifecycle and infusion changes are exactly what an audit trail exists to reconstruct.
findings.security_impact: An audit trail with a 22% floor of unaudited mutations cannot answer 'who changed this', and the hash chain's tamper-evidence applies only to what was written to it.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Mutations outside the chain are unreconstructable after the fact.
findings.operational_impact: Incident reconstruction and compliance evidence are incomplete by an unknown margin.
findings.scalability_impact: Session-level enforcement would add one insert per audited mutation; the chain is already serialized on last-hash read.
findings.legal_impact: ISO 27001 A.8.15 is cited in the audit service docstring; partial coverage weakens that claim.
findings.dependencies: NR-045 (canonical audit write repair, VERIFIED), NR-060 (consent audits all five decision branches).
findings.intersections: NR-045, NR-060, NR-021. NR-065 (the package blind spot this now measures around: app/national counts as auditing because interop.py does, while task_engine and workflow_runtime contain no audit call). NR-066 (what app/governance writes instead).
findings.contradictions: CLAUDE.md security invariant #2 states all mutations MUST write to the audit log; measurement shows at least 22% do not.
findings.recommended_fix: ENFORCE AT THE SESSION, NOT THE ROUTE. The mutation classes that must produce audit evidence are: clinical result/order state changes; authorization decisions including break-glass; identity lifecycle and role assignment; consent grant/revoke; blood product and controlled-substance lifecycle; financial and billing mutations; tenant/scope changes; and bulk export or disclosure of patient data. Enforcing per route has failed for 271 endpoints because it depends on an author remembering. A SQLAlchemy before_flush hook over a declared set of audit-worthy tables cannot be forgotten, sees the actual INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and can reuse infrastructure that already exists: database.py maintains per-request contextvars (request_id, endpoint, user_id, lab_id) for error correlation, which is exactly the actor context an audit row needs. NOT implemented here -- it changes write behaviour on every session and needs its own review.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_audit_chain_invariant.py ratchets the measured gap. Each declared package may shed unaudited mutations; none may gain them, no new unaudited package may appear, and a resolved entry must be removed rather than left as a stale allowance. The chain's own integrity (chain hash, previous-hash link, HMAC anchor, verifier) is asserted too, because the invariant is only worth enforcing while the chain is real. No runtime code changed.
findings.verification_method: 7 tests. Package ratchet (declared per-package counts, no new package, no stale entry), chain-integrity assertion, and a module-level aggregate ratchet. Negative-proven by removing app/governance from the ledger -- the guard fails naming it, proving the detector correction is load-bearing -- and by adding an unaudited mutating module, which fails the module ratchet with '131 modules ... up from 130'. Both restored byte-identical.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every mutation class listed above produces a hash-chained audit entry, enforced where it cannot be forgotten.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; tests only. The recommended session hook carries real risk and is deliberately not applied.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG for the lower bound (AST over the whole route surface); the upper bound is explicitly a proxy

findings.status: LATENT — RE-VERIFIED under sound resolution; precondition held, 75 dead create paths deliberately not rewritten — PHASE G: all 75 classified REACHABLE-BUT-INACTIVE; none is dead code
findings.title: 103 create paths splat an unvalidated request body into an ORM constructor; 75 set no tenant or actor
findings.description: Found while trying to resolve NR-022's nine REVIEW sites. They could not be decided from their call sites, and the reason mattered more than the question: the call sites are generic passthroughs. A route takes a bare `data: dict` with no request model and hands it to `Model(**data)`. Measured across app/: 103 such constructions. 28 set tenant and/or actor server-side; 75 set neither, so the request body would decide every column including lab_id, verified_by and is_deleted. PHASE G CLASSIFICATION, against the running application: LIVE 0, REACHABLE-BUT-INACTIVE 75, DEAD 0, UNKNOWN 0. All three modules (care_continuum_service 40, clinical_service 18, ehr_service 17) are a DIRECT import of a registered route module -- exactly NR-064's shape, where the route was clean and its service was not. So the only thing between these paths and a live mass-assignment surface is the absent table, which NR-022 and NR-059 both propose to create. A first pass classified ehr_service's 17 as DEAD and was wrong: app/routes/ehr.py:29 imports it through the package form the resolver could not see (NR-079). 'Dead' is the answer an undercounting instrument gives, and the most comfortable one to be wrong about.
findings.root_cause: Create paths were written as untyped dict passthroughs, so neither validation nor server-side tenancy has anywhere to live.
findings.evidence: AST scan for `Model(**param)` where param is a function argument, cross-referenced against the migration-derived built-table set. 103 sites; unguarded concentrated in care_continuum_service (40), clinical_service (18), ehr_service (17). The defensible pattern is `ClinicalTask(lab_id=lab_id, created_by=user_id, assigned_by=user_id, **data)` -- tenant and actor come from the authenticated user, a colliding body key raises TypeError rather than overriding, and those paths audit. CRITICAL SAFETY FACT: zero of the 75 unguarded sites targets a built table, so every such write currently fails with UndefinedTable before a row exists. The pattern is latent, not live. Detector note: server-setting occurs in two forms -- an explicit keyword and a pre-splat `data['key'] = value` mutation. The first version of this scan counted only the former and reported create_compliance_check as unguarded when it does set the actor by mutation; corrected before shipping, which moved the split from 27/76 to 28/75. findings.title: The citizen-relationship create endpoint queries national_citizens and national_patients, neither of which exists, and reports the failure as a generic 500
findings.description: POST /admin/citizen-relationships is registered at factory.py:599 and reachable by any actor holding platform:manage_users with ministry authorization. Its workflow validates the subject by querying `Citizen` (national_citizens) and, when a patient is named, `Patient` (national_patients). Neither table is created by any migration, so on a migrated database the query raises UndefinedTable before a row is ever written. The route catches `Exception` and returns 500 'Citizen relationship workflow failed', so the operator is told the workflow failed but not that the schema is absent.
findings.root_cause: niam_citizen_relationships was built ahead of the National Core subject tables it references. The migration guards the foreign keys on `_has_table(target)` -- correctly, or a fresh database could not migrate -- but the service still validates against the ORM class unconditionally.
findings.evidence: app/routes/citizen_relationship_admin.py:69 (POST) -> app/identity/services/citizen_relationship_service.py:144 `self.db.query(Citizen).filter(Citizen.id == citizen_id)` and :152 for Patient. app/national/domain/citizen.py / patient.py map to national_citizens / national_patients; both are absent from the migration-derived evidence-created-tables.json. Registration proved at factory.py:561/599. The FK-creation guard is at migrations/versions/20260811_0002_citizen_relationship_foundation.py:68-83.

findings.data_integrity_impact: None today: nothing is written. The two declared columns carry no database-level referential integrity because the migration could not create the constraints.
findings.operational_impact: The failure surfaces as an undifferentiated 500, so the cause is not visible to the operator who hits it.
findings.legal_impact: Delegated-access consent cannot be recorded through the intended audited path.

findings.contradictions: The workflow is otherwise exemplary -- explicit keywords, idempotency key, optimistic version, hash-chained audit -- which is why the missing schema is easy to miss. The workflow's own test suite was green throughout: it hands the service a fake session whose query() returns a SimpleNamespace, which cannot notice that the table behind a model does not exist. That is why the new guard is static.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the canonical subject for citizen_id and patient_id per NR-022 (CITIZEN and PATIENT classes respectively), build or re-point to that owner, then create the two foreign keys in the same migration. findings.status: DECIDED — organization-rooted; NR-070 no longer blocks it, NR-076 now does (the packages cannot persist what they are given)
findings.title: National orchestration tenancy is undecided; laboratory scope is now eliminated, and the untenanted surface is 84 of 113 national tables, not 15
findings.description: NR-059 left activation blocked on product intent. Unit 3 ran the checks the approved decision actually gates on and found two more blockers that do not depend on that question. All 15 task and workflow tables extend `BaseEntity` -- the one national base carrying neither TenantMixin nor AuditMixin, while TenantEntity, AuditEntity and TenantAuditEntity all exist alongside it. Only national_workflow_executions has a tenant column. The task listing path filters on status, priority, category, assignee, queue_id and a title LIKE, and on nothing else, because there is nothing else to filter on. Neither package contains a call reaching the hash-chained audit log, and there is no idempotency key or row lock anywhere in a package containing a saga engine and a workflow state machine. SHARPENED: the earlier reading of '1 of 15 tenanted' was too generous. `tenant_id` appears in exactly six places across both packages -- the column, a domain-entity field defaulting to None, a service parameter defaulting to None, the pass-through to the model and two serialisation points -- and NO route supplies it. The routes derive created_by from current_user.id and stop. So the column is written NULL on every path that could write it, and the surface is untenanted with one column that looks like tenancy and is not. UNIT 7 (platform-wide evidence): the earlier verdict listed four candidates and chose none, but it was reached from inside task_engine and workflow_runtime alone. RoleScopeType and MembershipScopeType -- the two vocabularies that decide what a role or membership may be scoped to -- are organization|facility|department|unit|workspace. Neither has a lab member or a governorate member, so a national artifact keyed by lab_id could not be named by any role assignment: nothing could be granted over it and nothing denied. The vocabulary is enforced rather than declared (MembershipService._validate_context raises 'Unsupported membership scope' on a miss; AuthorizationServiceV2 takes scope_type from the role, never from the caller) and every table behind it is built. niam_role_assignments.organization_id is nullable=False with facility/department/unit/workspace as nullable narrowings, all ULID String(26) into niam_* -- where TenantMixin.lab_id is an INTEGER into labs.id, so the laboratory option is also a type-level mismatch. TenantMixin is therefore eliminated, and governorate is eliminated as a *scope* because there is no governorate entity to point at: niam_organizations.governorate is a nullable String(50) attribute of an organization, not a level above or below one. Remaining question, still reserved: organization root, or genuinely national and deliberately unscoped. Surface re-measured across app/national: 113 tables, 84 untenanted, only 8 built; seven packages untenanted in full (background_platform, document_platform, ecosystem, observability, reference, rules_engine, task_engine = 49 tables, 6 built). Blanket tenancy would be the opposite error: app/national/ecosystem is six BUILT untenanted tables registering external partners, which sit outside every tenant by definition. Exactly two national tables carry lab_id (national_search_saved_searches, national_search_results) -- user-local saved searches, both built, declared as the one allowed exception rather than waived. UNIT 8 (DECISION): the two surviving candidates were the same candidate. app/identity/bootstrap/seed.py::seed_platform_organization creates the ministry -- 'GULA National Digital Health Platform' -- as a row in niam_organizations with org_type='ministry', so the national level IS an organization and RoleScopeType.organization at that row already expresses national scope. DECIDED: national orchestration is scoped at the canonical organization root using the authorization vocabulary unchanged; no 'national' scope member and no null-means-national convention, both of which would be a second spelling of one scope. Nine of the fifteen tables take NO scope column: they are children keyed by execution_id or task_id and inherit, so a column there duplicates the FK. The six roots take organization_id NOT NULL plus optional narrowings. Cross-organization coordination is expressed by participants, not by widening the owner column -- proved by national_referrals, a built cross-facility entity with referring_facility_id + receiving_facility_id and NO organization_id at all, which refutes any 'every national table needs one organization_id' rule. Scope must be server-derived on the ClinicalAuthorizationContextService pattern (fail-closed, five error types, no defaulting), never client-supplied. NOT YET IMPLEMENTED as columns, deliberately: see NR-070. UPDATE: NR-070 is fixed, so the reason given here for holding the scope columns -- 'a correct organization_id behind an unauthorized endpoint is a correctly-labelled open door' -- no longer applies. Building the tables is still wrong, for a new reason found by the NR-070 positive test: eleven of the fourteen concrete repositories in these two packages persist nothing (NR-076). Writing scope columns into tables whose repositories discard every row would produce correctly-scoped data loss instead of incorrectly-scoped data loss.
findings.root_cause: The two packages were implemented against the bare BaseEntity rather than TenantAuditEntity, and were never given a schema, so neither the tenancy gap nor the audit gap was ever exercised.
findings.evidence: AST over app/national/task_engine and app/national/workflow_runtime: 15 tables, 1 with a tenant column (national_workflow_executions). national_tasks has 22 columns and no tenant scoping of any kind. Zero word-boundary matches for log_action / audit_service / AuditLog( / log_access_decision in either package. national_task_audit_logs has 6 columns (task_id, action, actor_id, previous_status, new_status, details) -- no chain hash, no previous-hash link, no off-database anchor. WorkflowExecutionRepository.save loads by id, mutates and commits without reading `version`. | UNIT 7: app/identity/models/authorization.py RoleScopeType (5 members); app/identity/models/membership.py MembershipScopeType (5 members, identical); app/identity/services/membership_service.py:157-181 _validate_context; app/identity/services/authorization_service_v2.py:177 scope_type=role.scope_type; AST census of app/national = 113 tables / 84 untenanted / 8 built; backend/tests/test_national_scope_vocabulary.py (7 tests, all negative-proven). | UNIT 8: app/identity/bootstrap/seed.py:26-38 org_type='ministry'; app/national/domain/referral.py:18-22 referring/receiving facility pair, no organization_id; app/identity/services/clinical_authorization_context_service.py fail-closed derivation; 15 models = 6 roots + 9 children by execution_id/task_id.

They are; tenancy, audit and concurrency control are not. That estimate is corrected by this finding. The two available tenancy answers disagree and nothing in the repository prefers one: TenantMixin.lab_id is INTEGER against labs.id (a national workflow belongs to one laboratory), while the package's own signal is an optional VARCHAR(100) tenant_id (some facility, governorate or organization identifier). Re-basing on TenantAuditEntity would pick the first by default -- which is the decision, not a detail.
findings.recommended_fix: ANSWER THE TENANCY QUESTION FIRST: what is the tenant of a national workflow execution or task -- a laboratory, a facility, a governorate, or an organization? It is not derivable from this repository, and every other repair depends on it (the tenant column's type, the repository filters, the migration). Once answered: add the tenant column that answer implies and filter every repository read by it; route mutations through services/audit_service.log_action; add an idempotency key to task creation and workflow triggering plus a compare-and-set or row lock on execution advance; then one additive migration verified on PostgreSQL.

findings.title: The governance repository base writes an audit row into an unbuilt table from every create, update and delete
findings.description: CORRECTION to this finding's first record, which said governance 'writes rows; they are the wrong rows' and that 'rows exist, which is worse than none in one respect: it reads as coverage'. They do not exist and cannot. `gov_health_number_audit` is built by no migration, so the `HealthNumberAudit(...)` that `GovernanceRepository._write_audit` constructs from `add`, `update` and `delete` would raise UndefinedTable on flush -- taking the caller's own governance row down with it, because six of the tables its subclasses serve ARE built (gov_break_glass_accesses, gov_guardians, gov_identity_records, gov_merge_proposals, gov_qr_codes, gov_recovery_requests). The reason it has never happened is that nothing calls those repositories: their two persistence services are imported by no module outside app/governance/services, and the registered governance_router imports nine other service modules instead. The original observations still stand where they apply -- it is not the hash-chained AuditLog, the actor is the literal string "system", and the row is a health-number audit whatever entity was mutated -- but they describe code that cannot run rather than rows that exist. Severity lowered from P1 to P2 on that evidence.
findings.root_cause: A domain-specific audit model was wired into the generic repository base, and the authenticated actor was never threaded through to it.
findings.evidence: app/governance/repositories/base.py:36/:48/:60 call _write_audit; :69-75 define it; :70 constructs HealthNumberAudit. gov_health_number_audit is absent from the migration-derived evidence-created-tables.json while the six tables its subclasses serve are present. No importer of app/governance/services/citizen_platform_persistence.py or identity_persistence_service.py exists outside app/governance/services; factory.py:683 registers governance_router, whose module imports nine unrelated service modules.
findings.affected_components: app/governance/repositories/base.py and every governance repository inheriting it; 47 mutating endpoints
findings.affected_users: Anyone whose governance actions need to be attributable — identity governance, policy and stewardship changes
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect: governance decisions affecting identity resolution cannot be attributed to a person.
findings.security_impact: Latent. Attribution would be destroyed at the point of write if the code ran, but it cannot: the insert fails before a row exists, and no reachable caller reaches it. The residual risk is that making these repositories reachable silently breaks six built governance tables' mutations.
findings.data_integrity_impact: HealthNumberAudit.health_number is populated with arbitrary entity ids, so that table cannot be read as a health-number history.
findings.operational_impact: Masked NR-062's measurement of this package until word-boundary matching exposed it.

findings.status: MEASURED — reachable surface ratcheted; NR-064 was the first instance repaired — RE-MEASURED: 610 reachable across 24 modules, not 418 across 20 (NR-079)
findings.title: 773 query sites read, and 268 constructions write, tables no migration builds; 418 reads are reachable from a registered route
findings.description: NR-064 turned out to be one instance of a platform-wide class. Measured across app/ with model names resolved through each file's own imports -- absolute, relative and package re-exports: 773 `query(Model)` sites name a table no migration creates, and 418 of them are reachable from a registered router across 20 route modules, either in the route module itself or one import hop away (NR-064's exact shape: the route was clean, the service was not). Worst reachable: routes/clinical.py 57, routes/clinical_quality.py 55, routes/care_continuum.py 44, national/scheduling_platform 41. The write side: 268 ORM constructions target an unbuilt table -- app/services 106, app/governance 62, app/national 43 -- and writes fail differently, raising UndefinedTable on flush and taking the caller's own rows with them (NR-066 is that instance). CORRECTION: this finding first reported 483 reads / 267 reachable across 11 modules and 147 writes. Those figures were understated because the first guards resolved only absolute `app.*` imports and could not follow `from ..models import X` or `from app.ehr.models import CarePlan`. Nine route modules were invisible entirely and app/governance's write count went from 2 to 62. Resolution now lives once in backend/tests/orm_resolution.py. SCOPE CORRECTION (NR-079). The reachable figure was understated by a broken instrument, twice over. Registration was read by regex over factory.py, which does not match its bulk block (`from .routes import (admin, ehr, ehr_fhir, …)` then `for r in core_routes + feature_routes + …: app.include_router(r.router)`): 79 modules found against 142 the running application serves, with ZERO false positives. And import resolution dropped `from app.services import ehr_service` -- a package import naming a submodule, which resolves to app/services/ehr_service.py and not app/services.py. Four route modules were invisible entirely: app/routes/ehr_fhir.py (77), app/routes/ehr.py (63), app/governance/routes/governance_routes.py (47), app/governance/routes/analytics_routes.py (5). 418 + 192 = 610, and NOT ONE already-declared module's count changed -- the correction is purely additive, which is what distinguishes a repaired instrument from a regression. Registration is now read from the running application (route.endpoint.__module__), never from the file that configures it.
findings.root_cause: Whole subsystems were implemented against ORM models that were never given a schema, and nothing asserted that a reachable read resolves to a built table. Fake-session unit tests cannot detect it, because a fake answers query() regardless of whether the table exists.
findings.evidence: AST over app/ resolving each name through the file's own ImportFrom statements -- absolute, relative (level>0) and one hop through a package __init__ re-export -- cross-referenced with migration-derived evidence-created-tables.json; registered routers parsed from factory.py. A name resolving to no __tablename__ is excluded rather than guessed (GatewayMessage in app/integration is a plain class). Import resolution is load-bearing: 32 ORM class names map to more than one table, and bare-name matching has now caused four separate guard defects this session -- NR-065's audit detector, NR-062's ledger, NR-067's own first scan, and NR-063's model lookup.
findings.affected_users: Any caller of the affected endpoints
findings.clinical_impact: routes/clinical.py and routes/clinical_quality.py are the two largest reachable groups, so clinical read paths are the most affected.
findings.security_impact: Fails closed -- the query errors rather than returning data. The risk is operational opacity and the pressure to 'fix' it by creating tables without an activation review.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None directly; no write succeeds on these paths.
findings.operational_impact: Endpoints that cannot work are indistinguishable from endpoints that are merely failing, because the error surfaces as a generic 500.
findings.dependencies: Shares a root with NR-059 and NR-065 (implementation without schema).
findings.intersections: NR-064 (the first instance, now repaired), NR-059, NR-065, NR-054, NR-063.
findings.contradictions: The affected packages have passing unit tests. Fake sessions make an absent table invisible, so a green suite is not evidence that a read path can run.
findings.recommended_fix: Per module, decide: build the table under the §6 activation review (canonical owner, tenancy, actor, audit, state machine, idempotency, consumers), or stop reading it and withdraw the endpoint. Do not create tables to make the detector green.

No runtime code changed beyond the NR-064 repair itself.

Also negative-proven by restoring the pre-fix citizen relationship service (fails naming both lines), by adding an unbuilt read to app/routes/hospital.py, and by constructing an unbuilt model in app/pharmacy.
