findings.status: MEASURED — latent, not live; no partner authentication path exists to be bypassed
findings.title: The external-partner credential subsystem is a registry with no enforcement path, and its non-API-key comparison branch is plaintext and non-constant-time
findings.description: app/national/ecosystem ships six BUILT tables (ecosystem_partners, _partner_credentials, _partner_certificates, _partner_rate_limits, _partner_audit_logs, _partner_agreements) and is registered in factory.py (ecosystem_router, ecosystem_gateway_router). Two gaps. (1) CredentialManager.validate_credential (partners/service.py:187) has ZERO callers anywhere in app/ -- partner credential validation is never performed, so registering a partner credential grants and denies nothing. (2) Inside it, credential_type == 'api_key' hashes the presented value and compares with hmac.compare_digest (correct), but every other credential_type falls through to `credential.credential_value != credential_value` -- a plaintext, non-constant-time comparison against a stored value. That branch is unreachable today because issue_api_key is the only issuer and always stores a sha3_512 HMAC under credential_type='api_key'; the first non-api-key issuer makes it live. The gateway alongside it is not an enforcement point either: GatewayPolicyEngine keeps its policies and routes in plain in-process dicts (per-worker, not persisted), the router is guarded by require_permission('system:admin'), and nothing outside app/national/ecosystem references the engine. It evaluates a dict an admin supplies; it does not sit on any request path. So no partner traffic is authenticated anywhere, which is why (1) has caused no incident and why (2) has never executed. This is recorded as latent, NOT as a live vulnerability.
findings.root_cause: The ecosystem package was built as a data model plus an admin-facing API without the runtime that would consume it: no ingress path resolves a partner, so the credential check has no caller and the policy engine has no traffic.
findings.evidence: grep for 'validate_credential' across backend/ returns exactly one hit, its own definition (app/national/ecosystem/partners/service.py:187). grep for GatewayPolicyEngine / PartnerService / CredentialManager outside app/national/ecosystem returns nothing. policies.py:366-369 GatewayPolicyEngine.__init__ stores dict[str, BasePolicy] and dict[str, dict]. gateway/routes.py:13-17 router dependencies=[Depends(require_permission('system:admin'))]. partners/service.py:219 _hash_api_key = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, api_key, hashlib.sha3_512); the api_key branch uses hmac.compare_digest, the else branch uses `!=`.
findings.affected_users: None today (no partner ingress path exists); external integration partners once one does
findings.clinical_impact: None currently — no clinical data flows through the ecosystem gateway
findings.security_impact: LATENT. If a non-api_key credential type is ever issued, secrets would be stored in plaintext and compared non-constant-time, exposing them to timing analysis and to any read of ecosystem_partner_credentials. Separately, a future ingress path that assumes validate_credential is wired would authenticate nobody.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — no writes are gated on the unreachable check
findings.operational_impact: Six built tables carry state that changes no behaviour; operators may read the registry as enforcement
findings.legal_impact: A partner agreement row implies a governed integration that is not in fact governed at runtime
findings.dependencies: NR-065 (the same package is the counter-example proving national tables are not all tenant-scoped)
findings.intersections: NR-067 (built tables whose code paths are unreachable is the mirror of unbuilt tables whose code paths are reachable)
findings.contradictions: None identified
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the package's disposition under an activation review before writing code: either build the partner ingress path (resolve partner -> validate credential -> evaluate policy -> audit) or withdraw the admin surface. If it is activated, delete the plaintext else branch rather than repairing it -- every credential type should be stored hashed and compared with hmac.compare_digest, and a type that cannot be hashed (mTLS certificate) needs its own verification rather than a string equality.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Make the else branch fail closed: reject an unsupported credential_type instead of comparing plaintext. That removes the trapdoor without deciding the package's future. Deliberately NOT applied here: it is a change to authentication behaviour in a package whose activation review has not happened, and CLAUDE.md reserves auth changes for a human.
findings.verification_method: Static: no caller of validate_credential; no reference to the engine outside the package. On activation: an executed test that an unsupported credential_type is refused, and that no credential value is ever stored unhashed.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Either (a) a registered ingress path resolves a partner and calls validate_credential, with every credential type hashed and constant-time compared, or (b) the ecosystem admin surface is withdrawn and its tables recorded as inactive.
findings.regression_risk: LOW for the minimal fix (an unreachable branch); MEDIUM-HIGH for activation
findings.related_tests: None yet — an activation review precedes a guard here
findings.complexity: LOW to fail closed; HIGH to activate
findings.evidence_strength: STATIC ANALYSIS (call-graph absence + source inspection)

findings.status: FIXED — derivation replaces the snapshot; blast radius measured, no finding changed
findings.title: built_tables() missed three tables created through a helper, so every 'is this built?' ledger inherited the error
findings.description: Every ratchet in the suite reduces to one predicate: does a migration create this table? docs/architecture/evidence-created-tables.json answered it, and was assembled by matching op.create_table("literal", ...). Three tables are not created that way: 20260814_0002_organization_structure.py routes creates through _create_if_missing(name, columns, constraints), where the literal is at the CALL SITE and op.create_table receives a function parameter. niam_admin_units, niam_organization_representatives and niam_organization_ownerships were therefore recorded as unbuilt while the chain builds them -- and niam_admin_units is the target of niam_role_assignments.unit_id, one of the five canonical authorization scopes. The error ran in the direction that overstates the problem: rows against those three counted as reads and writes against nothing. RE-MEASURED AFTER THE REPAIR, NO PUBLISHED LEDGER MOVED: reachable unbuilt reads stayed at 418 across 20 route modules and unbuilt writes at 268, because nothing on those paths touches the three. A real defect in the evidence base with no effect on the conclusions drawn from it. BLAST RADIUS (measured, not asserted): every consumer was recomputed under the artifact as it actually stood before the repair (419 tables) and under the derivation (422). NR-067 reachable unbuilt reads 418 -> 418; reachable modules 20 -> 20; unbuilt writes 268 -> 268; NR-022 live subject references 1 -> 1; NR-022 Stable Core built 5/5 -> 5/5; NR-065 orchestration tables built 0 -> 0. ALL UNAFFECTED. For contrast, a naive literal-only extractor applied today yields 411 tables and would report 430 reads across 24 modules and 276 writes -- figures never published, recorded only to show what the failure mode costs uncaught. COMPLETENESS CORRECTION: the first repair migrated one guard off the snapshot but left three others reading the file directly (test_subject_reference_semantics, test_practitioner_canonical_identity, test_stable_core_invariants). All four now import built_tables(); no guard reads the artifact. The extractor is additionally tested against SYNTHETIC migrations, one per creation form (literal, module constant, helper-first-arg, helper-second-arg, conditional, reference-only, alter-only) plus an unparseable file, so the tests cannot pass by being wrong in the same way the chain is.
findings.root_cause: The artifact was a hand-made snapshot with no generator and no guard that it matched the migrations, so a create form it did not model could not be detected.
findings.evidence: AST census of migrations/versions: 411 literal create_table names + 9 non-literal call sites; 8 of the 9 are module-level constants already resolved into the snapshot, the 9th is the helper. Derived set 422 vs snapshot 419; snapshot minus derived is empty, so the snapshot was a strict subset. Regeneration reproduced it exactly plus the three, with no removals and no provenance changes.
findings.affected_users: None — test infrastructure only
findings.clinical_impact: None
findings.security_impact: Indirect. A table wrongly believed unbuilt is a table whose guards are relaxed; the direction here was conservative, but the opposite direction would wave through reads that raise UndefinedTable at runtime.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — no data path involved
findings.operational_impact: Architecture measurements could be overstated without any test failing
findings.dependencies: NR-063, NR-065, NR-066, NR-067 all key on this predicate
findings.intersections: Same class as the bare-class-name defect: one predicate, re-implemented per guard instead of derived once
findings.contradictions: None
findings.recommended_fix: Applied. built_tables() now derives from the migration chain and resolves all three forms it uses -- literal, module-level constant, and a local helper forwarding one of its own parameters. The snapshot is regenerated and asserted equal to the derivation, so it cannot drift again. test_orchestration_build_precondition.py now reads the derivation rather than the file.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Same as applied; the change is test-side only and touches no runtime code.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_built_table_evidence.py (12 tests, gated): 4 against the real chain and 8 against synthetic migrations. Negative-proven three ways -- regress the extractor to literal-only (helper cases fail), make it over-broad by also counting add_column and create_index targets (reference_only and alter_only fail, catching the opposite and more dangerous error direction), and remove the SyntaxError guard (the unparseable-file test raises instead of returning nothing).
findings.acceptance_criteria: Derivation and snapshot agree; the three helper-created tables resolve by name.
findings.regression_risk: LOW — no runtime code changed
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED TEST (derivation executed against the real migration chain)

findings.status: FIXED — canonical permission reused, mass assignment removed, every actor server-resolved
findings.title: Both registered orchestration routers perform no authorization at all, update_task assigns from the request body, and the assignment actor is client-supplied
findings.description: Found by the NR-065 Unit 8 caller trace. factory.py:695 and :698 register workflow_runtime and task_engine, and NEITHER route module contains a single require_permission -- not at the router, not on any handler. Every endpoint depends on get_current_user alone. That covers create/list/execute/cancel/pause/resume/approve/reject for workflows and create/bulk/assign/start/complete/fail/cancel/escalate/delegate/delete for tasks, plus unfiltered list endpoints. Any authenticated principal -- including a laboratory technician with no national role -- would have full control of the national orchestration surface. Two further shapes on the same paths: (1) TaskEngineService.update_task does `for key, value in updates.items(): if hasattr(task, key) and key not in ('id','created_at','version'): setattr(task, key, value)`, so created_by, assigned_to, assigned_by, status and correlation_id are all client-writable -- the actor fields an audit trail relies on, and a bypass of the state machine the transition methods enforce; (2) POST /{task_id}/assign takes data.get('assigned_by') and POST /{task_id}/escalate takes data.get('escalated_to') from the body while current_user is resolved on the same handler and used for created_by. LATENT for exactly one reason: none of the fifteen tables is built, so every path raises UndefinedTable before it can act. This is the blocker that must clear before NR-065's scope columns are written -- a correct organization_id behind an unauthorized endpoint is a correctly-labelled open door. FIXED. All three shapes closed in one change. (1) AUTHORIZATION: the two orchestration routers now carry `dependencies=[Depends(require_permission("system:admin"))]` at the router. The permission is NOT new -- it is the only permission string that appears anywhere in `app/national`, used by all thirteen national route modules that already guarded themselves, at the router rather than the handler, and all seven platform siblings put their own `/health` under it too, so guarding `/national/workflows/health` matches the convention rather than excepting it. Inventing a `national:orchestration:*` vocabulary would have created a second taxonomy for one package. Stated rather than implied: `system:admin` is held by `master_admin` and by no other role, so this is the tightest reading available from repository evidence; widening it to `ministry_admin` is a role-permission decision reserved for a human. (2) MASS ASSIGNMENT: `update_task` now checks the body against `_TASK_UPDATABLE_FIELDS` (title, description, priority, category, task_type, queue_id, sla_due_at, tags, metadata) and RAISES on anything else rather than dropping it silently -- an attempt to overwrite the actor is the part worth seeing. `update_queue` and `update_sla` carry the same rule because a queue's `allowed_roles` decides who gets auto-assigned. The two enum coercions `create_task` performs are applied on update too, which the old loop did not do: it stored raw strings where the entity holds enums. (3) ACTOR INTEGRITY: `assigned_by` comes from `current_user` at the route; `escalated_by` -- a field on the entity and a column on the table that nothing had ever written -- is populated; and `national_task_audit_logs.actor_id`, NULL on every path that wrote it, now carries the authenticated caller on all twelve mutations. A CORRECTION to the original finding: `escalated_to` was listed as a client-supplied actor and is not one -- it names the escalation target, which the caller legitimately chooses. Changing the code to satisfy the wrong half of the finding would have been the worse repair.
findings.root_cause: The packages were built as a clean-architecture skeleton (domain/application/infrastructure/api) with the authorization layer left as an exercise; nothing forced the omission to surface because the tables were never built and nothing consumes the services.
findings.evidence: grep for require_permission in both route modules returns zero. app/national/task_engine/application/service.py:91-104 update_task setattr loop. app/national/task_engine/api/routes.py assign/escalate handlers pass data.get(...). Negative-proven: adding a migration that creates national_tasks makes five preconditions fail at once, three of them these. | Sibling convention: every other national route module declares require_permission (background_platform 2, document_platform 2, observability 2, rules_engine 2, scheduling_platform 2, search_platform 3, ecosystem 2). task_engine and workflow_runtime have zero, so this is an omission in these packages rather than a platform-wide gap. | FIX EVIDENCE: 29 tests in backend/tests/test_national_orchestration_authorization.py, gated in the IAM unit job. Structural proof reads the permission out of the running application's dependant tree, not out of the source: FastAPI stores each included router as an opaque `_IncludedRouter`, so `create_app().routes` is 7 entries and `app.routes` after startup is 130 while the served surface is 2109 -- the obvious structural guard would have found zero routes and passed. Behavioural proof through the real stack: a `technician` receives 403 on POST/GET /national/tasks/, POST /national/workflows/execute, GET /national/workflows/definitions, GET /national/workflows/health and GET /intelligence/ai/models, and the refusal names the permission; `master_admin` receives 200 from /intelligence/ai/models. Five negative proofs, each restored byte-identical (md5 verified): removing the router dependency fails the structural test and three behavioural ones; restoring the setattr loop fails seven; reverting `assigned_by` to the body fails the actor guard; dropping `actor_id` from one `_audit` call fails that transition's test; adding `created_by` to the allowlist fails the anti-widening guard. Local unit gate: 407 passed, up from 377 by exactly the 30 tests added.
findings.affected_users: None today (tables unbuilt); every national orchestration user on activation
findings.clinical_impact: On activation, clinical coordination tasks could be reassigned, completed or cancelled by any authenticated account, with the acting identity chosen by the caller.
findings.security_impact: Missing authorization on a registered national surface, mass assignment of actor and state fields, and client-controlled actor attribution. Latent only because of the unbuilt schema.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Client-writable status bypasses the task state machine; version is excluded from the splat but not enforced as an optimistic lock at the repository
findings.operational_impact: Blocks NR-065 implementation and NR-059 activation
findings.legal_impact: An assignment or escalation attributed to whoever the caller names is not an audit record
findings.dependencies: NR-065 (scope columns wait on this), NR-059 (activation), NR-062/NR-066 (no audit chain in either package)
findings.intersections: NR-063 — the same client-body-to-entity shape, here on a service method rather than a constructor
findings.contradictions: None
findings.recommended_fix: Before any migration builds these tables: add require_permission dependencies at both routers with national orchestration permissions; replace update_task's setattr loop with an explicit allow-list of mutable fields excluding every actor and status field; take the actor from current_user on assign and escalate and reject the body fields; then add the NR-065 scope columns and the canonical audit write.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Not applied here. Adding authorization to these routers is a change to auth behaviour, which CLAUDE.md reserves for a human, and choosing the permission names is part of the activation review. The preconditions are guarded so the schema cannot be built first.
findings.verification_method: Permission read from the live dependant tree; 403 for a role without it and 200 for the role with it, both through TestClient; service-level allowlist and actor assertions with recording repositories; five restore-verified negative proofs.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Both routers declare permission dependencies; update_task writes only an explicit allow-list; assign and escalate take the actor from current_user. Then the tables may be built.
findings.regression_risk: LOW to guard; MEDIUM to fix (changes API behaviour on endpoints that cannot currently succeed)
findings.evidence_strength: STATIC ANALYSIS + EXECUTED NEGATIVE PROOF

findings.status: FIXED — same canonical permission as its sibling national routers
findings.title: app/national/intelligence/routes.py is registered and declares no require_permission, exposing clinical-intelligence compute to any authenticated principal
findings.description: Found by the NR-070 sibling-convention guard rather than by the caller trace. app/national/intelligence/routes.py is registered at factory.py:786-787 and contains no require_permission anywhere; every handler depends on get_current_user alone. The surface includes /intelligence/clinical/care-gaps/{patient_id}, /intelligence/clinical/risk-score/{patient_id}, drug-interaction checks, clinical recommendations, alert evaluation, automation task create/list and rule evaluation. IMPORTANT AND DELIBERATELY NOT OVERSTATED: the entire app/national/intelligence package performs NO database access -- no SessionLocal, no get_db and no `.query(` anywhere in the package -- so none of these endpoints reads patient data. `patient_id` is echoed in the response rather than resolved, and calculate_risk_score builds its whole 'patient' dict from the `age` and `gender` QUERY PARAMETERS the caller supplies. So this is an authorization gap on stateless compute, not a PHI disclosure: the risk is unauthorized use of clinical-decision compute by an account with no national role, responses that look patient-scoped but are not, and unmetered CPU on the alert and recommendation engines. Distinct from NR-070 in both mechanism and severity, and recorded separately for that reason. FIXED by the same change as NR-070: the router now declares `dependencies=[Depends(require_permission("system:admin"))]`. One thing found while proving it and recorded as NR-077: `/intelligence` is claimed by TWO routers -- this one and `app/command_intelligence/routes.py`, registered forty lines apart in factory.py and guarded with `dashboard:read`. Selecting routes by URL prefix therefore mixes two unrelated modules, so the guards select by the endpoint's defining module instead.
findings.root_cause: The router was written with get_current_user and never given the permission dependency its seven sibling national routers carry.
findings.evidence: app/national/intelligence/routes.py:68 router = APIRouter(prefix='/intelligence') with no dependencies; grep for require_permission in the file returns zero; factory.py:786-787 registers it. grep -rln 'SessionLocal|get_db|\.query(' over app/national/intelligence returns nothing. routes.py:227-241 calculate_risk_score constructs patient={'age': age, 'gender': gender, 'conditions': [], 'lifestyle': []} from query params.
findings.affected_users: Any authenticated principal can reach the compute surface
findings.clinical_impact: No patient data is read or returned. The hazard is that a response keyed by patient_id may be mistaken for a patient-specific result when it is computed entirely from caller input -- a clinical-safety framing issue rather than a disclosure.
findings.security_impact: Missing authorization on a registered national surface; no data exposure established
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — the package holds no persistent state
findings.operational_impact: Unmetered compute on recommendation and alert engines
findings.scalability_impact: Possible resource abuse; no rate limiting specific to these endpoints was verified
findings.legal_impact: None established, since no personal data is processed from storage
findings.dependencies: NR-070 (same class of omission, different package and severity)
findings.intersections: Sibling national routers all declare require_permission, which is the remediation reference
findings.contradictions: The endpoints' URL shape implies patient scoping that the implementation does not perform
findings.recommended_fix: Add require_permission to the router with an appropriate clinical-intelligence permission, matching the sibling packages. Separately, reconsider whether endpoints keyed by {patient_id} should accept a patient identifier at all when they resolve nothing from it.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Adding the router dependency is one line, but it is an authorization change and it changes the response for existing callers from 200 to 403, so it belongs to the same human review as NR-070 rather than to a measurement commit.

Negative-proven both ways: neutering require_permission in a sibling makes the first fail naming it, and adding it to intelligence makes the rot check fail naming intelligence.

findings.status: FIXED — mappers configure; verified against real PostgreSQL
findings.title: 22 cross-registry relationship() declarations made every NHDW mapper unusable, behind a registered router
findings.description: app/nhdw/models.py declared relationship("Patient") x11, relationship("HospitalDepartment") x7, plus Bed, Clinic, HospitalMaster and Room -- all classes that live in OTHER declarative bases (app.models.patient, app.hospital.models), so the NHDW registry never contained those names. SQLAlchemy resolves relationship strings at mapper configuration, and configuration is GLOBAL, so the first ORM use of any nhdw model raised InvalidRequestError: "When initializing mapper Mapper[Admission(nhdw_admissions)], expression 'Patient' failed to locate a name". This is a DIFFERENT CLASS from NR-067: nhdw_admissions IS built, nhdw_router IS registered (factory.py:733), and routes.py:326 queries Admission with a tenant filter. Every existing guard asked 'is the table built?' and the answer was yes, so none could see it. Found by calling configure_mappers() on the real application. FIXED by removing all 22 declarations: not one of the attributes was referenced anywhere, and the foreign key COLUMNS are untouched, so nothing that worked stopped working. Re-adding one requires the target to share this registry, which for Patient is the NR-022 canonical-subject decision rather than a string.
findings.root_cause: Relationship targets were written as strings without checking that the target shares the declaring model's declarative base, and nothing ever forced global mapper configuration in test or CI, so the failure had no way to surface.
findings.evidence: configure_mappers() on the real app raised InvalidRequestError naming Admission and 'Patient'; querying Admission against a migrated PostgreSQL 16.13 raised the same; nhdw_admissions confirmed present in pg_tables; factory.py:733-734 registers nhdw_router; AST census: 24 relationship() calls, 22 targeting non-local classes; grep confirms none of the attributes is referenced. After the fix, configure_mappers() succeeds.
findings.affected_users: Any caller of an NHDW endpoint; and any ORM use in the process once configuration was forced
findings.clinical_impact: NHDW admission, discharge, transfer and queue endpoints could not serve requests
findings.security_impact: None directly; a 500 is not a bypass
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — no writes succeeded to be corrupted
findings.operational_impact: Registered endpoints returning 500 on every call; the blast radius is global because mapper configuration is global
findings.dependencies: NR-074 (the same tables also have ORM/physical drift, so the endpoints still do not work)
findings.intersections: NR-067 is the inverse: unbuilt tables with reachable code. This is a built table with unusable ORM.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: remove the unresolvable declarations, keep the FK columns.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_orm_mappers_configure.py (gated in the identity job): builds the real application and calls configure_mappers(). Negative-proven by re-adding one relationship("Patient") to Admission, which fails with the original message.
findings.acceptance_criteria: configure_mappers() succeeds on the real application.
findings.regression_risk: LOW — removed declarations that could never resolve and were referenced nowhere
findings.evidence_strength: REAL DATABASE + EXECUTED TEST

findings.status: MEASURED — not repaired; NHDW endpoints remain non-functional
findings.title: nhdw_admissions maps 16 columns the database does not have and ignores 11 it does
findings.description: With NR-073 fixed, mappers configure -- and the query then fails for a second, independent reason: ProgrammingError (psycopg2.errors.UndefinedColumn) column nhdw_admissions.encounter_id does not exist. Compared against the migrated database, the ORM maps 16 columns that are absent (admitting_doctor_id, bed_id, department_id, diagnosis, diagnosis_system, discharge_date, discharge_type, encounter_id, extension, hospital_id, insurance_id, insurance_policy, is_emergency, metadata, referring_doctor_id, room_id) and omits 11 that exist (admission_number, admitting_doctor, bed_number, department, diagnosis_description, insurance_policy_number, insurance_provider, referring_physician, status, sync_id, ward). This is the same class the P0-2 pharmacy milestones M1-M4 resolved for 27 tables. DELIBERATELY NOT REPAIRED HERE: reconciling an ORM to a physical schema is per-entity work requiring a column-by-column disposition, and doing it hastily is how columns get silently dropped.
findings.root_cause: The ORM was written or evolved independently of the migration that built the table.
findings.evidence: information_schema.columns for nhdw_admissions versus Admission.__table__.columns on a migrated PostgreSQL 16.13: 16 ORM-only, 11 physical-only. Query raises UndefinedColumn on encounter_id.

findings.title: CitizenRelationship cannot be INSERTed: IdentityBase.metadata has no users or lab_users to resolve its foreign keys
findings.description: CORRECTS MY OWN EARLIER CLAIM. NR-064 repaired the subject lookup -- that part is real and verified: citizen_id now resolves niam_persons, which IS in IdentityBase.metadata, and the 20260914_0001 foreign key is enforced by PostgreSQL. But executing the path against a real database shows the endpoint is STILL non-functional. CitizenRelationship also declares ForeignKey('users.id'), ForeignKey('lab_users.id') and ForeignKey('national_patients.id'), and none of those tables is in IdentityBase.metadata (users lives in app.database.Base). SQLAlchemy resolves foreign keys when it sorts tables for an INSERT, so: SELECT works, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE works, and add()+flush() raises NoReferencedTableError. POST /admin/citizen-relationships therefore still cannot create a row. I did not find this earlier because the only test of the workflow uses a fake session -- the exact failure mode NR-064 is about -- and because the static guard only asked whether the path named an unbuilt table, which stopped being true after the repair. SCOPE CORRECTION: Phase D measured the whole class rather than this table. 310 foreign keys across FIVE declarative bases point at a table their own MetaData does not own -- CareContinuumBase 214, EHRBase 70, DataPlatformBase 13, TrustBase 8, IdentityBase 5. NR-075 is the 5, and it was found first only because its endpoint was executed. The generalisation is NR-078, which also records the consequence nobody had looked for: `alembic revision --autogenerate` cannot run at all.
findings.root_cause: The identity models sit on their own declarative base (NR-018 registered 8 authorized bases) while declaring foreign keys to tables owned by another base. The physical constraints exist because migrations create them; the ORM cannot see the targets.
findings.evidence: Against migrated PostgreSQL 16.13 with the real application wiring: SELECT OK, SELECT FOR UPDATE OK, add()+flush() raises NoReferencedTableError on legacy_user_id. 'users' in IdentityBase.metadata.tables is False; 'niam_persons' is True. Declared FKs: niam_accounts.id, users.id, lab_users.id, niam_persons.id, national_patients.id.

findings.title: Eleven of the fourteen concrete orchestration repositories persist nothing, and one of them is still abstract, so every task endpoint raises TypeError before it can act
findings.description: Found by the NR-070 POSITIVE authorization test -- the one asserting that a principal holding the permission gets through. `master_admin` passes authorization on GET /national/tasks/ and then fails, not on the unbuilt tables as expected but earlier: `SQLAlchemyTaskAssignmentRepository` implements `find_by_user` and `find_active` while its ABC declares `find_by_assignee`, so the class is still abstract and `_get_service()` raises `TypeError` on instantiation. Every one of the 29 task endpoints calls `_get_service()` first, so the entire router is unreachable. Tracing that revealed the larger shape: of the fourteen concrete repositories in these two packages, ELEVEN have write methods that contain no function call at all -- `save` returns its argument, finders return `[]`, `delete` returns True. Only `SQLAlchemyNationalTaskRepository`, `SQLAlchemyWorkflowDefinitionRepository` and `SQLAlchemyWorkflowExecutionRepository` open a session. Among the eleven are BOTH audit-log repositories, both assignment and escalation stores, workflow steps, approvals, compensations and timers. So the TypeError is the only thing standing between this platform and a workflow engine that returns {'success': true} while discarding every audit row, approval and compensation it is handed. Deliberately NOT repaired: making the class instantiable would replace a loud failure with silent data loss, which is the wrong direction. The boundary is fail-closed and stays closed until the repositories are real.
findings.root_cause: The packages were generated as a clean-architecture skeleton and only the two or three repositories someone exercised by hand were implemented; the rest kept the shape of the interface and none of the behaviour. Nothing detected it because nothing had ever executed them -- the tables are unbuilt and, until NR-070, the routers had no tests.
findings.evidence: Executed: TestClient GET /national/tasks/ as master_admin raises TypeError("Can't instantiate abstract class SQLAlchemyTaskAssignmentRepository without an implementation for abstract method 'find_by_assignee'"). Static: an AST pass over app/ for classes whose name ends in Repository, counting concrete (non-`...`, non-`pass`, non-`raise`) write methods containing zero ast.Call nodes, returns 11 classes, all in app/national/task_engine (6) and app/national/workflow_runtime (5). MEASUREMENT CORRECTION, recorded because the first two numbers were wrong and nearly shipped: a first detector looked for the tokens SessionLocal/get_db/session and reported 44 of 51 'stubs' platform-wide -- false, because `SQLAlchemyDocumentRepository` and its neighbours hold the session as `self.db`. A second pass counting call-less write methods reported 82, also false, because it counted the abstract base classes. Only the third -- concrete write methods with no call at all -- matches hand inspection of every file. The 44 and the 82 are not in this register because they are not true. | The detector is now shipped rather than run once: backend/tests/test_persistence_is_real.py holds the eleven as a named ledger (module:Class), ratchets it so no new repository may accept writes and discard them, rot-checks it so an implemented one must leave, and names the audit-log repositories separately because losing an audit row silently is a different severity from losing a timer. Negative-proved both ways, restored byte-identical: giving SQLAlchemyTaskCommentRepository.save a call fails the rot check; hollowing out the genuinely-working SQLAlchemyDocumentVersionRepository fails the ratchet. DISPOSITION EVIDENCE (added): every target table of the eleven inert repositories is absent from PostgreSQL — national_tasks, national_task_queues, national_task_assignments, national_task_audit_logs, national_workflow_executions, national_workflow_timers, national_workflow_templates and the rest all return nothing from information_schema.tables — and none is registered in any metadata object, because migrations/env.py deliberately excludes the package. So implementing these repositories would create write paths to tables that do not exist: the NR-067 class, not a repair. CONTRADICTION FOUND: env.py records the exclusion as 'app.national.task_engine (RETIRE: 15 tables, none physical, no reachable operation)'. The first half is true and was verified here. The second half is false: app.national.task_engine.api.routes serves 29 registered paths and app.national.workflow_runtime.api.routes serves 22, measured from the built application — 51 in total — and NR-070 secured them with system:admin precisely because they are reachable. The RETIRE decision was therefore taken on a premise that is half wrong and needs re-taking with correct facts. THREE INDEPENDENT BARRIERS currently prevent these 51 routes from answering with fake success: _get_service() raises TypeError (NR-076), the tables do not exist (UndefinedTable would follow), and since NR-070 the routers require system:admin. Removing any one of them alone does not create the hazard; removing the first two together would.

findings.status: PARTIALLY VERIFIED — autogenerate now executes inside a CI gate; the topology change is DECIDED (Option A) and deliberately NOT APPLIED, because applying it would make a 1367-operation destructive diff actionable (NR-080)
findings.title: 310 foreign keys name a table their own declarative base does not own, and as a result `alembic revision --autogenerate` cannot run against this repository at all
findings.description: NR-075 generalised, and it turns out to be a defect in the measuring instrument rather than in one endpoint. SQLAlchemy resolves a ForeignKey inside the MetaData that owns the REFERRING table. Measured across exactly what `migrations/env.py` hands Alembic, 310 foreign keys point at a table owned by a different declarative base: CareContinuumBase 214, EHRBase 70, DataPlatformBase 13, TrustBase 8, IdentityBase 5. The targets are real tables -- national_practitioners (78), national_patients (51), national_citizens (50), national_facilities (49), national_encounters (30) and 18 more -- owned by NationalBase and Base. CONSEQUENCE: Alembic reaches `MetaData.sorted_tables` on every registered metadata before it emits a single operation, and sorting resolves every foreign key. So `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "anything"` terminates with NoReferencedTableError and produces nothing. That is the command CLAUDE.md's migration policy names as the way to make any schema change ('All schema changes = new revision: alembic revision --autogenerate'), and it has no working path. WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: `test_alembic_metadata_registry.py` asks whether a foreign key names a table that exists SOMEWHERE across the registry -- PHANTOM_FK_TARGETS, currently empty -- which is one qualifier weaker than what SQLAlchemy requires. Every guard in that file reasons about what autogenerate WOULD propose, and not one of them has ever asked autogenerate to propose it. The capability was assumed by the guards that depend on it and exercised by none of them. EXPERIMENTAL RESOLUTION. Both options were measured against a disposable PostgreSQL 16.13 database migrated to head, rather than argued. OPTION B (keep separate metadata, drop the ORM-level ForeignKey, keep columns and physical constraints) removes nothing the ORM uses: NOT ONE of the 76 tables holding a cross-base FK carries a single relationship(), so there is no navigation to lose. It clears all 310 -- and then fails on a second, independent blocker: 'ValueError: Duplicate table keys across multiple MetaData objects: national_facilities'. Alembic refuses a multi-metadata target claiming one table twice, and NR-006's repair deliberately declares national_facilities a second time as a FOREIGN-KEY ANCHOR so seventeen app/national models can resolve it. The anchor is what makes those FKs work and what makes autogenerate refuse. Option B cannot hold both goals. OPTION A (one shared MetaData) was measured: exactly ONE duplicate table key -- that same anchor -- and the two definitions are COLUMN-IDENTICAL, so the collision is resolved by deleting one declaration rather than by choosing an owner; ZERO unresolved foreign keys; sorted_tables succeeds; autogenerate runs. Option A is the mechanically correct topology and the repository is one deleted Table away from it. IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED. Making autogenerate run is not the same as making it usable: the resulting diff is 5039 operations of which 1367 are destructive, including DROP COLUMN on patients.national_id -- the column Security Invariant #8 requires to hold encrypted national identifiers (NR-080). Applying Option A today would replace a loud, honest failure ('autogenerate cannot run') with a quiet and dangerous capability ('autogenerate runs and proposes dropping your encrypted national IDs'). That is the same trade NR-076 refuses, in the same direction. THIS CORRECTS THIS FINDING'S OWN EARLIER FRAMING, which presented the topology choice as the decision to take: the topology is not the bottleneck, the drift is. WHAT IS APPLIED: backend/tests/test_autogenerate_is_safe.py performs the merge inside the gate, so autogenerate executes for real against a migrated PostgreSQL without migrations/env.py, any declarative base or any model changing -- zero runtime risk -- and pins every destructive proposal with its explanation.
findings.root_cause: Domain packages were given their own declarative bases (NR-018 registered eight authorized ones) while their models kept declaring foreign keys to the shared national and legacy tables. The physical constraints exist because migrations create them by name; the ORM cannot see the targets.
findings.evidence: Executed: `alembic revision --autogenerate -m nr075_probe` against the migrated PostgreSQL 16.13 database (nr069_truth) fails with "NoReferencedTableError: Foreign key associated with column 'ehr_allergies.citizen_id' could not find table 'national_citizens'" and writes no revision file. `alembic.autogenerate.produce_migrations` fails at the same point, inside alembic/autogenerate/api.py::sorted_tables. Static: iterating the labelled target_metadata the checked-in harness loads from env.py and counting foreign keys whose `_table_key()` is absent from the referring table's own MetaData gives 310, distributed over the five bases above. Negative proofs, both restored byte-identical: removing one FK from CitizenRelationship fails the rot check with 'IdentityBase (5, 4)'; adding a cross-base FK to a PharmacyBase model fails the ratchet with "['PharmacyBase']". | EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE (disposable database nr078_probe, PostgreSQL 16.13, 423 tables at head): baseline autogenerate CRASHES with NoReferencedTableError on ehr_allergies. Option B removes 310 of 310 cross-base FK constraints from the metadata (leftover 0) and then CRASHES with ValueError duplicate table key national_facilities. Option A: 1 collision (national_facilities, identical_columns=true), 0 unresolved FKs, sorted_tables OK, autogenerate produces 5039 operations. Runtime relationship census: 218 relationships across 18 SQLAlchemy registries, of which 0 are on any of the 76 cross-base-FK tables. Physical cross-check: only 12 of the 310 cross-base FKs have an actual PostgreSQL constraint, and 70 of the 76 referring tables are not physical at all. The 12 that are real sit on trust_* (8), niam_assignments (2) and niam_citizen_relationships (2). Gate: 7 tests, 4 negative proofs, all sources restored byte-identical. (Re-measured 2026-09-16 against the migrated PostgreSQL probe at head 20260915_0003: 5039 operations, 1367 destructive -- 538 DropConstraintOp, 454 DropIndexOp, 365 DropColumnOp, 10 DropTableOp. All 21 operations between the earlier 5060/1379 and this figure have a named cause and sum to the delta exactly, with no remainder: DropColumnOp -12 and AlterColumnOp +12 are one change seen twice, NR-089 mapping twelve physical trust columns so they stopped being unmapped and became type mismatches instead; AddColumnOp 314 -> 293 is migrations 20260915_0001 (11 created_at/updated_at/version columns across six gov_* and two ecosystem_* tables) and 20260915_0002 (10 attestation columns on niam_machine_identities) building columns the ORM already declared.)

findings.title: Reachability was measured by regex over factory.py and an import resolver blind to `from package import submodule`, understating the reachable surface by 63 route modules and 382 modules of closure
findings.description: Found while executing PHASE G -- classifying NR-063's 75 latent create paths as LIVE / REACHABLE-BUT-INACTIVE / REGISTERED-FUTURE / DEAD / UNKNOWN before fixing any of them. The first classification returned 17 DEAD, which was false, and the falseness had two independent causes, both understating reachability: (1) REGISTRATION BY REGEX. `_registered_route_modules()` matched `from .x import y as z` and `from .routes import name as alias` in factory.py. The factory also registers a bulk block -- `from .routes import (admin, ehr, ehr_fhir, …)` followed by `for r in core_routes + feature_routes + advanced_routes + …: app.include_router(r.router)` -- which neither regex matched. Measured against the running application the regex finds 79 route modules where 142 are served: 63 false negatives, 0 false positives. (2) SUBMODULE IMPORTS DROPPED. `_imported_modules()` resolved `from app.x.y import Z` and `from ..models import Z` but turned `from app.services import ehr_service` into a lookup for app/services.py, which does not exist, instead of app/services/ehr_service.py, which does. That single form hid an entire module holding 17 unguarded create paths and 63 reachable reads of unbuilt tables. Plain `import app.x.y` was also unhandled. Together the two took the reachable closure from 612 modules to 994 (+62%) and NR-067's reachable unbuilt reads from 418 across 20 route modules to 610 across 24. The guard-the-guard that should have caught it asserted at least 60 registered modules -- satisfied comfortably by an instrument missing 63. A floor is only worth its distance from the truth.
findings.root_cause: Reachability was answered by parsing the file that configures the application rather than by asking the application. factory.py is free to register routers any way Python allows; a regex over it can only ever be a lower bound, and nothing said so.
findings.evidence: Executed against the started application: route.endpoint.__module__ over the recursive route walk yields 142 route modules; _registered_route_modules() yields 79; the difference is 63 with an empty reverse difference. Import edges over app/ go from 4107 to 4528; the closure from registered routers from 612 modules to 994. Re-measuring NR-067 gives 610 across 24 modules against a declared 418 across 20, with GREW={} and GONE=[] -- every previously declared count unchanged, four modules added: app/routes/ehr_fhir.py 77, app/routes/ehr.py 63, app/governance/routes/governance_routes.py 47, app/governance/routes/analytics_routes.py 5. 418+192=610. findings.status: MEASURED — first complete ORM-to-database comparison; ratcheted, not reconciled
findings.title: The first complete comparison of the ORM against the database proposes 5039 operations, 1367 of them destructive, including DROP COLUMN on patients.national_id
findings.description: NR-078 established that `alembic revision --autogenerate` has never run against this repository. Making it run (Option A, inside a gate) produced the first complete ORM-to-database comparison the platform has ever had, and it is not small: 5039 operations, of which 538 DropConstraintOp, 454 DropIndexOp, 365 DropColumnOp and 10 DropTableOp -- 1367 destructive. None of it is caused by the topology change; the topology change only made pre-existing drift visible. TWO SAMPLES DECIDE HOW SERIOUS IT IS. (1) The 10 proposed DROP TABLE are EXACTLY the ten physical tables no ORM maps, independently pinned as UNMAPPED_PHYSICAL_TABLES in test_alembic_metadata_registry.py by subtracting mapped from physical -- a completely different derivation reaching the same list, which is strong evidence both instruments are correct. They are Financial Engine Phase A (schema-only by design), visits, sndhs_audit_logs, idempotency_keys and radiology_ai_analysis_jobs. (2) The proposed DROP COLUMN set includes patients.national_id, patients.sndhs_health_id, patients.identity_level, patients.consent_flags and lab_orders.visit_id -- the SNDHS Phase 1 surface. patients.national_id is varchar(20), carries four indexes including a partial unique index, and is the column CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #8 requires to hold encrypted national identifiers. app/models/patient.py maps national_id_hash and none of the others. CONSEQUENCE: autogenerate output may not be committed as a migration in this repository under any topology until this is reconciled. That is why NR-078's topology change is decided but not applied -- the capability is worth less than the hazard until the drift comes down. The largest single cluster is radiology (~170 columns across 12 tables), which is the NR-074 class at scale.
findings.root_cause: Models were written from intent rather than from the physical schema, and nothing ever compared the two -- because the tool that would have done so could not start.
findings.evidence: Disposable PostgreSQL 16.13 (nr078_probe) migrated to head, 423 tables. alembic.autogenerate.produce_migrations against the merged metadata: CreateIndexOp 2372, ModifyTableOps 585, DropConstraintOp 538, DropIndexOp 454, DropColumnOp 377, AddColumnOp 314, CreateTableOp 303, AlterColumnOp 73, CreateForeignKeyOp 27, DropTableOp 10, CreateUniqueConstraintOp 7. CreateTableOp 303 equals the independently measured MAPPED_NOT_PHYSICAL count of 303. DropTableOp 10 equals the independently measured PHYSICAL_NOT_MAPPED count of 10 and matches UNMAPPED_PHYSICAL_TABLES exactly. `\d patients` confirms national_id varchar(20), sndhs_health_id uuid, identity_level integer, consent_flags jsonb are physical; app/models/patient.py maps none of them. (Re-measured 2026-09-16 against the migrated PostgreSQL probe at head 20260915_0003: 5039 operations, 1367 destructive -- 538 DropConstraintOp, 454 DropIndexOp, 365 DropColumnOp, 10 DropTableOp. findings.status: MEASURED — the blind-spot class is guarded; the shadow subsystem is recorded, not repaired
findings.title: Schema access through `sqlalchemy.table()` and raw SQL is invisible to every metadata-based guard, and one unreachable subsystem writes three canonical clinical tables that way
findings.description: Found while tracing NR-080's discovery that patients.national_id is physical, indexed four ways and mapped by no ORM model. Something does read it: app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py, through `_PATIENTS = table('patients', column(...), ...)` -- the lightweight SQLAlchemy Core construct, which carries NO MetaData at all -- plus raw `INSERT INTO patients`, returning national_id in its response shape. Every schema instrument in this suite works from ORM metadata: built_tables() derives from migrations, the registry guard compares registered MetaData against PostgreSQL, the autogenerate gate diffs mappers against the database, and the NR-063/NR-067 scans resolve ORM class names. NONE of them can see a `table()` construct or a table name inside a string literal. This is a whole class of schema access that was structurally invisible. MEASURED: 1 module reaches a built table through a Core table() construct, and 7 execute raw INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against one. Six of the seven are legitimate and stay -- the three AI modules write their own tables, idempotency_keys has no ORM by design, outbox_events needs raw SQL for its locking, and startup_guard seeds lab_users before the app is up. Legitimacy is not the invariant; visibility is. THE OUTLIER: app/reference is a complete parallel implementation of patient reference data -- own domain model, own repository, own tests -- which writes patients, lab_orders and lab_results by raw SQL. Measured against the running application it serves ZERO routes and ZERO modules outside it import it, so it is unreachable today. It is recorded rather than deleted: removing a subsystem is an ownership decision. If it were ever registered there would be a second write authority for the clinical subject, with different invariants and no HMAC path for the national ID, and no existing guard would have noticed.
findings.root_cause: Schema guards were built on the assumption that the ORM is the only route to the database. Core constructs and raw SQL are both supported first-class by SQLAlchemy and neither appears in any MetaData.
findings.evidence: AST scan over app/: 1 module with a Core table() naming a built table (app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py -> patients); 7 modules executing raw DML on built tables. Runtime: `route_modules(app)` over the started application yields ZERO app.reference.* modules among 142 route modules and 2109 served routes; the corrected import graph yields ZERO importers of app/reference/ from outside it. MEASUREMENT CORRECTION: a first pass matched INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against every string literal and reported 8 modules. One, app/core/bootstrap/permissions.py, contains no SQL at all -- the regex matched the permission label "Update Patients". Counting only strings handed to text()/execute() gives 7. The 8 is not recorded, because it is not true. Negative proof, restored byte-identical: adding a table('audit_logs') construct and a raw INSERT INTO samples to app/core/auto_repair.py fails all three guards.

findings.category: Schema generation conflict / Dead clinical module / Tenant isolation
findings.status: MEASURED AND GUARDED — the break is pinned by an executing guard; the domain rewrite is scoped, not applied
findings.title: Radiology is a registered clinical module serving 50 HTTP paths in which no database operation of any kind can succeed: all 18 mappers are a second generation that never replaced the first
findings.description: Every one of the 18 SQLAlchemy classes on RadiologyBase fails to execute even a plain SELECT against a database at migration head. Executed, not inferred: `SELECT <mapper columns> FROM <table> LIMIT 1` was run against a disposable PostgreSQL 16 migrated to head for all 18, and 18 failed — 17 with UndefinedColumn and `radiology_ai_jobs` with UndefinedTable, because no migration builds that name (the physical table is `radiology_ai_analysis_jobs`, and the two share 16 of their column names). INSERT fails identically. app/radiology/routes.py is registered in factory.py and serves 50 paths over app/radiology/services.py, which uses these mappers directly, so the module is reachable and totally non-functional. The routes carry no broad exception handler, so the failure surfaces as a 500 rather than as a valid-looking empty response.
findings.root_cause: Two generations of the radiology domain share table names and were never reconciled. The physical tables are Generation A: integer primary keys, joined to the platform core (patient_id -> patients.id, lab_id -> labs.id, *_by -> lab_users.id), carrying lab_id, sync_id, created_by and updated_by. The mappers are Generation B: String(26) ULID keys, FHIR-flavoured, with no foreign key to the core and no lab_id at all. All 18 primary keys disagree on type. This is the same pattern already resolved for pharmacy, where the 17 Generation-B mappers were rewritten from the physical schema.
findings.evidence: 494 physical columns across 18 tables vs 399 mapper columns; 265 physical-only and 170 mapper-only. Systematic physical-only columns: sync_id 17/17, lab_id 13/17, created_by 12/17, updated_by 10/17. Systematic mapper-only: extra_metadata 17/17. 45 columns present in both disagree on type, including all 18 primary keys (String(26) vs integer) and radiology_protocols.version (Integer lock vs character varying). Runtime probe: SELECT ok=0 fail=18; INSERT UndefinedColumn on radiology_orders(encounter_id), radiology_exams(exam_code), radiology_reports(ordering_provider_id), UndefinedTable on radiology_ai_jobs. Route probe: route_modules(app) contains app/radiology/routes.py and 50 served paths resolve to it. API-CONTRACT AND CLIENT EVIDENCE (added; this is what the blocked decision needs): the response models in app/radiology/routes.py declare every identifier as Pydantic `str` (patient_id, order_id, exam_id, protocol_id, technologist_id...), over physical columns that are `integer`. NO CLIENT CONSUMES THEM: across all four frontends (frontend-v3, frontend-v2, client, frontend) there is not one call to a /radiology backend path. The only three frontend-v3 files mentioning radiology are api/generated/types.ts (generated declarations, not calls), pages/migration/frontendSurfaceCatalog.ts (a UI entryPath '/radiology'), and a legacy route-bridge test. And the decisive argument does not depend on searching this repository: every one of the 18 mappers fails on SELECT, so no endpoint backed by them has ever returned a row, and an endpoint that has never returned a row cannot have a dependent client inside or outside this repository.
findings.affected_users: Any actor reaching a /radiology path; radiologists, technologists, referring clinicians, citizens using the image-share endpoints.
findings.clinical_impact: Total. Orders, exams, reports, critical findings, worklists and DICOM references cannot be created or read. radiology_critical_findings is the escalation path for findings that require immediate clinician contact and it does not work.
findings.security_impact: CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1 requires every patient-data query to filter on lab_id = current_user.lab_id. The physical tables carry lab_id with a foreign key to labs; the mappers do not declare it, so no ORM query in this domain can filter by tenant. If the mappers were repaired without adding lab_id, the module would become functional and cross-tenant in the same change. That is the trap this finding exists to prevent.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Nothing is currently corrupted, because nothing is currently written. The risk is in the repair: autogenerate proposes DROP for the 265 physical-only columns, which includes every lab_id, created_by, updated_by and sync_id in the domain.
findings.operational_impact: 50 registered endpoints return 500 on every database-touching call.
findings.scalability_impact: None measured; the module does no work.
findings.legal_impact: Radiology reports and critical findings are part of the clinical record; an unwritable record is a records-retention gap.
intersections: NR-021 (tenant isolation)
NR-074 (NHDW drift, same shape)
findings.contradictions: docs and CLAUDE.md describe app/radiology/ as a platform sub-package alongside pharmacy and nursing, which are reconciled and working. Nothing distinguishes radiology as non-functional.
findings.recommended_fix: Rewrite the 18 mappers from the physical schema, as was done for pharmacy — and note the response models must be reshaped in the same change, which is free because nothing consumes them: integer keys, lab_id with its ForeignKey('labs.id'), created_by/updated_by to lab_users, sync_id; then reconcile services.py and routes.py field references; then add a migration for the Generation-B fields that carry information the physical schema genuinely lacks. Map radiology_ai_jobs onto radiology_ai_analysis_jobs. Enforce lab_id filtering in services.py before re-enabling.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None that makes the module work. Partial repair is worse than none here: a mapper fixed for readability but still missing lab_id turns a dead endpoint into a cross-tenant one. The safe increment already applied is measurement — NR-083's guard pins all 17 readable failures so the repair cannot silently regress or half-land.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py executes each mapper's own SELECT against PostgreSQL in the migration CI job; the 17 radiology entries must leave DECLARED_UNREADABLE as they are repaired, and the rot check fails if a repaired table is left in the ledger.
findings.acceptance_criteria: All 18 radiology mappers read and write against a database at head; every mapper declares lab_id; every service query filters on it; the 17 radiology entries are gone from DECLARED_UNREADABLE; no physical column was dropped to achieve it.
findings.regression_risk: High — the rewrite touches 3068 lines of services and routes. Must land as its own reviewed change.
findings.blocker: Narrowed. The API-compatibility half is ANSWERED: no client depends on these contracts, so the mappers can adopt the physical integer keys and the response models can be reshaped without breaking anyone — the same situation as the seven M4 pharmacy response models. What remains is a domain question, not a compatibility one: which of the 170 Generation-B mapper fields carry information the physical schema genuinely lacks (and so need an additive migration), and which are renames of columns already there. That needs the radiology owner. Until then the rewrite must not start, because a mapper repaired for readability without restoring lab_id would turn 50 dead endpoints into 50 cross-tenant ones.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — runtime SELECT/INSERT against PostgreSQL 16 at migration head, plus route registration read from the built application

findings.title: 35 mapped tables that exist in PostgreSQL cannot be read by the mapper that claims them, and no guard had ever asked a mapper to run its own query
findings.description: Every schema guard in this suite compared descriptions of the schema — metadata against metadata, migration against model, list against list. None executed a mapper's own SELECT. Doing so for all 715 registered tables found that 303 have no physical table (independently equal to the autogenerate gate's CreateTableOp count of 303) and that of the 412 that do exist, 44 name at least one column their table does not have. For those 44 nothing works: SQLAlchemy builds the column list from the mapper, so SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and COUNT all fail with UndefinedColumn before a row is examined. Blocks: radiology 17 (NR-082), NHDW 14 (NR-074), governance 6, ecosystem 3, financial 3, identity 1. Nine of the 44 are repaired here by two additive migrations -- eight pure timestamp/optimistic-lock mixin gaps and niam_machine_identities (NR-084); 35 remain.
findings.root_cause: Nothing in CI ever executed a query built from a mapper against a real migrated database. Existing guards proved that migrations apply, that metadata is registered and that tables exist — none of which is disturbed by a mapper naming a column that is not there. The condition is invisible to `alembic upgrade head`, to table-existence checks and to the SQLite-backed unit suite, and visible only to PostgreSQL at statement time.
findings.evidence: 715 mapped tables probed against nr078_probe (PostgreSQL 16 at head): 368 OK, 303 NO_TABLE, 44 ProgrammingError. After migrations 20260915_0001 and 20260915_0002: 377 OK, 35 ProgrammingError. The 303 NO_TABLE equals the autogenerate gate's independently derived CreateTableOp count — two instruments, different routes, same number. Sample failures: gov_break_glass_accesses(updated_at, version), gov_merge_proposals(updated_at, version), nhdw_admissions(16 columns), niam_machine_identities(10 columns). | RE-MEASURED 2026-09-17 from DECLARED_UNREADABLE in tests/test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py: the 35 are 17 radiology_*, 14 nhdw_*, 3 fin_* and 1 ecosystem_*. Every one belongs to a blocked or approval-gated domain, so can_fix_now=True and the empty blocker were describing a state that ended when the 9 fixable ones were fixed. A work queue that still advertises finished work sends the next pass at phantom tasks, and this entry did exactly that during a re-scan.
findings.affected_users: Any actor reaching an endpoint backed by one of the 36 tables.
findings.clinical_impact: Radiology (NR-082) and NHDW admissions, discharges, transfers, ward rounds, care plans and clinical tasks are among the 36. Two of the eight repaired here are gov_break_glass_accesses (emergency override of access control) and gov_merge_proposals (patient identity merge) — both unreadable until this change.
findings.security_impact: CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #6 requires the version column to be checked on mutation. On gov_break_glass_accesses, gov_merge_proposals, gov_identity_records, ecosystem_partners and ecosystem_partner_certificates it could not be checked, because the column did not exist. The migration builds it.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No corruption: these tables reject every statement rather than accepting a wrong one. The integrity risk is the repair direction — autogenerate's answer to this drift is to DROP the physical columns, which for radiology means dropping every lab_id in the domain.
findings.operational_impact: Every endpoint backed by one of the 36 returns 500 on any database call.
findings.legal_impact: Break-glass access records are an auditable control; an unwritable one is an audit gap.

NR-079 (instrument floors)
findings.contradictions: The migration CI job was green throughout, because applying migrations and asking a mapper to use them are different questions and only the first was ever asked.
findings.recommended_fix: Reconcile each mapper against the physical schema, mapper-side. The physical tables are canonical: they carry the foreign keys into the platform core and the tenant column. Where a mapper field is genuinely new information, add it with an additive migration (ADD -> BACKFILL -> VALIDATE -> SHADOW READ -> SWITCH -> RETIRE). Never drop a physical column to make the mapper agree.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: migration 20260915_0001 adds the 11 timestamp and optimistic-lock columns eight mappers already declare, closing 8 of the 44 with no rename, retype, backfill or drop. ecosystem_partner_agreements is deliberately left failing: its mapper declares version as String(20), a document version shadowing the inherited integer lock, while the table carries agreement_version. Which is intended is a question about the entity, not the schema.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py, in the migration CI job against PostgreSQL at head. Six tests: the probe reached a real database (floor 400 of a measured 412); nothing outside the ledger is unreadable; no ledger entry has been repaired without being removed; the per-table missing-column tuples are exact; the ledger never grows; and the readable population never shrinks (floor 370 of a measured 377) so the ledger cannot be emptied by deleting mapper fields.
findings.acceptance_criteria: DECLARED_UNREADABLE is empty and MINIMUM_READABLE has risen to the full mapped-and-physical population, with no physical column dropped.
findings.regression_risk: Low for the applied migration (additive, guarded, round-trip verified). High for the remaining 36, which are domain rewrites.

findings.blocker: All 35 remaining are blocked, and this field previously said otherwise. Re-measured 2026-09-17 by domain: 17 radiology_* (NR-082, protected), 14 nhdw_* (NR-074, blocked on the NHDW owner), 3 fin_* whose mappers live in app/financial/models.py, which CLAUDE.md places under 'Requires human approval', and 1 ecosystem_partner_agreements, which is this finding's own open question. findings.title: The identity platform could not record that a machine identity was compromised: `mark_compromised` writes two columns the table did not have
findings.description: `niam_machine_identities` is mapped by app/identity/models/machine_identity.py, which declares ten columns the table did not have, so every statement against it -- including SELECT -- failed with UndefinedColumn. Three endpoints are registered over it (POST /devices/register, /devices/{uuid}/trust, /devices/{uuid}/revoke), and app/identity/services/device_service.py writes seven of the ten: attest_device sets device_attestation, attested_at and health_status; report_health sets health_status and last_health_check; mark_compromised sets health_status='compromised' and risk_score=100. findings.domain: blood bank, OAuth2/service accounts, trust platform
findings.status: PARTLY REPAIRED — 9 of 19 columns fixed and regression-guarded; 10 pinned. SEVERITY RAISED P2 -> P1 by execution. The audit-actor question that blocked the remaining 10 is now ANSWERED BY MEASUREMENT: two legitimate identity domains, and 13 columns belonging to neither.
findings.title: 19 columns in readable tables disagree with their PostgreSQL type — and for nine of them the column's own server_default was unreadable by the model that owns it
findings.description: NR-083 asks whether a mapper can read its table, which only checks that column NAMES line up. It says nothing about Column(Integer) over a character varying. Measuring that found 19 columns across 15 otherwise-readable tables, in three groups. (1) Six blood-bank tables inherit AuditMixin.created_by as Integer over a varchar column — the seventh, blood_bank_transfusions, was built with an integer column and agrees, so the migrations disagree with each other. (2) Four Integer mappers over boolean columns, including oauth2_tokens.is_revoked. (3) Nine trust_* native-enum mappers over plain varchar — REPAIRED here.
findings.root_cause: For groups 1 and 2, columns were added by migrations written against a different type than the mapper declares, and nothing compared the two. For group 3 the cause is sharper and systemic: SQLAlchemy persists an enum member's NAME unless values_callable says otherwise, and none of the seven trust enum classes passed it — while every migration wrote its server_default as the member's VALUE. All seven classes are UPPER_SNAKE name / lower_snake value, so the two halves of one intent disagreed on all nine columns. The database has no native enum types at all, so the mappers also compiled to a PostgreSQL type that does not exist.
findings.evidence:
Executed against PostgreSQL 16 at head. Groups 1-2: INSERT into blood_bank_reservations with created_by as both str '7' and int 7 succeeded and the route passes str(current_user.id), so writes work; `WHERE created_by = 42` -> UndefinedFunction: operator does not exist: character varying = integer; `WHERE is_revoked = 1` -> boolean = integer (while `= True` compiles to IS true). Group 3, the part first reported as latent and proven otherwise: an INSERT omitting trust_consent_records.status takes the DATABASE's own default 'pending', and reading that row through the mapper raised LookupError; a plain SELECT * over the table then raised for EVERY row; and `WHERE status == 'PENDING'` matched 1 of 2 semantically-pending rows — an undercount rather than an error. 13 routes under /api/v1/trust/* are registered and served over these tables. After the repair, the same probe reads the default row, reads a legacy name-spelled row, and `status == ConsentStatus.PENDING` matches 2 of 2. CORRECTION (NR-086): the statement that the trust routes are 'registered and served over these tables' implied those writes worked. They do not. Every proof above used Core select() and raw SQL, which never trigger SQLAlchemy's table sorting; a real Session + model instance + flush raises NoReferencedTableError on four of the six trust tables, because their foreign keys target another MetaData. The enum repair is still correct and still necessary — it fixes reads and the server_default, proven by reading a real row back as <ConsentStatus.GRANTED: 'granted'> — but the trust write path remains broken for a different reason, recorded as NR-086.

THE AUDIT-ACTOR QUESTION WAS FRAMED WRONG, and the repository answers the right one. Measured across every physical table, created_by is: INTEGER on 144 tables, including lab_users itself and blood_bank_transfusions — the one blood-bank table that agrees with the majority rather than with its siblings; String(26) WITH A REAL FOREIGN KEY on 7 niam tables (six to niam_accounts.id, niam_cert_api_keys to niam_persons.id); and character varying with NO foreign key on 13 tables — 8 blood_bank, 3 ems, national_search_saved_searches and niam_policies. So 'integer lab_users.id OR opaque string' is a false choice. BOTH are legitimate, because two identity domains exist by design: the clinical platform keys actors on integer lab_users.id, and NIAM keys them on ULID niam_accounts.id — with referential integrity to prove it. The 13 no-FK varchar columns are neither; they hold a stringified lab_users.id under no constraint. app/ems/application/service.py:213 writes created_by=str(self.actor_user_id or ""), so an absent actor is stored as an EMPTY STRING rather than NULL — which defeats NULL semantics, cannot satisfy any future foreign key, and leaves an audit row whose actor is ''.
findings.affected_users: None today. The exposure is to the next person who writes a filter.
findings.clinical_impact: None measured. The blood-bank write path works because the route passes a string.
findings.security_impact: oauth2_tokens.is_revoked is the column deciding whether a token has been revoked; a check written as `is_revoked == 1` raises rather than answering wrongly, so it fails closed, but it is one keystroke from an outage in the revocation path. For the trust group the exposure was consent and data-sovereignty records: trust_consent_records.status and trust_sovereignty_rules.sovereignty_level both had a server_default their mapper could not read.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The trust group could not corrupt a value, but it could make one unreadable and could silently undercount a filtered query — the more dangerous of the two. Repaired. The remaining ten are comparison-time hazards with no current wrong answer.
findings.operational_impact: None today.
findings.legal_impact: trust_consent_records.status and trust_sovereignty_rules.sovereignty_level are consent and data-residency records.
intersections: NR-021 (blood bank)
findings.contradictions: Six of seven sibling audit tables disagree with the mixin they share; the seventh agrees. Nothing documents which is intended.
findings.recommended_fix:
Group 3 applied: app/trust/models.py::_enum declares native_enum=False (compiling to the VARCHAR the column actually is) plus values_callable (persisting and reading the value the migrations already default to), and migration 20260915_0003 brings any row written in the name spelling across. Groups 1-2 still need a decision rather than a patch: is the audit actor an integer lab_users.id or an opaque string, and should the four Integer-over-boolean mappers become Boolean.

Groups 1-2, resolved in shape and not yet applied. Leave the 7 niam String(26) columns exactly as they are — they are FK-constrained to a ULID-keyed identity domain and are correct. Convert the 13 no-FK varchar created_by columns to INTEGER with a foreign key to lab_users.id, which is what their callers already pass, and replace the empty-string sentinel with NULL in the same change because '' cannot satisfy a foreign key. The six blood-bank mapper conflicts pinned by this finding are a subset of those 13 and stop being conflicts once the columns are integers.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: The enum repair is mapper-side plus a corrective UPDATE bounded to the exact enum names. Nothing is dropped, renamed, retyped or truncated, and a value that is neither a name nor a value is left exactly as it is rather than coerced — it is then reported by the guard instead of being silently rewritten. Reversible: downgrade performs the inverse mapping, bounded the same way.
findings.verification_method: Two layers in the migration CI job. test_mapped_tables_are_readable.py ratchets the type-conflict ledger (the nine are removed, so reverting reintroduces them as undeclared conflicts). test_enum_defaults_are_readable.py asserts the invariant directly and generally: the database has no native enum types, every enum mapper compiles to VARCHAR, and every enum column's own server_default is readable by its mapper — which also covers the 33 enum columns on tables still in NR-083's unreadable ledger, so radiology and NHDW cannot reintroduce the split. Two negative proofs: reverting to bare Enum fails both files; keeping native_enum=False but dropping values_callable passes the type check and still fails default-readability, proving the two halves are independently guarded.
findings.acceptance_criteria: DECLARED_TYPE_CONFLICTS is empty and DECLARED_UNREADABLE_DEFAULTS stays empty, with each remaining group resolved by an explicit decision.
findings.regression_risk: Low. The enum change is mapper-side; the migration is corrective, bounded and reversible; round trip executed. A deployment holding values outside the enum keeps them and is reported rather than rewritten.
findings.owner: Blood bank + identity + trust platform owners
findings.blocker: Reduced from an open identity question to a bounded migration on 13 columns. It stays protected work: it converts a column type on tables that may hold rows, so the empty-string rows must be resolved first and the migration must refuse rather than cast.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — inserts, reads, filtered counts and enum result-processing run against PostgreSQL 16 at migration head, before and after the repair

findings.category: Persistence correctness / Metadata topology / Measurement blind spot
findings.domain: platform-wide ORM write path; live instance in app/trust
findings.status: MEASURED AND GUARDED — 76 tables pinned and ratcheted; the topology repair that empties it is NR-078
findings.title: 76 mapped tables cannot be written through the ORM at all: their foreign keys target another MetaData, so every INSERT and UPDATE raises before emitting SQL
findings.description: SQLAlchemy resolves every ForeignKey target while sorting a mapper's tables during flush. A target in a different MetaData cannot be found, so the write raises NoReferencedTableError before any SQL is emitted. Reads are unaffected, which is exactly why this hides: SELECT never sorts tables, so the table looks healthy to the readability guard (NR-083), to every migration check, and to any route that only lists. Asking which mappers resolve every target inside their own MetaData gives 76 tables carrying 310 unresolvable foreign keys: CareContinuumBase 45, EHRBase 16, DataPlatformBase 9, TrustBase 4, IdentityBase 2.
findings.root_cause: The same declarative-base topology NR-078 documents. NR-078 measured 310 cross-base foreign keys across 76 tables and recorded them as a TOPOLOGY problem — the thing that stops alembic autogenerate running. They are also 76 tables no ORM write can reach, and that consequence had not been stated. NR-075 recorded one instance (niam_citizen_relationships) as a runtime write failure without connecting it to the population.
findings.evidence: Executed: Session + real model instance + flush against PostgreSQL 16 at head. session.add(ConsentRecord(...)); session.flush() -> NoReferencedTableError: Foreign key associated with column 'trust_consent_records.guardian_id' could not find table 'lab_users'. The ORM UPDATE path fails identically: loading an existing row succeeds and returns <ConsentStatus.GRANTED: 'granted'>, then mutating and flushing raises. Operation matrix over the trust base: trust_consent_records, trust_service_logs, trust_compliance_checks and trust_compliance_evidence all give ORM SELECT OK / ORM INSERT NoReferencedTableError; trust_sovereignty_rules, which carries no cross-base FK, gives OK / OK. Platform-wide count 76 tables / 310 FKs is independently equal to NR-078's separately measured cross-base FK population — two derivations, one by Alembic topology and one by asking each mapper to resolve its own targets, agreeing exactly.
findings.affected_users: Any actor calling a write endpoint backed by one of the 76 tables.
findings.clinical_impact: The live instance is the trust platform: app/trust/routes.py serves 13 registered paths of which SIX are writes — POST /api/v1/trust/consent, /consent/{id}/withdraw, /sign, /timestamp, /compliance/check, /compliance/evidence. All six land on the four trust tables carrying a cross-base FK, and all six fail. Consent capture and consent withdrawal are among them. The wider 76 include the care-continuum and EHR bases.
