findings.security_impact: Consent withdrawal cannot be recorded. A platform that cannot persist a withdrawal has no mechanism to honour it, and the failure is a 500 rather than a refusal, so nothing downstream learns the withdrawal was not stored.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No corruption: the write raises before SQL is emitted, so nothing partial is persisted. The integrity risk is the absence of records that callers believe they created.
findings.operational_impact: Six registered trust endpoints return 500 on every call; the same holds for any write endpoint backed by the other 72 tables.
findings.legal_impact: Consent records and their withdrawal are a legal control under any health-data regime.
findings.contradictions: My own NR-085 commit message stated that thirteen trust routes are 'registered and served over these tables, including consent creation and withdrawal', which implied they worked. They do not, and never have. Every NR-085 proof used Core select() and raw SQL, which never trigger table sorting. Corrected here rather than left standing.
findings.recommended_fix: This is NR-078's repair, not a separate one. Option A (one shared MetaData) resolves all 310 at once, and NR-078 has already measured that NOT ONE of these 76 tables carries a relationship(), so no ORM navigation is lost either way. The alternative — replacing each cross-base ForeignKey with the plain column it should be — is equally available and equally safe for the same reason. Neither may be applied before the NR-080 drift is reconciled, because Option A also makes autogenerate propose dropping patients.national_id.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None that is safe today, and that is the finding rather than a gap in it. The increment applied is measurement: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_writable.py pins the 76 with their exact FK counts and ratchets both ends, so no new table can join them unnoticed and the ledger cannot be emptied by deleting mappers.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_mapped_tables_are_writable.py in the unit CI job. The invariant is static and needs no database — the question is whether a mapper's declared targets exist in its own metadata, answerable from the registry alone. Five tests: the probe walked the registry (floor 700 of a measured 716); no undeclared table is unwritable; no ledger entry has been repaired without being removed; the per-table FK counts stay exact; and the writable population never shrinks (floor 630 of a measured 640). Three negative proofs, sources restored byte-identical — including adding a cross-base ForeignKey to trust_sovereignty_rules, which is currently writable, and watching it be caught.
findings.acceptance_criteria: DECLARED_UNWRITABLE is empty and MINIMUM_WRITABLE has risen to the full mapped population.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change — measurement only.
findings.blocker: NR-078's topology change, which is itself blocked on the NR-080 drift reconciliation.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — real Session, real model instance, real flush against PostgreSQL 16 at migration head; plus a static registry walk cross-checked against NR-078's independent count

findings.category: Parallel write authority / Dead code disposition / Latent security defect
findings.status: DISPOSITION ESTABLISHED — RETIRE is safe and ACTIVATE-AS-IS is unsafe; both proved by execution. Retirement itself is the user's call.
findings.title: app/reference is a second, raw-SQL write authority over the three core clinical tables; it is unmounted and schema-incompatible, and activating it as written would store plaintext national IDs
findings.description: app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py issues raw INSERT and SELECT statements against patients, lab_orders and lab_results — the three most sensitive tables on the platform — through app.database.get_db, i.e. the production database, not a fixture or a separate store. It is a complete parallel persistence stack (domain models, services, repositories, three routers) that duplicates the canonical one. NR-081 asked whether it should be activated or retired. Both halves are now answered by execution rather than by route count, which §21 explicitly forbids relying on. It cannot work: every one of its statements names columns the physical schema does not have. And it must not be made to work as written: it writes a raw national ID into patients.national_id with no hashing and no encryption, which the canonical path does not do.
findings.root_cause: The module was written against a different schema generation from the one the migrations actually built — the same Generation-A/Generation-B split as NR-080 and NR-082, but expressed in raw SQL instead of ORM mappers. Because it was never mounted, nothing ever executed a statement, so the divergence was never observed. Its national-ID handling predates the HMAC scheme in app/routes/register.py and was never brought forward.
evidence: REACHABILITY: no include_router for app.reference anywhere in backend/app. Outside its own package it is referenced only by 4 test files and reports/PHASE_10_BACKEND_ENDPOINT_INVENTORY.md (which marks its 7 endpoints IMPLEMENTED_SOURCE but UNVERIFIED). The two apparent production hits (app/national/services/__init__.py, app/national/api/routes/__init__.py) are a different 'reference' — national reference data — and are false positives. No importlib/__import__ plugin machinery in backend/app could load it dynamically: the only such calls are __import__('datetime') and __import__('uuid'). 8 route decorators are declared across the three routers and 0 are served.

TARGET DATABASE: app/reference/infrastructure/dependencies.py:6 — 'from app.database import get_db', used at lines 23, 31 and 44. This is the production session, so the 'it points at some other database' explanation is ruled out.

EXECUTED against PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, each in its own rolled-back transaction: repositories.py:56 INSERT INTO patients -> ERROR: column "name" of relation "patients" does not exist; repositories.py:211 INSERT INTO lab_orders -> ERROR: column "test_type" of relation "lab_orders" does not exist; repositories.py:314 INSERT INTO lab_results -> ERROR: column "analyte" of relation "lab_results" does not exist.

FULL MAGNITUDE (information_schema, not first-error): patients 4 of 9 named columns absent (name, date_of_birth, address, updated_at — physical is full_name and birth_date, and there is no address or updated_at column at all); lab_orders 5 of 9 absent (test_type, priority, notes, updated_at, performed_by); lab_results 9 of 13 absent (analyte, min_value, max_value, min_critical, max_critical, is_critical, flagged, notes, performed_by). So only 4 of 9, 4 of 9 and 4 of 13 columns respectively exist. This is a different schema generation, not a typo.

READS FAIL IDENTICALLY: the SELECTs at lines 95, 169, 242, 271, 353, 369 and 402 name the same absent columns (name, test_type, analyte), so the module is dead in both directions. This matters because NR-086 established that raw SQL BYPASSES the NoReferencedTableError barrier that stops ORM writes — so schema incompatibility, not that barrier, is what makes this module inert.
NOT-NULL columns with no default that the statements never supply, so even a column-rename fix would still fail: patients.full_name, lab_results.test_name, lab_results.token.

LATENT SECURITY DEFECT: repositories.py:83 binds 'national_id': patient.national_id straight into patients.national_id. patients has no triggers and national_id has no column default, so there is no database-level protection; encryption is application-level (shared.security.encryption.encrypt_national_id, used by app/citizen_platform/identity.py). The canonical path instead HMAC-SHA256s the value with NID_HMAC_KEY into national_id_hash (app/routes/register.py:337-358), and app/models/patient.py does not map national_id at all. A naive activation that fixed only the column names would therefore write plaintext national IDs, violating CLAUDE.md Security Invariant 8.

CANONICAL OWNERSHIP (unambiguous, single owner each): patients, lab_orders and lab_results are all in Base.metadata and no other registered metadata object, verified against the live target_metadata registry.

MIGRATION OWNERSHIP: all three tables are created by migrations/versions/20250322_0000_create_base_schema.py, the immutable bootstrap snapshot (lab_orders is further altered by 20250323_0004_core_enforcement.py). app/reference owns no migration and has never owned one.

PRIOR DECISION ALREADY IN THE REPOSITORY: backend/tests/test_side_door_hardening.py:81-87 asserts that app/reference/routes/patients.py, orders.py and results.py each contain require_permission("system:admin"). The routers were hardened in place against accidental activation rather than retired, so a decision was taken here before and stopped short of removal.
findings.affected_users: None today — nothing is served. Every patient in a lab, if the module were activated as written.
findings.clinical_impact: None today. If activated, a second write path to lab_orders and lab_results that does not share the canonical order state machine (app/domain/order_state.py) or the LabResult optimistic lock, so clinical state could be advanced without the transitions the canonical path enforces.
findings.security_impact: Latent and specific: plaintext national IDs in patients.national_id, bypassing the NID_HMAC_KEY scheme. Also no audit-log write on any of its three save() paths, so mutations through it would be invisible to the hash chain.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None today. If activated: a parallel writer with no optimistic-lock check and no audit row, over the three tables that carry all patient data.
findings.operational_impact: None today. 8 declared routes that cannot be reached and would 500 if they could.
findings.legal_impact: Plaintext national-ID storage would be a data-protection exposure on Iraqi civil-registry identifiers, and unaudited clinical mutations would break the audit-trail guarantee.
intersections: NR-086 — raw SQL bypasses the NoReferencedTableError barrier, so this module is NOT protected by the thing that protects the ORM write paths; its inertness rests on schema mismatch alone.
NR-080 / NR-082 — same Generation-A vs Generation-B schema split, expressed in raw SQL here rather than in ORM mappers.
NR-076 — the same disposition shape: a persistence layer that cannot reach its tables. There the tables do not exist; here they exist and disagree.
contradictions: reports/PHASE_10_BACKEND_ENDPOINT_INVENTORY.md lists 7 /reference/* endpoints as IMPLEMENTED_SOURCE. None is served and none could answer if it were. The report's own UNVERIFIED marking on every other column is what keeps this from being a false claim.
test_side_door_hardening.py treats these three routers as sensitive live surface needing a system:admin guard, while no application code mounts them.
findings.recommended_fix: RETIRE app/reference in a single change that removes the package and its three routers together, and drops the three entries from test_side_door_hardening.py's parametrisation in the same commit. Retiring routers separately from their package is how a retired subsystem becomes reachable again (the NR-076 lesson). It is a product decision, not an engineering one, so it is not applied here.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Change nothing and leave all three barriers in place: not mounted, schema-incompatible, system:admin-guarded. This is the current state and it is safe. What is NOT safe, and is the reason this finding exists, is the one-commit 'fix the column names' change that an engineer reading these files would naturally reach for — that alone would produce an unaudited parallel writer storing plaintext national IDs.
findings.verification_method: Executed the three INSERT shapes verbatim against a PostgreSQL 16 database at migration head, each in a rolled-back transaction; cross-checked every named column against information_schema; queried pg_trigger and column_default for database-level national-ID protection; resolved canonical metadata ownership from the live target_metadata registry; swept the repository for any mount or dynamic-import activation path.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Either the package and its routers are removed together with the test parametrisation updated, or the decision to keep it dormant is recorded with the plaintext-national-ID hazard named, so the next reader does not activate it by fixing the column names.
findings.regression_risk: None for retirement — nothing imports it outside its own package and four test files.
findings.complexity: low (retirement); the hazard is in the tempting partial fix, not in the removal
findings.blocker: Product decision — retire the package or record the dormancy. Engineering evidence is complete.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — every claim above was produced by running something, not by reading.

findings.category: Tenant isolation / Raw-SQL blind spot / Latent cross-tenant read
findings.domain: app/national/search_platform, app/insurance — raw SQL over patients
findings.status: MEASURED AND GUARDED — 6 untenanted sites pinned, 1 of them already executable; the invariant is ratcheted on executability, not on count
findings.title: Six raw-SQL reads of patients carry no lab_id constraint — four in a registered package serving 14 paths — and what keeps them inert is a bare string and a wrong column name, not tenant isolation
findings.description: Security Invariant #1 requires every patient-data query to filter by lab_id. Every guard that checks it works from ORM metadata, and NR-081 established that none of them can see a table name inside a string literal. Asking the SQL directly: of 335 .execute() call sites in app/, eight read patients. Two constrain lab_id and are correct. Six do not, across app/national/search_platform (four) and app/insurance/services/coverage_engine.py (two). The search package IS registered and serves 14 paths; app/insurance serves none and nothing outside it imports it, so those two sites are NR-087's class rather than this one. None currently succeeds — but not one of them is stopped by anything to do with tenancy, and every barrier is the kind a developer removes while fixing something else.
findings.root_cause: The same Generation-A/Generation-B schema split as NR-080, NR-082 and NR-087, plus SQLAlchemy 2.0's rejection of bare strings. Because no statement has ever executed, nobody noticed that the tenant filter was missing as well as the column names. The search module is internally inconsistent — three call sites pass a bare string and a fourth is correctly wrapped in text() — which is itself evidence it was never run.
evidence: POPULATION: 335 `.execute(...)` call sites in backend/app; 8 carry SQL reading `patients`; 2 constrain lab_id (app/ai/agent_runtime.py:68, app/routes/stats.py:272) and are correct; 6 do not.
app/national/search_platform/application/interfaces.py contains ZERO occurrences of `lab_id`.
EXECUTED, the three bare-string sites: passing a raw Python str to execute() raises `ObjectNotExecutableError: Not an executable object` under SQLAlchemy 2.0 before any SQL is sent.

EXECUTED, get_facets (the fourth site, properly wrapped in text() and therefore executable): `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM patients WHERE to_tsvector('simple', name || ' ' || COALESCE(phone,'') || ' ' || COALESCE(national_id,'')) @@ to_tsquery('simple', :q)` -> `ProgrammingError: column "name" does not exist`. Substituting the column the table actually has: `full_name` -> EXECUTES, COUNT = 0. So ONE COLUMN RENAME separates GET /facets from a working cross-lab count whose predicate matches on national_id.

EXECUTED, the insurance sites: `SELECT date_of_birth FROM patients WHERE id = :pid` -> `UndefinedColumn` (the table has birth_date), but `SELECT gender FROM patients WHERE id = :pid` with text() -> EXECUTES. That one is VALID SQL keyed on a caller-supplied id with no lab_id filter, inert solely because of the bare string. The fix for ObjectNotExecutableError is to wrap it in text() — a one-token change — and that change alone makes it a live cross-lab read.

EXECUTED, the citizen branch of the search union: `SELECT id FROM national_citizens` -> `UndefinedTable: relation "national_citizens" does not exist` — the same table NR-064 established no migration creates.

The national_id predicate is a full-text index over a national identifier. patients.national_id has no trigger and no column default (NR-087), and the canonical mapper deliberately does not expose it — app/models/patient.py maps national_id_hash only.

REACHABILITY, measured by walking the STARTED application recursively (2102 served routes): app/national/search_platform serves 14 paths, registered at factory.py:712, with PostgresFullTextSearch imported by routes.py:10 and instantiated per request over the app session (routes.py:51); both guarded by require_permission("system:admin") at the router (routes.py:26) and in _get_service (routes.py:44). app/insurance serves ZERO paths: factory.py:541/605 registers app/routes/insurance.py, a DIFFERENT module of the same name, and nothing outside app/insurance imports the package (the one apparent hit, app/national/domain/__init__.py, is a third homonym, app.national.domain.insurance). Cross-checks from the same walk: task_engine 29 + workflow_runtime 22 = 51 (NR-076 confirmed), app/reference 0 (NR-087 confirmed).

MEASUREMENT CORRECTION, recorded because the wrong number was published first. The original NR-088 write-up said both packages were registered. That came from grepping factory.py for 'insurance' and reading the hit as this package; it is a different module. A second probe then reported ZERO served paths for every package, which was also wrong: FastAPI stores an included router as an opaque _IncludedRouter, so one pass over app.routes sees 123 entries against a served surface of 2102. tests/orm_resolution.py::every_route already recurses for exactly this reason. Only the third measurement is recorded here.
findings.affected_users: None today — no statement succeeds. Every patient in every lab, if any barrier is removed without a tenant filter being added.
findings.clinical_impact: None today. GET /facets, /search and /suggest return 500.
findings.security_impact: Latent cross-tenant disclosure (Security Invariant #1) on a registered router serving 14 paths, plus a full-text match over a national identifier. The insurance age/gender checks are keyed on a caller-supplied patient_id with no tenant constraint, which is IDOR-shaped once executable — though that package is currently unreachable.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — all six sites are reads.
findings.operational_impact: 14 search routes that 500. The insurance coverage rules are unreachable.
findings.legal_impact: A searchable plaintext national identifier would be a data-protection exposure on Iraqi civil-registry identifiers.
intersections: NR-081 — this is exactly the blind spot NR-081 measured: no ORM-metadata guard can see a table name inside a string literal, so tenant isolation went unchecked here.
NR-087 — same class and same Generation split; there the module is unmounted, here both packages are registered.
NR-082 — same hazard shape: repairing for functionality without restoring lab_id turns a dead endpoint into a cross-tenant one.
NR-064 — the national_citizens branch targets the table NR-064 established no migration creates.

NR-087 — app/insurance is a third instance of that class: an unreachable package whose raw SQL over patients is schema-incompatible. Its two sites are ledgered here because the SQL is the same hazard, but its disposition belongs with NR-087's.
contradictions: migrations/env.py:186-189 records app.national.task_engine as 'RETIRE: 15 tables, none physical, no reachable operation'. task_engine alone serves 29 paths and workflow_runtime a further 22. That half of the note is false, as NR-076 recorded. The SAME NOTE IS CORRECT about app.insurance ('DEFER ... no reachable operation'): it serves zero. An earlier version of this finding claimed both halves were wrong; that claim was itself wrong and is corrected here.

app/routes/compliance.py:103 and :780 publish `national_id_storage: "Hashed with HMAC-SHA256 - not reversible"` and `PASS`, while app/national/search_platform builds a full-text index over a plaintext patients.national_id column.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the disposition of app/national/search_platform first — it is the NR-087 question again, for a package that IS registered. If it is to work, the mappers/SQL must be rewritten from the physical schema WITH lab_id restored and enforced, the national_id term removed from the full-text expression (search a hash, never the identifier), and the national_citizens branch resolved against a table that exists. If it is to be retired, the 14 routes go in the same change. app/insurance is unreachable and its disposition is NR-087's question, not this one; if it is ever activated, both coverage checks need the tenant filter and date_of_birth corrected to birth_date in that same change.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Change nothing and leave the barriers in place; they hold today. The hazard is the partial fix: wrapping a bare string in text() to clear ObjectNotExecutableError, or renaming name to full_name to clear UndefinedColumn, without adding lab_id. The guard makes exactly that fail.
findings.verification_method: AST scan over every .execute() call site in backend/app resolving literal, variable-bound and text()-wrapped SQL; each classified site then executed against PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, both as written and after the one-line repair a developer would make.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Either every raw-SQL read of patients constrains lab_id, or the packages are retired with their routes. The ledger must reach zero by tenant filters being added, not by entries being declared.
findings.regression_risk: None — the guard is static and no runtime code changed.
findings.owner: Platform security + national search / insurance product owners
findings.complexity: low to guard; the repair is a product disposition
findings.blocker: Product disposition for app/national/search_platform and app/insurance. The guard is applied now and is not blocked.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — every barrier and every removal of a barrier was run against PostgreSQL.

findings.category: Declarative mixin never mixed in / Live service failure / Latent hard delete
findings.status: TRUST HALF FIXED AND VERIFIED; governance half LATENT and guarded at zero callers
findings.title: A soft-delete mixin declared and never mixed in, in two domains — five served trust routes raised AttributeError, and governance's soft delete silently falls through to a hard DELETE for 38 of 61 models
findings.description: app/trust/base.py defines TrustSoftDeleteMixin with is_deleted, deleted_at, soft_delete(), restore() and an is_active property — and TrustBaseEntity(TrustTimestampMixin, TrustBase) does not list it. Six service methods filter on it regardless, so they raised AttributeError while BUILDING the query, before SQLAlchemy emitted anything and before any schema guard could look. app/governance/base.py has the identical mistake with GovernanceSoftDeleteMixin, and there the failure mode is worse in kind though currently unreachable: GovernanceRepository.delete falls through is_deleted -> is_active -> a hard self._db.delete(entity), with soft defaulting to True.
findings.root_cause: A mixin is only a mixin if something inherits it. Nothing in the ORM, the schema guards or the type checker objects to a Column-carrying class that no mapped class lists as a base, and the attribute error surfaces only when a query touches it. Both domains wrote the mixin, matched it to the physical schema, and never attached it.
evidence: EXECUTED: TrustBaseEntity.__bases__ == ['TrustTimestampMixin', 'Base']; TrustSoftDeleteMixin in ConsentRecord.__mro__ is False; ConsentRecord.is_deleted and .deleted_at both raise AttributeError.

EXECUTED against PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003 with a real Session, BEFORE the fix: ConsentService.get_patient_consents(1) -> AttributeError: type object 'ConsentRecord' has no attribute 'is_deleted'; SovereigntyService.get_all_rules() -> the same for 'SovereigntyRule'.
Six call sites: app/trust/services.py lines 88, 105, 116, 136, 157, 223, over ConsentRecord, SovereigntyRule and TrustServiceLog.
Five served routes call them: app/trust/routes.py verify_consent (113), get_patient_consents (124), withdraw_consent (147), get_all_rules (172), verify_document_integrity (256).

PHYSICAL: all six trust_* tables carry is_deleted and deleted_at as `timestamp with time zone`, nullable, no default (migration 20260716_0013) — exactly what the mixin declares. The mixin was written to match the schema and simply never attached, so the repair needed no migration.
EXECUTED after the fix: the same two service calls return [] against real PostgreSQL.

SECOND INSTRUMENT: NR-080's column-drop classification independently proposed dropping exactly those twelve trust columns. Mixing the mixin in took the total DropColumnOp from 377 to 365 — the first reduction in that budget rather than a re-measurement of it.

GOVERNANCE, measured: 38 of the 61 GovernanceBase mapped classes carry neither is_deleted nor is_active, so delete(entity) with its default soft=True reaches self._db.delete(entity). Among them gov_national_audit_events, gov_ai_audit_events, gov_health_number_audit, gov_merge_proposals, gov_merged_identities, gov_professional_licenses, gov_emergency_admin.

GOVERNANCE REACHABILITY: zero callers. Nothing in app/ calls a governance repository delete; the governance router IS registered (factory.py:683) and exposes no delete; the one nearby hit, app/document_intelligence, deletes a different model by raw query. Latent, not live.
findings.affected_users: Any caller of the five trust routes, until the fix. None for the governance half.
findings.clinical_impact: Consent verification and consent withdrawal returned 500 rather than an answer.
findings.security_impact: Latent audit-trail destruction in governance: a request to soft-delete an audit row performs a hard DELETE. CLAUDE.md forbids reducing audit-log coverage, and three audit tables are in the affected set.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None realised — the governance path has no caller. The hazard is activation.
findings.operational_impact: Five trust routes raised before the fix; they now execute SQL.
findings.legal_impact: Consent withdrawal failing is a data-protection matter; that path is NR-086's to finish.
intersections: NR-086 — this EXTENDS rather than corrects it. NR-086 recorded trust_sovereignty_rules as ORM SELECT OK / ORM INSERT OK and said reads are unaffected; both statements are accurate about ORM TABLE operations. This is an earlier barrier in the service layer, so the one healthy trust table was still unreachable through SovereigntyService. The trust write paths remain blocked by NR-086 and this fix does not change that.
NR-080 — the twelve trust columns were 12 of its 377 proposed drops; the fix removed them.
findings.recommended_fix: Trust: DONE — TrustBaseEntity now lists TrustSoftDeleteMixin. No migration; the columns already exist with matching types. Governance: give the 38 models a soft-delete flag, or make delete() refuse rather than fall through, BEFORE any delete endpoint is wired. The guard holds the caller count at zero until then.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: The one-line mixin attachment, which is what was applied.
findings.verification_method: Attribute access and real service calls executed against PostgreSQL 16 at migration head, before and after; physical column types read from information_schema; governance model flags read from GovernanceBase.registry.mappers; reachability by repository-wide caller search.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every attribute a trust service filters on exists, and no governance delete has a caller.
findings.regression_risk: Low — two nullable columns that already exist physically become mapped; no write path changes.
findings.complexity: trivial to fix, easy to miss
findings.blocker: Governance half needs a product decision: add flags to 38 models, or make delete() fail closed.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the defect and the repair were both run against real PostgreSQL.

findings.title: The government compliance report attested to tenant isolation it was breaking in the same response, and described a 16-role access model as 4 roles
findings.category: False compliance attestation / Cross-tenant read / Stale hard-coded verdict
findings.status: FIXED AND VERIFIED — both leaks closed and proved by execution; the residual unmeasurable claims are pinned at 23 and ratcheted
findings.blocker: None for the fixed half. The 23 remaining hard-coded verdicts name controls in nginx, the TLS terminator and the deployment, which this process cannot observe; whether to measure, qualify or remove them from an auditor's checklist is a product decision.
findings.complexity: trivial to fix, serious in consequence
findings.regression_risk: Low — two COUNT(*) values become lab-scoped and one report string becomes derived. No key is added to or removed from any response; `scope` is additive.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — both the defect and the repair were run against real PostgreSQL with two labs of fixture data.
findings.verification_method: Fixture rows for two labs inserted into audit_logs on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003 inside a transaction, the endpoints' own SQL extracted from the module by AST and executed verbatim, then rolled back. The probe database holds zero rows before and after.
findings.affected_users: Any lab admin or master_admin calling /compliance/security-report or /compliance/system-status — both endpoints are registered in app/factory.py and served.
findings.description:
/compliance/security-report and /compliance/system-status describe themselves as reports for government and ISO 27001 auditors. Three separate ways of being untrue were found in them.

(1) CROSS-TENANT READ, contradicted in the same response. security_report printed 'multi_tenant': 'PASS - per-lab data isolation enforced at query level' two keys above failed_logins_24h, which ran SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit_logs WHERE action='login_failed' AND created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours' with no lab_id. system_status carried a second copy of the same query, which a grep for the triple-quoted form missed and the AST guard caught on its first run. audit_logs.lab_id exists and carries its own index (ix_audit_logs_lab_id), so the omission was not a schema limitation.

(2) A STALE LITERAL. 'rbac': 'PASS - 4 roles: master_admin, admin, staff, technician' was a string constant. ROLE_PERMISSIONS carries 16. The twelve undisclosed roles include ministry_admin and province_admin, which are not lab-scoped at all, and the entire six-role financial separation-of-duties set (cashier, finance_operator, finance_controller, finance_auditor, reconciler, refund_reviewer). An auditor was told the access-control model was a quarter of its real size.

(3) A TRUE MEASUREMENT UNDER A FALSE LABEL. /compliance/audit-integrity verifies the hash chain platform-wide, which is correct and unavoidable — audit_service._get_last_chain_hash selects the newest chain_hash across all labs, so every lab's entries interleave in one id-ordered sequence and a per-lab chain would not verify. The endpoint then set result['lab_id'] = current_user.lab_id onto that result, presenting a platform-wide entries_checked as the caller's own.
findings.root_cause: The report asserts rather than measures. 23 of its verdicts are string literals that no code computes, so nothing fails when the system they describe changes — nobody edits a literal when they add a role, and nothing links the isolation claim to the queries beneath it. The two measured values it does carry (the chain result and the active-user count) lend their credibility to the literals beside them.
findings.security_impact: A lab admin was served a count of every lab's failed logins, from two separate endpoints. The disclosure is aggregate rather than row-level, but it is a cross-tenant read that CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1 forbids, in the endpoint that certifies Invariant #1 is held.
findings.legal_impact: The stated audience is government and ISO 27001 auditors. A report that understates the access-control model by twelve roles, including two that cross lab boundaries and the whole financial separation-of-duties set, misinforms a regulator about the controls under review.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — every change is to a read path. No write, schema or migration is touched.
findings.clinical_impact: None — no clinical data is read or written by these endpoints.
findings.operational_impact: Two COUNT(*) values fall to the caller's own lab, so dashboards reading them will show smaller numbers that are now correct.
findings.scalability_impact: Marginally positive — both counts now hit ix_audit_logs_lab_id instead of scanning every lab's rows.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Add AND lab_id = :lab_id to both queries; derive the rbac line from ROLE_PERMISSIONS; add an additive 'scope' key to the chain result rather than removing 'lab_id'.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied. The remaining 23 unmeasurable verdicts need a product decision, not an engineering one.
acceptance_criteria: Both failed-login counts return only the caller's lab, proved against PostgreSQL with two labs of fixture data.
No 'rbac' verdict in the module is a string literal.
/compliance/audit-integrity records that the chain result is platform-wide.
The hard-coded verdict count does not rise above 23.
evidence: EXECUTED against PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, three lab-1 and five lab-2 failed logins inserted in a transaction: the shipped security_report query returned 8 to a lab-1 caller; the same query with lab_id returned 3. Five of the eight rows belonged to lab 2.

EXECUTED after the fix, both endpoints' SQL extracted from the module by AST and run verbatim: security_report and system_status each return 3 as lab 1 and 5 as lab 2. Probe database rows before and after: 0.

MEASURED: app.security.rbac.ROLE_PERMISSIONS has 16 entries — admin, cashier, citizen, doctor, finance_auditor, finance_controller, finance_operator, lab_admin, lab_staff, master_admin, ministry_admin, province_admin, reconciler, refund_reviewer, staff, technician. The report named 4.

READ from the database: audit_logs.lab_id exists, is indexed as ix_audit_logs_lab_id, and the table carries trg_audit_logs_no_update and trg_audit_logs_no_delete — so the report's separate immutability claim is one of the true ones.

STATIC: audit_service._get_last_chain_hash runs SELECT chain_hash FROM audit_logs ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1 with no lab filter, and _compute_chain_hash's record omits lab_id entirely. The chain is global by construction, and tenant attribution is not covered by it.
AST: 23 hard-coded PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL verdicts remain across the two reports (20 in security_report, 5 in system_status, less the 2 rbac literals now derived).

Negative proof, all four guards, source restored byte-identical (md5 verified): removing the lab_id clause, restoring the rbac literal, dropping the scope key and adding one more PASS verdict each fire their own assertion.
Gate: unit 434 -> 438 passed, 4 deselected, by exactly the four tests added.
intersections: NR-088 — the same class of defect (a raw-SQL read missing lab_id) in a different table. NR-088's guard watches app-wide reads of `patients` only, so neither of these two audit_logs sites was in its scope. The two guards now cover two tables; nothing covers the rest.
NR-062 — audit coverage. This finding is about reading audit_logs, not writing them, and does not change the coverage measurement.

The three audit_logs reads in this one router use three different tenant-scoping strategies: audit_summary scopes by LabUser.id membership, security_report now scopes by lab_id, and verify_audit_chain is deliberately unscoped. There is no canonical way to scope an audit query, which is why each site invented one.
contradictions: routes/compliance.py printed 'per-lab data isolation enforced at query level' as PASS while two of its own queries read every lab's audit rows.

findings.title: HTTP idempotency is implemented four times; the dormant DB-backed one leaks a cached response across tenants, and POST /samples has no replay protection at all
findings.category: Duplicate source of truth / Latent cross-tenant disclosure / Coverage gap on a clinical write
findings.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — §32-A answered and implemented (POST /samples and POST /batch/orders now claim idempotency); §32-B answered REWRITE, not retire, and the rewrite is blocked on a schema decision. The dormant module remains pinned at zero application wirings.
findings.blocker: §32-B: retirement is NOT available. §26 requires proving no test dependency before retiring, and tests/test_idempotency.py has eleven tests against this module. Rewriting it is the right disposition because NR-095 shows the cache-backed store is correct only when Redis is present, but the rewrite needs idempotency_keys' primary key widened from (key) to (lab_id, key) — a deliberate schema decision.
findings.complexity: the proof is small; the decisions behind it are not
findings.regression_risk: None from this change — no application code was modified. Guards only.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the dormant module's own three SQL statements, extracted by AST, run verbatim against PostgreSQL 16 with two labs.
findings.verification_method: Two labs and one shared idempotency key inserted on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003 inside a transaction, then rolled back; the module's SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE taken from the source by AST rather than retyped. Probe rows before and after: 0.
findings.affected_users: None today — the dormant module is reachable from nothing. Any lab, if it is ever wired as written.
findings.description:
app/core/idempotency.py is a FastAPI dependency whose docstring names four clinical write endpoints it is for (POST /api/orders, /api/results, /api/results/{id}/validate, /api/samples) and states as a rule: 'Keys are scoped per lab (prevents cross-lab replay attacks)'. Nothing imports it. idempotency_check is used as a Depends nowhere and purge_expired_keys is called by nothing, so the rule has never been exercised — which is the only reason the following are latent.

The rule is not implemented, and three defects compound.

(1) A CACHED RESPONSE CROSSES TENANTS. idempotency_keys has PRIMARY KEY (key) alone, so a key is globally unique, while cache() runs UPDATE idempotency_keys SET status_code, response_body WHERE key = :key with no lab_id. Executed: lab A claims a key and caches an order for its own patient; lab B presents the same key, its SELECT misses on lab_id so it is told the request is new, it proceeds, and its cache() overwrites lab A's row — which keeps lab_id = 901. Lab A then replays its own key and is served {'order_id': 222, 'patient': 'LAB-B PATIENT'}.

(2) A NULL-LAB ROW REPLAYS TO EVERY LAB. The lookup reads WHERE key = :key AND (lab_id = :lab_id OR lab_id IS NULL). lab_id comes from getattr(current_user, 'lab_id', None), so any principal without one — a citizen, ministry_admin, province_admin or service account — stores a row matching every lab's lookup. Executed: one such row was readable by lab 901 and lab 902 alike.

(3) THE RESERVATION DOES NOT RESERVE. The insert is ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING and rowcount is never read, so a key already held by another lab silently yields is_duplicate=False. Executed: rowcount 0, and the caller cannot tell.

Meanwhile a correct implementation is live. app/services/order_service.py::create_order keys its cache f'idempotency:order:{lab_id}:{idempotency_key}' — tenant in the key rather than in a filter, so two labs cannot name the same entry — fingerprints the clinical payload so a key cannot be reused for different content, and claims atomically with set_if_absent. app/routes/results.py:177 passes the Idempotency-Key header through to it, so POST /orders is genuinely protected.

COVERAGE, measured rather than assumed: POST /orders is protected by the live mechanism. POST /samples (app/routes/samples.py:48) has no idempotency of any kind. POST /orders/{id}/validate uses an If-Match ETag instead, which is a different and arguably sufficient control for a state transition. app/routes/batch.py:68 passes idempotency_key=None explicitly, so a retried bulk order creation duplicates every row in it.
findings.root_cause: Four independent idempotency mechanisms exist with no canonical one: the dormant DB-backed dependency, the live Redis-backed order path, app/integration/esb/idempotency.py for message dedup, and idempotency_key_hash blind-index columns on identity ORM models. Nothing names which is authoritative, so the dormant one kept a docstring asserting coverage that another mechanism actually provides, for only one of the four endpoints it claims.
findings.security_impact: Latent. If the dormant dependency is wired as written, a lab replaying its own idempotency key can be served another lab's cached response body — which for these endpoints contains order and result payloads, so patient data. No path reaches it today.
findings.clinical_impact: POST /samples is replayable: a client retry after a timeout creates a second sample record. The batch order path is replayable for every row it carries. CLAUDE.md exempts /results, /orders and /samples from concurrency shedding because patient-safety operations must never be shed; replay protection is the other half of that guarantee and is present on only one of them.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Duplicate samples and duplicate batch-created orders on retry. No corruption of existing rows.
findings.operational_impact: None from this change. idempotency_keys is physical with an FK to labs and an index on lab_id, but no ORM maps it — it is one of NR-030's ten DROP candidates, so it is currently written by nothing.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Leave the dormant module unwired. The guard fails if anyone imports it while the three defects remain.
findings.recommended_fix: Do not repair app/core/idempotency.py in place. Either retire it, or rewrite it on the live design — tenant in the key, payload fingerprint, atomic claim, rowcount checked — and make idempotency_keys' primary key (lab_id, key) rather than (key). Separately, decide whether POST /samples and the batch order path must require an Idempotency-Key.
acceptance_criteria: app/core/idempotency.py is imported by nothing while its three defects remain.
If a defect is repaired, the ledger pinning it is updated in the same change.
The live cache key keeps lab_id and the claim stays atomic.
evidence: EXECUTED on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, module SQL extracted by AST and run verbatim: lab A caches under key 'shared-key-0001'; lab B's lookup returns None; lab B's INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING returns rowcount 0; after lab B's UPDATE the row's lab_id is still 901; lab A's replay returns {'order_id': 222, 'patient': 'LAB-B PATIENT'}.
EXECUTED: a row inserted with lab_id NULL was returned by the module's own SELECT for lab 901 and for lab 902.

READ from the database: idempotency_keys PRIMARY KEY is btree (key) alone; lab_id is nullable, indexed as ix_idempotency_keys_lab_id, with FK idempotency_keys_lab_id_fkey to labs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE.
STATIC: no module in app/ imports app.core.idempotency. idempotency_check appears as a Depends nowhere; purge_expired_keys has no caller.

STATIC: app/routes/results.py:177 passes idempotency_key=request.headers.get('Idempotency-Key') into create_order. app/routes/samples.py:48 passes nothing. app/routes/batch.py:68 passes idempotency_key=None explicitly.

Negative proof, four guards, both sources restored byte-identical (md5 verified): importing the dependency into a route module, half-fixing the lookup, dropping lab_id from the live cache key and removing set_if_absent each fire their own assertion.
Gate: unit 438 -> 442 passed, 4 deselected, by exactly the four tests added.

§32-A ANSWERED — MANDATORY for both. POST /samples creates a physical specimen record with no natural uniqueness: samples.barcode is NOT NULL and UNIQUE but generate_barcode() mints SMP- + secrets.token_hex(6) per INSERT, so the constraint guarantees barcode uniqueness rather than request identity, and (order_id, sample_type) must not be unique because an order legitimately carries several tubes of the same type. POST /batch/orders passed idempotency_key=None explicitly for up to 50 orders. Both now claim through the canonical helper; the batch claims once for the whole request, since a retry must reproduce the same outcome including its per-item errors.

§32-B ANSWERED — REWRITE, not retire and not canonicalise-as-is. Retire is unavailable: eleven tests in tests/test_idempotency.py depend on the module, so §26's precondition fails. Canonicalise-as-is is unsafe: the three defects above are unchanged. Rewrite is correct because NR-095 shows the live cache-backed store degrades to per-worker without Redis, and PostgreSQL is the only store the application cannot run without.

EXTRACTED, not rewritten: the one correct implementation, inline in order_service.create_order, is now app/services/idempotency.py and is used by all three endpoints. Behaviour preservation proved differentially — the pre-refactor block and the helper were run over the same seven scenarios (no key, first use, retry, different payload, in-flight, retry while in flight, different lab) and produced IDENTICAL outcomes in every one.

FALSE GREEN FOUND in the module's own suite: test_same_key_different_lab_is_not_duplicate was documented as 'lab 2 cannot replay lab 1's response', a tenant-isolation guarantee. It exercises idempotency_check only, never cache(), which is the half that crosses tenants. The assertion is kept; the docstring now states what it covers and what it does not.
intersections: NR-030 / NR-080 — idempotency_keys is one of the ten physical tables no ORM maps, and one of the ten DropTableOp autogenerate proposes. It must not be dropped: it is the store a corrected implementation would need.
NR-087 — the same disposition. A dormant module whose natural repair would create a live unsafe path, so it is held unreachable rather than fixed in place.
NR-090 — both found a docstring asserting a security property the code beneath it did not implement.
contradictions: app/core/idempotency.py's docstring states 'Keys are scoped per lab (prevents cross-lab replay attacks)' while its UPDATE matches on key alone and its SELECT treats a NULL lab_id as a wildcard.
The same docstring lists POST /api/samples among the endpoints it supports; that endpoint has no idempotency of any kind.

findings.title: Two of three clinical agent tools read lab results with no tenant constraint, on a served endpoint whose arguments come from an external model — and all three are broken against the physical schema, which is the only thing that was containing it
findings.category: Latent cross-tenant clinical disclosure / AI-supplied arguments / ORM-schema mismatch
findings.status: TENANT CONSTRAINT FIXED AND GUARDED; the schema mismatch is deliberately NOT repaired — making a clinical AI surface functional is a product decision
findings.blocker: Whether POST /api/ai/v2/agents/execute's clinical tools should work at all is a clinical product decision. Repairing the column names activates an AI path over patient data and is not taken here.
findings.regression_risk: None observable — all three tools raised before the change and raise after it. The constraint only takes effect if the column names are ever corrected.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — all three tools' SQL run verbatim against PostgreSQL 16 with two labs, before and after, plus the counterfactual repair.
findings.verification_method: Two labs, two patients, one order and one result each, inserted on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003 inside a transaction and rolled back; each tool's SQL extracted from the module by AST rather than retyped. Probe rows before and after: 0.
findings.affected_users: None today — every tool raises. Any lab, if the column names are corrected without the tenant constraint.
findings.description:
POST /api/ai/v2/agents/execute is registered in app/factory.py and served. A caller submits a free-text task; AgentRuntime._plan_tools sends it to an external model (app.gateways.google_ai.generate_chat), json.loads the plan it returns, and execute_plan dispatches the tool and parameters that plan names — so the patient_id of a clinical read originates in a model's reading of user text.

The runtime is right about the boundary: execute_tool calls tool.fn(**kwargs, lab_id=context.lab_id, user_id=context.user_id), so the authenticated tenant is injected and the model cannot supply its own (a lab_id in its params raises TypeError for a repeated keyword). The tenant is the runtime's to decide, not the model's, which is the correct placement.

Two of the three clinical tools took that lab_id into **kwargs and never used it. _get_recent_results and _analyze_lab_pattern selected from lab_results JOIN lab_orders on lo.patient_id alone. _lookup_patient in the same file filtered (lab_id = :lab OR :lab IS NULL) — scoped, but fail-open if the tenant were absent.

None of it was reachable, and the reason is not a control. All three name columns the database does not have: patients has full_name not name, and lab_results has created_at not result_date. Executed, all three raise; each catches the exception and returns {'error': ...}, so callers get an error string and no data. The clinical agent-tool surface is non-functional, and that is what was containing it.

Which makes correcting the column names a trap, and that was executed too: with the names fixed and the same WHERE clause, a lab-901 session asking for patient 7002 (lab 902) received ['SECRET-LAB-B']. Adding lo.lab_id returns [] for that request and still returns ['SECRET-LAB-A'] for the session's own patient.
findings.root_cause: lab_results carries no lab_id of its own — it is tenanted transitively through lab_orders — so a developer writing a query against it has nothing local to filter on and has to know to constrain the join. _lookup_patient, over a table that does have lab_id, got it right; the two over lab_results did not.
findings.security_impact: Latent. Correcting two column names, with no other change, turns a served endpoint into a cross-tenant read of clinical lab results whose patient_id is chosen by an external model's interpretation of caller text. The tenant constraint is now in place, so that repair is safe whenever someone makes it.
findings.clinical_impact: The clinical agent tools return an error string for every call. No clinical AI assistance is actually being delivered by this surface.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — all three paths are reads.
findings.operational_impact: None observable; behaviour before and after the change is identical.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: constrain lo.lab_id on both lab_results queries and bind lab_id unconditionally in _lookup_patient, leaving the column names untouched.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide whether this AI surface should function. If yes, correct the column names — the tenant boundary is already enforced and guarded.
acceptance_criteria: No registered agent tool reads a tenant-owned table without a lab_id constraint.
No agent tool treats an absent tenant as a wildcard.
execute_tool keeps injecting context.lab_id, so the tenant never comes from the planning model.
If the schema mismatches are repaired, the ledger is updated in the same change.
evidence: EXECUTED on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003, tool SQL extracted by AST: lookup_patient RAISES 'column "name" does not exist'; get_recent_results and analyze_lab_pattern both RAISE 'column lr.result_date does not exist'. Each is caught and returned as {'error': ...}.

EXECUTED counterfactual: with result_date corrected to created_at and no tenant filter, a lab-901 session asking for patient 7002 (lab 902) received ['SECRET-LAB-B']. With AND lo.lab_id = :lab_id it received [], and ['SECRET-LAB-A'] for its own patient 7001.

READ from the database: lab_results has no lab_id column at all — order_id, test_type_id, test_name, value, value_text, unit, normal_range_low, normal_range_high, flag, token, token_hash, expires_at, created_at, clinical_engine_version, version. patients has full_name, not name.

STATIC: app/ai/agent_runtime.py:175 reads tool.fn(**kwargs, lab_id=context.lab_id, user_id=context.user_id) — the runtime injects the authenticated tenant into every tool call and the model cannot override it.
STATIC: 5 tools are registered; 3 touch tenant tables; before this change 1 of those 3 constrained lab_id. After, 3 of 3, with no fail-open wildcard.
AST: _plan_tools sends the caller's task to app.gateways.google_ai.generate_chat and json.loads the returned plan, whose params become the tool arguments.

Negative proof, four guards, source restored byte-identical (md5 verified): removing the constraint, restoring the wildcard, stopping the runtime injection and correcting the column names each fire their own assertion.
Gate: unit 442 -> 446 passed, 4 deselected, by exactly the four tests added.
intersections: NR-087 and NR-091 — the third instance this session of the same shape: a path held safe only by being broken, whose natural repair makes it unsafe. The containment in all three cases was accidental.

NR-088 / NR-090 — the same missing-lab_id class in raw SQL, in different modules. The platform-wide sweep that found this one measured 19 raw-SQL sites reading a lab_id-bearing table without lab_id, of which most are correct by design (the audit chain hash, a startup backfill, a janitor sweep) or already pinned.
NR-074 — an ORM naming columns the database lacks. Here the same mismatch is in raw SQL rather than a mapper, so no schema guard in this suite was watching it.
contradictions: app/routes/ai_platform.py serves these tools behind _require_doctor and passes lab_id=current_user.lab_id into run_session, so the route believes the call is tenant-scoped; two of the three tools then discarded it.

findings.title: POST /api/ai/v2/agents/execute accepted any session_id and resumed that conversation — reading another user's AI history into a prompt sent to an external model, and writing back into it
findings.category: Broken object-level authorization (IDOR) / Cross-tenant and cross-user read and write / External AI exposure
findings.status: FIXED AND GUARDED — the control the module already had, applied to the third endpoint that needed it
findings.blocker: None. Whether ConversationMemory.get_session should also constrain the tenant itself (defence in depth) is open; the route-layer check is the one the codebase already uses and is sufficient.
findings.complexity: one call; the reasoning is in what it reaches
findings.regression_risk: Low — a request with no session_id behaves exactly as before. A request naming a session the caller does not own now gets 404 instead of resuming it, which is the intent.
findings.evidence_strength: STATIC, traced end to end through the call graph and the SQL it reaches. No execution was needed: the missing call is a fact about the source, and what it guards is read directly from run_session and get_session.
findings.verification_method: AST over app/routes/ai_platform.py enumerating handlers that accept a session_id and the calls each makes; source trace of AgentRuntime.run_session -> ConversationMemory.get_session/get_history/add_message; three negative proofs with sources restored byte-identical.
findings.affected_users: Any doctor-role caller who knows another user's session id. Sessions are uuid4, so not guessable — but ids are returned by POST /sessions, travel in request bodies and logs, and run_session's own fallback id is f"agent-{time.time()}".
findings.description:
app/routes/ai_platform.py defines _assert_session_owner, whose docstring is 'Prevent cross-user and cross-lab access to AI conversation history'. It raises 404 unless the conversation's user_id AND lab_id both match the caller.

Three served endpoints take a session_id from the caller. POST /sessions/message and GET /sessions/{session_id} called it. POST /agents/execute did not, and AgentRequest.session_id is a plain optional string on the request body.

AgentRuntime.run_session treats that id as a resumable conversation: it calls memory_store.get_session(session_id), creates a new one only if that returns None, then add_message(session_id, 'user', task) and get_history(session_id, max_tokens=500), and passes the history into _plan_tools -- which sends it to app.gateways.google_ai.generate_chat. ConversationMemory.get_session runs SELECT id, lab_id, user_id, session_id, title, metadata FROM ai_conversations WHERE session_id = :sid with no tenant constraint, loads every message of that conversation, and caches it.

So naming another user's session made the endpoint read that conversation's history, include it in a prompt sent to an external model, and append the caller's task and the run's summary back into it — a cross-user and cross-tenant read AND write, plus exposure of another lab's conversation content to a third party.

Fixed by calling the module's own _assert_session_owner when body.session_id is supplied. A request without one still gets a fresh session.
findings.root_cause: The control existed and was correct; it was applied per-endpoint by hand, and one of the three endpoints that needed it was missed. Nothing enumerated which handlers accept a session_id, so nothing could notice the omission.
findings.security_impact: Live broken object-level authorization on a served endpoint. Mitigated only by session ids being uuid4 and the caller needing the doctor role — neither of which is an authorization control. CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1 requires tenant isolation on patient-data queries; AI conversation history about patients is within that spirit, and the module's own docstring already said so.
findings.legal_impact: Another lab's conversation content could be sent to an external AI provider, which §27 of the operating brief forbids by default.
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect: a doctor's agent session could be polluted with another user's conversation history, which becomes planning context for clinical tool selection.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The caller's task and the run summary were appended to another user's conversation, and persisted by add_message's INSERT via a subquery on ai_conversations.session_id.
findings.operational_impact: None — the no-session_id path is unchanged.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: call _assert_session_owner on body.session_id in execute_agent, exactly as the two sibling endpoints do.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied. Optionally also constrain ConversationMemory.get_session by lab_id for defence in depth — the route check must stay regardless, because it also compares user_id, which a tenant filter does not.
acceptance_criteria: Every handler accepting a caller-supplied session_id calls _assert_session_owner.
_assert_session_owner keeps comparing both user_id and lab_id.
If the underlying lookup becomes tenant-scoped, the reasoning recorded here is revisited.
evidence: STATIC: app/routes/ai_platform.py:48 defines _assert_session_owner comparing conversation.user_id != current_user.id or conversation.lab_id != current_user.lab_id. Before the fix it was called at two sites (add_message, get_session) and not in execute_agent.

STATIC: AgentRuntime.run_session calls get_session(session_id), then add_message(session_id, 'user', task) and get_history(session_id, 500), and passes that history to _plan_tools, which calls app.gateways.google_ai.generate_chat.

STATIC: ConversationMemory.get_session executes SELECT ... FROM ai_conversations WHERE session_id = :sid with no lab_id or user_id constraint, then loads all rows of ai_conversation_messages for that conversation and caches the result in self._sessions.
STATIC: create_session mints uuid.uuid4(); run_session's fallback for an absent id is f"agent-{time.time()}".

Negative proof, three guards, sources restored byte-identical (md5 verified): reverting to the pre-fix route file names execute_agent; removing the user_id half of the comparison fires the second; tenant-scoping the underlying lookup fires the third.

Detector self-audit: the third guard's first version was a substring check and did NOT fire on its own negative proof, because appending 'AND lab_id = :lab' leaves the prefix intact. It was rewritten to extract the statement by AST and inspect the whole WHERE clause, and then fired.
Gate: unit 446 -> 449 passed, 4 deselected, by exactly the three tests added.
intersections: NR-092 — the same endpoint, a different boundary. That finding was about the tenant of the clinical data a tool reads; this is about the tenant of the conversation the request resumes. Both were reachable through POST /agents/execute.
NR-090 — both are a control that exists and is applied to some call sites but not all.
contradictions: _assert_session_owner's docstring claims to 'prevent cross-user and cross-lab access to AI conversation history' while the endpoint that resumes a conversation did not call it.

findings.title: claims.idempotency_key was unique across the whole platform, so one lab's choice of key made that key permanently unusable for every other lab
findings.category: Tenant isolation (availability) / Idempotency scope / ORM-schema constraint drift
findings.status: FIXED AND VERIFIED — migration applied, round-trip executed, platform-wide invariant now guarded
findings.blocker: None. The migration is non-destructive and provably always-applicable; its downgrade is the narrowing direction and refuses rather than deleting another tenant's claims.
findings.complexity: one index; found only by census
findings.regression_risk: Very low. Widening a unique key rejects no row that was previously accepted. Both application read paths were already lab-scoped and are unchanged.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the collision, the fix, and the full migration round-trip were all run against real PostgreSQL.
findings.verification_method: Two labs and one shared key on PostgreSQL 16, before and after; alembic upgrade -> downgrade -1 -> upgrade round-trip; autogenerate drift re-measured to confirm the ORM and schema moved together.
findings.affected_users: Any lab whose client chose an idempotency key another lab had already used. The failure is a refused INSERT, not a disclosure.
findings.description:
A census of every column matching %idempotency% across the physical schema found twelve. Nine scope uniqueness by a tenant discriminator (lab_id, tenant_id, institution_id, subscription_id). claims did not: the model declared idempotency_key with unique=True, producing a global claims_idempotency_key_key, even though the table carries lab_id.

Both application read paths were already correct — services/claims_service.py::create_claim and insurance/api/claims.py::create_claim each filter lab_id alongside the key — so nothing was disclosed. What broke was the other tenant's ability to write. Executed on PostgreSQL 16 at head 20260915_0003:

    lab 901 creates a claim with key 'INV-2026-001'  -> OK
    lab 902's lab-scoped idempotency lookup finds     -> 0, so it proceeds
    lab 902's INSERT                                  -> REFUSED,
        duplicate key value violates unique constraint "claims_idempotency_key_key"

Idempotency keys are chosen by the client. Clients choose invoice numbers, counters and dates, which collide across tenants by construction, so this is not a rare edge.

Fixed by migration 20260916_0001, replacing the global constraint with uq_claims_lab_idempotency (lab_id, idempotency_key) — the convention the nine other tables already use.
findings.root_cause: unique=True on a column is the easiest thing to write and is correct only for a globally unique value. An idempotency key is namespaced by whoever chose it. Nothing enumerated the idempotency columns, so the one table that got it wrong looked exactly like the nine that got it right.
findings.security_impact: Tenant isolation in the availability dimension: lab A's action determined whether lab B could write. No cross-tenant read was possible — the lookups were scoped. CLAUDE.md invariant #1 and §8 of the operating brief both require that one lab cannot affect another's data operations.
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect: an insurance claim that could not be created blocks reimbursement for delivered care. No clinical record is altered.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — no row was written incorrectly; the defect refused writes rather than corrupting them.
findings.operational_impact: Claims creation failures that would have appeared as unexplained 500s, more likely as tenants grow and key spaces overlap.
findings.scalability_impact: Positive: collision probability grew with tenant count, so this was a defect that got worse at national scale.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: drop claims_idempotency_key_key, create uq_claims_lab_idempotency (lab_id, idempotency_key), and mirror it in the ORM.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied.
acceptance_criteria: Every idempotency-bearing column's unique index includes a tenant discriminator, or the table is declared an exception with a reason.
claims specifically has uq_claims_lab_idempotency and no globally unique index over the key.
Two labs can use the same key; one lab cannot reuse its own.
Declared exceptions are rot-checked so a stale exemption cannot hide a regression.
evidence: CENSUS against the live schema: 12 columns match %idempotency%. Scoped: billing_invoices, clinical_command_receipts, device_outbox_messages, integration_inbox_events, pay_financial_control_requests, pay_payment_intents, pay_subscription_usage_events, pharmacy_sales (8 by tenant discriminator). Unscoped by design: niam_account_creation_requests, niam_citizen_relationships (national scope, no tenant column). No unique index by design: edge_tasks. Wrong: claims.
EXECUTED before the fix on PostgreSQL 16: lab 902's INSERT refused by claims_idempotency_key_key after lab 901 used 'INV-2026-001'.
EXECUTED after the fix: lab 901 OK, lab 902 with the SAME key OK, lab 901 reusing its own key still REFUSED by uq_claims_lab_idempotency; 3 claims with NULL keys coexist (NULLs stay distinct).
MIGRATION round-trip executed: upgrade 20260915_0003 -> 20260916_0001 leaves only the scoped index; downgrade -1 restores claims_idempotency_key_key; re-upgrade returns to 20260916_0001 (head).

SAFETY PROOF: widening a unique key can never fail on existing data — two rows sharing (lab_id, idempotency_key) would share idempotency_key and would already have been refused. The downgrade is the narrowing direction and refuses with a counted explanation rather than deleting another tenant's claims.

AUTOGENERATE DRIFT re-measured after the change: 5039 operations / 1367 destructive, every operation kind identical to before. The ORM and the schema moved together, so the change introduced no drift. test_schema_fidelity and test_built_tables_match_database agree.

Negative proof, sources restored byte-identical (md5) and the schema restored: an actual alembic downgrade fires both the general invariant and the claims-specific assertion; a stale exemption fires the rot check; a census pattern that matches nothing fires the guard-the-guard.
Gate: migration 113 -> 117 passed, 5 xfailed, by exactly the four tests added.
intersections: NR-091 — the same defect shape. There it was latent in a dormant module (PK on key alone); here it was live in the physical schema of a table with real writers. NR-091's analysis is what prompted the census that found this.
NR-080 — the drift ledger was re-measured after this schema change and is unchanged, because the mapper and the migration moved in lockstep.
contradictions: app/models/claim.py's own module docstring says 'All queries MUST filter by lab_id (security invariant)' — the queries did; the constraint did not.

findings.title: Idempotency protection silently disappears without Redis: the claim store falls back to a per-worker in-memory dict, so a retry handled by another gunicorn worker creates a duplicate clinical write
findings.category: Conditional loss of a clinical safety control / Deployment-dependent correctness
findings.status: MEASURED AND SURFACED — the degradation is now published as a measured state; the durable fix is a database-backed store and is not yet built
findings.blocker: Making the claim store database-backed needs idempotency_keys' primary key changed from (key) to (lab_id, key) — a schema decision on a table that NR-030 lists among the ten no ORM maps. Worth doing deliberately rather than as a side effect of this finding.
findings.complexity: small to surface, real work to fix durably
findings.regression_risk: None from this change — reporting only.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — two _MemoryStore instances, standing for two workers, were shown not to share a claim.
findings.verification_method: _build_cache() inspected with REDIS_URL unset; two independent _MemoryStore instances exercised with the same key.
findings.affected_users: Every lab, in any deployment where REDIS_URL is unset or Redis is unreachable, whenever a client retries a clinical write.
findings.description:
app/security/redis_client.py::_build_cache falls back to a process-local _MemoryStore when REDIS_URL is unset or Redis is unreachable. In production it logs CRITICAL and continues in degraded mode. Its own log line says 'not shared across workers'.

gunicorn runs WEB_CONCURRENCY workers (the pool budget in CLAUDE.md assumes 3), each with its own _MemoryStore. Executed:

    worker A claims the key                  : True
    worker A sees it                          : True
    worker B sees it                          : False
    worker B's retry claims the SAME key      : True

So a retry landing on a different worker is treated as a new request and the clinical write is repeated. This applies to POST /orders, and now equally to POST /samples and POST /batch/orders, which were given the same mechanism under NR-091's follow-up.

Nothing surfaced this. The mechanism exists, its tests pass (single-process), and the security report asserted protection. /compliance/system-status now publishes idempotency_store as MEASURED_PASS or MEASURED_FAIL from idempotency.is_shared(), so the degraded state is visible rather than assumed away.
findings.root_cause: Idempotency was built on an optional cache. Redis is explicitly optional in this platform -- the fallback is deliberate and useful for development -- but a correctness control must not be optional. PostgreSQL is the only store the application cannot run without, which is why idempotency_keys exists.
findings.security_impact: None directly. The failure is duplication, not disclosure.
findings.clinical_impact: A duplicated order or sample is a clinical-safety issue: two accession records for one specimen, or two orders for one clinical intent. CLAUDE.md exempts these endpoints from concurrency shedding because patient-safety operations must never be shed; replay protection is the other half of that guarantee.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Duplicate clinical rows on retry, in the degraded configuration only.
findings.operational_impact: Deployments without REDIS_URL believe they have replay protection and do not. The report now says so.
findings.scalability_impact: Worsens with worker count: more workers, lower the chance a retry lands on the one holding the claim.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: publish the store topology as a measured state so the gap is visible. Set REDIS_URL in any deployment that relies on idempotency.
findings.recommended_fix: Move the canonical claim to PostgreSQL. idempotency_keys already exists with lab_id, an FK to labs and an index; it needs its primary key widened from (key) to (lab_id, key) — the same correction NR-094 made to claims — and a rewritten writer, because the module that currently owns it is unsafe (NR-091).
acceptance_criteria: The security report publishes the claim store's topology as a measured state, never as an unconditional PASS.
is_shared() stays a measurement and never gates a clinical write.
If a database-backed store is built, idempotency_keys is keyed (lab_id, key).
evidence: STATIC: _build_cache() returns _MemoryStore when REDIS_URL is falsy, logging CRITICAL first if IS_PRODUCTION. The non-production log line reads 'REDIS_URL not set — using in-memory store (not shared across workers)'.
EXECUTED: with REDIS_URL unset, _build_cache() returns _MemoryStore. Two instances: A claims a key (True), A sees it (True), B does not (False), and B's set_if_absent on the same key returns True.
STATIC: _MemoryStore holds a plain dict guarded by a threading.Lock — process-local by construction.

Gate: /compliance/system-status now reports idempotency_store as MEASURED_PASS or MEASURED_FAIL, computed from idempotency.is_shared(), and a guard requires both the call and the MEASURED_FAIL branch to remain.
intersections: NR-091 — that finding named the dormant DB-backed module unsafe. This one explains why a DB-backed store is nonetheless the right destination: the cache-backed one is correct only when an optional dependency is present.
NR-090 — the same report that asserted unmeasurable controls now carries this as a measured one, which is the pattern §32-D asks for.
NR-030 — idempotency_keys is one of the ten physical tables no ORM maps. It must not be dropped; it is the store the durable fix needs.
contradictions: The security report asserted replay protection while the store backing it could be per-worker. That specific claim is now measured.

findings.title: The clinical AI agent surface was kept inert only by a column-name typo; §32-C assessed it NOT READY and the safety is now a deliberate flag instead of a bug
findings.category: AI governance / Fail-safe by accident / Information disclosure
findings.status: ASSESSED AND GATED — decision recorded, gate installed and proved; activation is a clinical product decision
findings.blocker: Activating the surface requires an audit path for tool invocations, a deterministic layer ahead of the planning model, and a decision about sending free text and conversation history to an external model. All three are product/clinical decisions, not engineering ones.
findings.regression_risk: None. All three tools raised before this change and return a disabled response after it; neither reaches the database.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the gate was exercised against a live PostgreSQL connection and no tool reached the database.
findings.verification_method: Each registered tool invoked directly with the flag off; AST assertions that the gate precedes next(get_db()); three negative proofs.
findings.affected_users: Doctor-role callers of POST /api/ai/v2/agents/execute. The surface returned error strings before and returns a disabled response now.
findings.description:
§32-C asked whether the AI clinical agent tools should become operational. Assessed against the operating brief's criteria:

  READY   tenant isolation   - NR-092: the runtime injects the authenticated lab_id into every tool and the planning model cannot override it (a lab_id in its params raises TypeError).
  READY   authorization      - _require_doctor on the route, plus session ownership after NR-093.
  NOT     schema correctness - all three tools name columns the database lacks (patients.full_name not name; lab_results.created_at not result_date), so every call raises.
  NOT     audit              - agent_runtime.py calls log_action ZERO times. No record exists that an AI tool read a patient's demographics or results.
  PARTIAL provenance         - ai_suggest/approval_store exist but only run for requires_approval=True tools; all three clinical tools are registered with requires_approval=False.
  NOT     external exposure  - _plan_tools sends the caller's free text and up to 500 tokens of conversation history to Google Gemini to choose both the tool and its patient_id. §27 forbids exposing patient data to external AI by default.
  NOT     deterministic layer- §15 requires rule -> SQL/search -> small model -> large model. Here the model is first and picks the patient.
  WRONG   fallback shape     - on any planner failure it silently substitutes a different tool (search_knowledge_graph) rather than declining.
  NOT     evaluation         - ai/governance.py INSERTs ai_evaluations with no lab_id.
  NOT     failure behaviour  - each tool returned {'error': str(exc)} to the caller, which is how 'column lr.result_date does not exist' became an API response.

VERDICT: do not activate. Six criteria fail and three of them are structural, not bugs.

The more important finding is what was holding it. The ONLY thing keeping this surface inert was a column-name mismatch: correcting two identifiers during a tidy-up would have switched on a clinical AI path with no audit and an external planner. Safety that depends on a bug is not safety. ENABLE_AI_CLINICAL_AGENT_TOOLS now gates all three tools, defaults to false, and is read at call time so the switch is effective without a restart. The raw-exception disclosure is closed in the same change.
findings.root_cause: The surface was built and registered before the governance it needs existed, and then stopped working for an unrelated reason. Nothing recorded that it was not supposed to work, so its brokenness read as a defect to fix rather than a boundary to keep.
findings.security_impact: The failure path disclosed schema (table and column names) to any doctor-role caller. Closed.
findings.clinical_impact: None today — the surface returns a disabled response. Activating it without an audit path would put unlogged AI reads of patient results into clinical use.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — every tool is a read.
findings.operational_impact: Callers now receive an explicit 'not enabled' response rather than a database error.
findings.scalability_impact: Positive: a disabled tool opens no database session.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: gate all three tools on ENABLE_AI_CLINICAL_AGENT_TOOLS (default false), checked before next(get_db()), and stop returning str(exc).
findings.recommended_fix: Before activation: audit every tool invocation, put a deterministic layer ahead of the planner, decide the external-model exposure question, and scope ai_evaluations by lab.
acceptance_criteria: Every clinical agent tool checks the gate before opening a database session.
The flag defaults to False.
No tool returns a raw exception to the caller.
Tenant scoping from NR-092 remains in place, so activation is safe on that axis whenever the rest is ready.
evidence: EXECUTED with a live PostgreSQL DATABASE_URL and the flag off: lookup_patient, get_recent_results and analyze_lab_pattern each returned the disabled envelope, and none produced a schema error — so none reached the database.
STATIC: grep for log_action / audit in app/ai/agent_runtime.py returns nothing. Tool invocations are unaudited.
STATIC: _plan_tools builds a prompt from the caller's task and memory_store.get_history(session_id, max_tokens=500) and passes it to app.gateways.google_ai.generate_chat, which posts to Gemini.
