STATIC: the planner's except branch returns [{'tool': 'search_knowledge_graph', 'params': {'query': task}, 'required': False}] — a different tool, substituted silently.
STATIC: all three clinical tools are registered with requires_approval=False, so the ai_suggest/approval path does not run for them.

Negative proof, sources restored byte-identical (md5): moving the gate after next(get_db()) fires the ordering assertion; flipping the default to true fires the default assertion; restoring str(exc) fires the disclosure assertion.
Gate: unit 470 -> 473 passed, 4 deselected, by exactly the three tests added.

CORRECTION to this finding's own evaluation criterion, measured after it was written. The criterion said 'ai/governance.py INSERTs ai_evaluations with no lab_id', which is true of the statement but implied a live write. It is not one: app.ai.governance.evaluator.evaluate() has ZERO callers across app/. The only `.evaluate(` hits belong to different objects entirely — the certification evaluator, the governance policy engine, the research platform's early-warning SDK. app/routes/ai_platform.py imports the AI evaluator but uses only get_stats(), which reads an in-memory list. So _persist is unreachable and ai_evaluations has no writer at all; the table is physical with zero rows written. The criterion stands as a readiness gap — if the evaluator is ever wired, it will store prompts and responses with lab_id NULL despite the column carrying an FK to labs — but it is latent, not live, and this record previously did not say so.
intersections: NR-092 — that finding made the surface tenant-safe; this one records that tenant safety was necessary but nowhere near sufficient.
NR-087 and NR-091 — the same shape a third and fourth time: a path safe only because it is broken. This is the first of them where the accidental safety has been replaced by a deliberate switch.

findings.title: §32-D: twelve of the compliance report's twenty-three hard-coded verdicts now measure, name where they cannot be measured, or name the gate that holds them
findings.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — 12 of 23 converted and the ratchet tightened 23 -> 11; the remaining 11 are app-internal and derivable
findings.blocker: The remaining eleven are weaker claims rather than false ones. Turning them into measurements is possible but each needs its own probe; whether an auditor's checklist should carry them at all is a product decision.
findings.complexity: small per claim, eleven still to go
findings.regression_risk: Low. Every change is to a reported string; no control was altered. security_report gained a `request` parameter, which FastAPI injects.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the audit-immutability measurement was exercised in all four of its states against real PostgreSQL and SQLite.
findings.verification_method: Trigger dropped inside a transaction and re-measured, then rolled back; the same call made against SQLite; AST recount of the remaining literals.
findings.affected_users: Auditors and anyone reading the compliance endpoints.
findings.description:
NR-090 fixed the two statements in these reports that were outright false. This is the rest: 23 verdicts that were string literals no code computed, so nothing failed when the system they described changed.

Classified per §32-D. Twelve converted:

  UNOBSERVABLE (5) — data_in_transit, rate_limiting, server_disclosure, attack_path_blocking, no_new_privileges. Each names a control in nginx or the container runtime, which this process cannot see, and now says where it would have to be verified instead of asserting PASS.

  MEASURED (5) — tamper_detection, immutability and audit_immutability now ask pg_trigger whether trg_audit_logs_no_update and trg_audit_logs_no_delete exist; request_body_limit and security_headers ask app.user_middleware what is actually installed rather than what factory.py intends.

  ENFORCED_BY_GATE (2) — multi_tenant and object_level_auth. A blanket PASS from inside one request cannot speak for the whole codebase, and this platform has found four tenant-scope defects in as many days (NR-088, NR-090, NR-092, NR-094). The verdict now names the CI guard that holds each invariant, so an auditor can ask for its output.

The eleven remaining are app-internal and derivable — a hasher in use, a route registered. Weaker than measured, but not the same species as telling an auditor this process verified nginx. The guard's ceiling came down 23 -> 11 with them, because a ratchet that keeps its old headroom is not a ratchet.
findings.root_cause: The report was written as a description of the system rather than as an observation of it. A description is correct on the day it is written and silently stops being correct afterwards, with nothing to notice.
findings.security_impact: None directly. The risk was an auditor forming a false picture of controls that were never checked.
findings.legal_impact: The stated audience is government and ISO 27001 auditors. Five claims about infrastructure this process cannot observe were being presented as verified findings.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None — reporting only.
findings.clinical_impact: None.
findings.operational_impact: The audit-immutability verdict now reports MEASURED_FAIL if the triggers are ever absent, which is a real operational signal the report previously could not give.
findings.scalability_impact: Negligible: one catalogue query per report.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied for twelve. The rest stay literal and are pinned at 11.
findings.recommended_fix: Continue converting the remaining eleven, or decide with the compliance owner which belong on the checklist at all.
acceptance_criteria: No verdict that names infrastructure outside this process reports PASS.
The audit-immutability verdict reflects the actual trigger state, including MEASURED_FAIL and UNOBSERVABLE.
The hard-coded verdict count does not rise above 11.
evidence: EXECUTED against PostgreSQL 16: with both triggers present the verdict is 'MEASURED_PASS - trg_audit_logs_no_delete, trg_audit_logs_no_update present on audit_logs'.

EXECUTED with trg_audit_logs_no_update dropped inside a transaction: 'MEASURED_FAIL - audit_logs is NOT append-only: trg_audit_logs_no_update absent. Rows can be updated or deleted.' Rolled back; the verdict returned to MEASURED_PASS.

EXECUTED against SQLite, where pg_trigger does not exist: 'UNOBSERVABLE - the audit trigger catalogue could not be read on this backend; verify on the PostgreSQL primary'. It does NOT fall back to PASS, which is the rule §32-D sets.
AST recount: hard-coded PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL literals across both reports fell from 23 to 11, and the guard's declared ceiling was lowered to match.
Gate: unit 473 passed, 4 deselected — unchanged, because this converts assertions rather than adding tests.
intersections: NR-090 — that finding fixed the two false statements; this one addresses the unmeasured ones behind them.
NR-095 — idempotency_store was the first verdict converted to a MEASURED state, in that finding rather than this one.
NR-088 / NR-092 / NR-094 — the reason multi_tenant became ENFORCED_BY_GATE rather than staying PASS.

findings.title: The served /clinical/orders router let one lab read, cancel and complete another lab's clinical orders, and records those orders in a module-level dict
findings.category: Tenant isolation / Clinical safety / Non-persistent write path
findings.status: RESOLVED — tenant scoping applied to all four stores, the surface gated default-off, and route shadowing corrected
findings.regression_risk: Low. The router had no reachable consumer: frontend-v3 binds it in endpoints.ts, but client.ts's own read guard does not allowlist /clinical/orders and no view imports the hooks. The /api/v1/clinical/orders the frontend does call is the clinical_gateway router, which is a different, persisting surface.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the cross-tenant read, the cross-tenant cancel and the route shadowing were all reproduced against the module before the fix and re-run after it.
findings.verification_method: Direct handler invocation with two LabUser identities; Starlette path_regex resolution order inspected directly; 8 CI-gated guards with 6 negative proofs, every perturbed source restored byte-identical (md5).
findings.affected_users: Every lab on a deployment, for medication, radiology, procedure, lab, consultation, referral, nutrition and nursing orders.
findings.description:
app/routes/clinical_orders.py is registered at factory.py:675 and served at /clinical/orders. Three defects on one surface.

1. CROSS-TENANT READ AND MUTATION. create_order recorded lab_id on every row; no reader consulted it. Executed before the fix: lab 901 listed lab 902's order CLN-ORD-000002 with patient P-B-777 and its notes, fetched it by id, and cancelled it. _ORDER_TEMPLATES, _RECURRING_ORDERS and _STANDING_ORDER_ASSIGNMENTS were shared the same way.

2. ROUTE SHADOWING. GET /{order_id} was declared before GET /templates, /recurring and /standing. Starlette resolves in declaration order and /clinical/orders/{order_id} matches /clinical/orders/templates, so all three reads were unreachable while POST /templates and POST /recurring still accepted writes. This is the fourth instance in this register of a path that is safe only because it is broken (NR-087, NR-091, NR-092, NR-096 are the others), and its trap is specific: correcting the ordering alone would have opened three cross-tenant reads as a side effect of a tidy-up. Ordering, scoping and gating were therefore applied together.

3. NO PERSISTENCE. Every handler declares db: Session = Depends(get_db) and none uses it. The backing store is a module-level dict: per-process, lost on restart, invisible to the other gunicorn workers. A clinician can POST a medication order, receive 201 with an id, and have that order exist nowhere. Nothing is audited. That is a patient-safety problem rather than a missing feature, so the whole surface is now gated behind ENABLE_CLINICAL_ORDERS_STUB, default false, and returns 503 naming /orders as the persisting alternative.

The tenant scoping is applied regardless of the flag, because a gate that can be flipped must not uncover a cross-tenant read.
findings.root_cause: The module was written to the shape of a persisted API — Session dependency, lab_id on every row, pagination — without either half being connected. The lab_id was written and never read; the Session was injected and never used. Both look like a working implementation at a glance, which is why neither was noticed.
findings.security_impact: Cross-tenant read of patient identifiers, order contents and clinical notes, plus cross-tenant mutation of clinical order status. Violates CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1.
findings.legal_impact: Patient data from one laboratory was readable by another on the same deployment.
findings.data_integrity_impact: A foreign lab could set another lab's order to cancelled or completed. No audit record of any of it.
findings.clinical_impact: Two ways: a cancelled order a clinician still believes is active, and an order that returns 201 while being recorded nowhere. Both are the same class — the clinician's belief about an order diverges from reality.
findings.operational_impact: The surface now returns 503 by default. No known consumer loses a working call, because the three sub-resource GETs were unreachable and the frontend's own read guard blocks the rest.
findings.scalability_impact: The dict grows unbounded per worker for as long as the process lives; gating it default-off removes that too.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied: _mine()/_owned() scope all four stores, _require_enabled() on all ten handlers, literal paths declared before /{order_id}.
findings.recommended_fix: Either back this router with real lab_orders rows and audit writes, or retire it. §26 applies to the retirement: it has a frontend endpoints.ts binding and three hooks, so those go first.
acceptance_criteria: No lab can read, cancel or complete another lab's clinical order, template, recurring order or standing order.
Every @router-decorated handler in the module calls _require_enabled() as its first statement, including any added later.
ENABLE_CLINICAL_ORDERS_STUB defaults to false.
GET /templates, /recurring and /standing resolve to their own handlers, not to get_order.
evidence: EXECUTED before the fix: lab 901 LISTS clinical orders -> rows belonging to another lab: 1 (CLN-ORD-000002, lab_id=902, patient P-B-777, notes 'LAB-B: confidential'); lab 901 FETCHES it by id -> same row; lab 901 CANCELS it -> status is now cancelled.
EXECUTED before the fix, route resolution: GET /clinical/orders/templates -> get_order (declared as /clinical/orders/{order_id}); same for /recurring and /standing.

EXECUTED after the fix: all ten handlers return 503 with the flag off; with the flag on, lab 901's list returns 1 row and 0 foreign rows, and GET/CANCEL/COMPLETE of lab 902's order each return 404 with lab 902's order still 'pending'.
EXECUTED after the fix, route resolution: /templates -> list_order_templates, /recurring -> list_recurring_orders, /standing -> get_standing_orders_for_patient, /CLN-ORD-000001 -> get_order.
404 not 403 on the foreign-order paths, so a caller cannot learn that an order exists.

Six negative proofs, each failing with its intended message and every source restored byte-identical (md5): gate removed from one handler; get_order moved back above the literal paths; _ORDER_TEMPLATES read unscoped; _owned matching on id alone; a new ungated handler appended; the flag defaulted to true.
intersections: NR-087 / NR-091 / NR-092 / NR-096 — the same pattern: a capability that was safe only because it was broken. Here the breakage was route shadowing rather than a wrong column name.
NR-092 — the sibling defect where a correct control existed but was not applied to every call site; here the control did not exist on any reader at all.
clinical_gateway — /api/v1/clinical/orders is a different, persisting router and is the one the frontend actually reads.
contradictions: Every handler declares an unused db: Session dependency, which makes the module read as though it persists. That is what the gate's 503 message corrects.

findings.title: Thirty literal routes are unreachable because a parameterised sibling is declared before them
findings.domain: 13 route modules across app/national, app/pharmacy, app/routes, app/identity, app/governance, app/public_health
findings.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — 6 of 30 fixed; 20 of the remaining 24 are blocked on NR-065/NR-076, not on this finding
findings.blocker: 20 of the 24 remaining entries are in app/national packages whose tables are not built; that is blocked on the NR-065 tenancy decision and NR-076, both reserved for a human.
findings.complexity: small per module, thirteen modules; each fix ACTIVATES a handler that has never served a request, so each needs its tenant scoping confirmed first
findings.regression_risk: Low per route and the reorder is mechanically verifiable — the four applied here are pure reorders, proved by an identical sorted-line multiset before and after. The real risk is not the reorder but what it switches on.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — resolution confirmed through the application's own matcher, not a reimplementation of it.
findings.verification_method: create_app(), flatten the route tree through _IncludedRouter.original_router, then resolve each path with the routes' own matches()/path_regex. Auth comparison via each route's solved FastAPI dependant.
findings.affected_users: Anyone calling the affected endpoints, including three live frontend callers.
findings.description:
Starlette resolves routes in declaration order. GET /pharmacy/drugs/{drug_id} matches /pharmacy/drugs/search, so a /drugs/search declared later never runs: the request lands in get_drug with drug_id='search'. Thirty routes across thirteen modules are in that state.

Measured, not inferred. The first version of this scan reported zero, because this FastAPI (0.141.1) mounts included routers as _IncludedRouter rather than flattening them into app.routes, so isinstance(r, APIRoute) matched nothing. Zero looked like good news. The corrected scan finds 2102 routes and 30 shadowed; ten were then re-checked one by one through the app's own matcher and all ten resolved to the parameterised sibling.

SEVERITY. This is P2 rather than P1 because it does not weaken authorization: on all thirty pairs the swallowing handler's solved dependency set is equal to or stricter than the intended handler's, so no request reaches a weaker check than the one its path was meant to hit. That property is now itself a test — if it ever stops holding, the finding is P1.

What it does do is make thirty endpoints dead, three of them with live frontend callers: PublicHealthApiPage.tsx calls /public-health/disease-cases/stats, and useApi.ts calls /hospital/occupancy and /hospital/appointments. POST /hospital/appointments is not shadowed, so appointments can be created and not listed — the same write-reachable, read-shadowed shape as NR-098.

FIXING IT ACTIVATES CODE. Reordering makes a handler reachable that has never served a request, which is precisely the trap NR-098 names. An entry therefore leaves the ledger only with the reorder that fixes it and only after its handler is shown to scope reads to the caller's tenant. A crude regex over handler bodies called 28 of 30 unscoped; reading them showed that verdict is unreliable — the pharmacy handlers carry tenancy through _get_pharmacy_service(db, user), which passes user.lab_id into a service that filters DrugBatch.lab_id. That false positive is why each module is being read rather than pattern-matched.
findings.root_cause: Route order is a global property of a router but is edited locally, one handler at a time. A sub-resource added below an existing /{id} handler is dead on arrival and nothing says so: no import breaks, no test fails, and the endpoint returns a plausible 404 from the wrong handler.
findings.security_impact: None measured. Verified across all thirty pairs that the swallowing handler's dependency set is a superset of the intended one's; that check is now a standing test.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None. No shadowed route writes; the writes at these paths use methods that are not shadowed.
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect. /pharmacy/batches/expiring is the expiring-stock read, and /hospital/appointments the appointment list; both silently return nothing useful.
findings.operational_impact: Six /health sub-resources across the national platform routers are shadowed, so those platform health probes have never reported.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Move each literal declaration above its parameterised sibling, in tranches, confirming tenant scoping per handler.
findings.recommended_fix: Complete the remaining 26, then keep the guard with an empty ledger.
acceptance_criteria: No literal route is matched by an earlier parameterised route.
No shadowed route is served by a handler with weaker authorization than the route addressed.
The ledger shrinks and never grows, and a fixed route must be removed from it.
The scan fails rather than passing vacuously if it stops seeing the route table.
evidence: EXECUTED: 2102 routes flattened; 30 shadowed. Ten re-resolved through the app's own matcher: /pharmacy/drugs/search -> get_drug, /pharmacy/batches/expiring -> get_batch, /national/tasks/health -> get_task, /national/notifications/templates -> get_notification, /hospital/occupancy -> get_hospital, /clinical/documentation/templates -> get_document, /governance/workers/ranking -> get_worker, /public-health/disease-cases/stats -> get_case, /national/observability/traces/search -> get_trace. 10/10.
EXECUTED: auth comparison over all 30 pairs — 0 with a weaker swallower, 0 where an unauthenticated route moved behind auth, 30 equal or stricter.

APPLIED to 4 (pharmacy 2, hospital 2). Both files: the sorted-line multiset is identical before and after, so the change is a pure reorder with no content change. After: /pharmacy/drugs/search -> search_drugs, /pharmacy/batches/expiring -> get_expiring_batches, /hospital/occupancy -> occupancy_stats, /hospital/appointments -> list_appointments, and the parameterised siblings /drugs/DRUG-1, /batches/B-1, /hospital/7 still resolve to get_drug, get_batch, get_hospital.

Tenant scoping confirmed before activating each of the four: hospital passes current_user.lab_id into HospitalService; pharmacy passes user.lab_id into PharmacyService, whose get_expiring_batches filters DrugBatch.lab_id == self.lab_id.

Five negative proofs, each failing with its intended message, every source restored byte-identical (md5): a fixed route re-shadowed; a ledger entry dropped without a fix; a fixed route left in the ledger; the scan's floor raised so it goes blind; the intended handler given a guard its swallower lacks.

DISPOSITION of the 24 still in the ledger, measured against built_tables() on PostgreSQL at head (422 physical tables): 20 are in app/national packages whose tables DO NOT EXIST — no national_* task, notification, job, document, rule or trace table is built, and no gov worker table either. NR-065 records the same for the fifteen task/workflow tables. Those routes already fail at the database, and building the tables is blocked on the NR-065 organization-rooted tenancy decision and NR-076. Reordering them now would change one failure into another, and would pre-position an untenanted read for whenever the tables are built. They stay in the ledger deliberately. 2 (certificates) ARE backed — niam_cert_certificates is built — and are authenticated, via include-level dependencies (see below). 1 (public-health stats) was backed and is fixed here. 1 (governance/workers/ranking) has no backing table.

GUARD CORRECTION. The walk reads each router's own routes, which are PRE-include, so a dependency attached by include_router(..., dependencies=[...]) is invisible to it. app/identity/api/router.py mounts the certificates router with _AUTH_REQUIRED = [Depends(get_current_niam_actor)], and reading that router's routes directly shows no auth at all — which is what the first pass reported for /certificates/expiring and /certificates/authorities. The pair comparison is still sound, but only because both sides of every pair come from the same module and are mounted together. The guard now ASSERTS that rather than assuming it, and the test's docstring says explicitly that it does not establish absolute authentication.

APPLIED to /public-health/disease-cases/stats: pure reorder, identical line multiset before and after. Safe to activate because the whole router carries dependencies=[Depends(require_permission('system:admin'))] and its sibling GET /disease-cases is already reachable at the same scope, so the aggregate adds no exposure class the list does not already have. PublicHealthApiPage.tsx calls this path.
intersections: NR-098 — the same defect on /clinical/orders, found first because that router was being read for a different reason. This is the platform-wide measurement of it.

NR-054 — the frontend calls /niam/certificates/expiring, which does not exist on the backend at all; the backend path is /certificates/expiring and is shadowed. Two different orphaning mechanisms on one feature.

findings.title: One lab could read and electronically sign another lab's clinical notes; the whole medical-record router is a module-level dict
findings.category: Tenant isolation / Clinical record integrity / Non-persistent write path
findings.status: RESOLVED — lab_id stamped at the store, every reader scoped, surface gated default-off, /templates un-shadowed
findings.regression_risk: Low. GET /templates was unreachable (NR-099) and the frontend binds these endpoints in endpoints.ts without any view importing the hooks.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the cross-tenant list, fetch, version-history read and electronic signature were all reproduced against the module before the fix and re-run after it.
findings.verification_method: Direct handler invocation with two LabUser identities; Starlette path_regex resolution inspected directly; 10 CI-gated guards with 7 negative proofs, every perturbed source restored byte-identical (md5).
findings.affected_users: Every lab on a deployment, for SOAP, progress, nursing, consultation, operation and emergency notes.
findings.description:
Found by following NR-099: /clinical/documentation/templates was one of the thirty shadowed routes, and reordering it would have ACTIVATED an unscoped read. Reading the module to check that first is what surfaced this.

The module is registered in factory.py and served. Every handler declares db: Session = Depends(get_db). The module makes ZERO database calls — _DOCUMENTS, _TEMPLATES and _VERSION_HISTORY are module-level dicts.

1. NO TENANT FIELD AT ALL. Unlike NR-098, where lab_id was written but never read, _store_document did not record lab_id, so no reader could have scoped by it even in principle. Executed before the fix: lab 901 listed lab 902's operation note with patient P-B-777 and findings 'LAB-B: confidential operative findings'; fetched it by id; read its version history.

2. CROSS-TENANT ELECTRONIC SIGNATURE. lab 901 called POST /sign on lab 902's operation note. The document came back is_signed=True, signed_by=11 — a lab 901 user — and the version history recorded the action. An electronic signature is a legal attestation on a medical record, and one organisation could apply it to another organisation's operative note.

3. NO PERSISTENCE, NO AUDIT. A signed operation note lives in one gunicorn worker's memory until the next restart. log_action is never called.

FIX. lab_id is stamped inside _store_document rather than at each of the six create handlers, so a seventh create cannot forget it. _owned_doc() gates get/sign/version-history on the caller's lab and returns 404 rather than 403, so a caller cannot learn a document exists. list_documents and list_structured_templates filter by lab_id. All twelve handlers are gated behind ENABLE_CLINICAL_DOCUMENTATION_STUB (default false). The scoping applies regardless of the flag. GET /templates was then moved above GET /{document_id}, closing one NR-099 entry.
findings.root_cause: Same as NR-098 and from the same hand: a module written to the shape of a persisted API — Session dependency, pagination, version history — with neither half connected. Here it went one step further, because the tenant column was never introduced at all, so there was nothing even to forget to read.
findings.security_impact: Cross-tenant read of clinical narrative (operative findings, nursing assessments, emergency notes) and cross-tenant write of an electronic signature. Violates CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #1, and #2 as well: no mutation here was audited.
findings.legal_impact: An electronic signature attributable to a clinician of one organisation could be applied to another organisation's medical record. That is a records-integrity failure, not only a privacy one.
findings.data_integrity_impact: is_signed, signed_by, signed_at and a version-history entry could all be written by a foreign lab. No audit record of any of it.
findings.clinical_impact: The medical record is the artefact here. A note that appears signed but was signed by someone outside the treating organisation, and a note that disappears on restart, are both direct patient-safety problems.
findings.operational_impact: The surface now returns 503 by default. Nothing loses a working call: GET /templates was unreachable, and no frontend view imports the hooks.
findings.scalability_impact: Three dicts grow unbounded per worker for the process lifetime; the default-off gate removes that too.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied.
findings.recommended_fix: Back the router with real tables and audit every signature, or retire it. §26 applies: endpoints.ts binds it, so that goes first.
acceptance_criteria: Every document records the lab that created it.
No lab can list, fetch, sign or read the version history of another lab's clinical document.
No foreign-lab signature can be left on a document even if a future change stops the call from raising.
Every @router-decorated handler calls _require_enabled() first, including any added later.
ENABLE_CLINICAL_DOCUMENTATION_STUB defaults to false.
GET /templates resolves to list_structured_templates, not get_document.
evidence: EXECUTED before the fix: 'is lab_id recorded on the document at all? False'. lab 901 LISTS -> 2 documents including CLN-DOC-000002 (lab 902, patient P-B-777, 'LAB-B: confidential operative findings'); lab 901 FETCHES it; lab 901 SIGNS it -> is_signed=True signed_by=user 11 (a lab 901 user); lab 901 reads its version history -> ['created', 'signed'].
EXECUTED before the fix: db.query/execute/add/commit calls in the module: 0.

EXECUTED after the fix: all 12 served handlers return 503 with the flag off (ungated: 0). With the flag on: lab_id recorded as 902; lab 901's list returns 1 document with 0 foreign rows; GET, SIGN and VERSIONS of lab 902's note each return 404; the note's is_signed is still False; lab 901 sees only its own template.
EXECUTED after the fix: GET /clinical/documentation/templates resolves to list_structured_templates, /CLN-DOC-000001 to get_document.

Seven negative proofs, each failing with its intended message, every source restored byte-identical (md5): lab_id no longer stamped; sign_document matching on id alone; list_documents losing its filter; one handler losing the gate; /templates re-shadowed; a new ungated handler appended; the flag defaulted to true.
intersections: NR-098 — the same defect class on /clinical/orders. This one is worse: there lab_id was written and not read; here it was never written.
NR-099 — this was found by checking a shadowed route before activating it, which is exactly what that finding's ledger discipline is for. Fixing it closes one NR-099 entry.
NR-045 — audit coverage. No mutation on this router is audited, signatures included.
contradictions: All twelve handlers declare an unused db: Session dependency, so the module reads as though it persists.

findings.title: ph_disease_cases extends TenantEntity and not one line in the public_health package reads or writes the tenant column
findings.owner: Public health product owner / Platform security
findings.status: OPEN — measured, not fixed. Which scope is correct is a product decision (§27).
findings.blocker: Whether national disease surveillance should be tenant-scoped is a policy question, not an engineering one. §27 reserves changes to canonical scope semantics.
findings.complexity: small to apply once the semantics are decided
findings.regression_risk: Applying a tenant filter would CHANGE what existing callers see. That is why it is not being applied unilaterally.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — grep over the whole package and the built-table check; the count is zero, not small.
findings.verification_method: grep for tenant_id|lab_id across app/public_health (0 hits); model base read from source; ph_disease_cases confirmed present in built_tables() against PostgreSQL at head.
findings.affected_users: Anyone with system:admin on any deployment.
findings.description:
Found while deciding whether /public-health/disease-cases/stats was safe to un-shadow (NR-099).

DiseaseCaseModel extends TenantEntity, so ph_disease_cases carries a tenant column, and the table is built. Across the entire app/public_health package the strings tenant_id and lab_id appear ZERO times. Nothing writes the column and nothing filters on it: list_cases, get_case and get_case_stats all read every row.

This is the third instance this session of a tenant column that exists and is not used (NR-098 wrote lab_id and never read it; NR-100 never wrote it). The difference is that here the unscoped behaviour may well be CORRECT. The router is gated on require_permission('system:admin'), and national disease surveillance is cross-lab epidemiology by purpose — a per-lab view of an outbreak is close to useless.

So the finding is not 'this is a leak'. It is: the model declares a tenancy the code does not implement, and nothing records which of the two is intended. Either the column is vestigial and should be justified in the model, or surveillance is meant to be scoped and the filter is missing. A reader cannot tell, and neither could I.

What this record deliberately does NOT do is apply a filter. Adding one would change what every existing system:admin caller sees, and §27 reserves changes to canonical scope semantics.

Note the row contents: patient_national_id, patient_age, patient_gender, location_lat/lng, travel_history and exposure_history. If the intended answer is 'scoped', the exposure is patient-level.
findings.root_cause: TenantEntity was chosen as the base — plausibly for created_at/updated_at/soft-delete rather than for tenancy — and the tenant column came along with it. Inheriting a mixin is not the same as adopting its semantics, and nothing in the codebase distinguishes the two.
findings.security_impact: Conditional. If surveillance is meant to be national, none. If it is meant to be scoped, every system:admin principal reads every lab's reportable disease cases including patient national IDs and travel history.
findings.legal_impact: Depends on the same decision. Iraqi national IDs appear in these rows.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None. The column is simply never populated.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly.
findings.operational_impact: None.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Record the decision. If national: document why the tenant column is unused, or drop it in a later migration once §11 is satisfied. If scoped: add the filter to all three readers and populate the column on report_case, with a backfill plan for existing rows.
findings.recommended_fix: Ask the public health product owner which scope is intended, then apply one of the two above.
acceptance_criteria: The intended scope of ph_disease_cases is recorded somewhere a reader can find it.
If scoped: list_cases, get_case and get_case_stats all filter, and report_case populates the column.
If national: the unused tenant column is justified in the model or removed under the §11 sequence.
evidence: EXECUTED: grep -rn 'tenant_id|lab_id' app/public_health/ returns 0 lines.
app/public_health/infrastructure/models.py:6 — class DiseaseCaseModel(TenantEntity), __tablename__ = 'ph_disease_cases'.
ph_disease_cases IS present in built_tables() against PostgreSQL at head, so this is a live table rather than an unbuilt one.
The router carries dependencies=[Depends(require_permission('system:admin'))], so the surface is not open, which is why this is P2 rather than P0.
Row contents include patient_national_id, patient_age, patient_gender, location_lat, location_lng, travel_history and exposure_history.
intersections: NR-099 — found while deciding whether this route was safe to un-shadow.
NR-098 / NR-100 — the same shape (a tenant column no reader uses), but those were unambiguous defects and this one is a genuine question.
NR-065 — the same class of question for national orchestration, decided there as organization-rooted.
contradictions: The model declares tenancy via TenantEntity; the package implements none. One of the two is wrong and nothing records which.

findings.title: The five-rights medication safety check answered 'All five rights verified' from five booleans the caller supplied
findings.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — the false claim is gone and the attestation is now recorded; verifying against the record is NR-102's open half
findings.blocker: Actually verifying the five rights needs a clinical decision: the right-time tolerance, and what must happen when a check fails (warn, block, require override with reason). That is not an engineering judgement.
findings.complexity: small for the honesty fix (applied); medium for real verification
findings.regression_risk: Low. The endpoint had no consumer — no frontend call site and no backend caller — so no working call changed shape. The response gained fields rather than losing any.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED — the old and new responses were both produced by calling the handler.
findings.verification_method: Direct handler invocation with log_action captured; AST/type-hint scan over all 2102 served routes for request bodies that are entirely client booleans; 5 CI-gated guards with 7 negative proofs, every source restored byte-identical (md5).
findings.affected_users: Nursing staff administering medication, and any future consumer of this endpoint.
findings.description:
POST /nursing/medication-admin/verify was summarised 'Verify five rights'. Its request body is five booleans — right_patient, right_drug, right_dose, right_route, right_time — all supplied by the caller. The service computed all(checks) and returned, for five trues:

    {"passed": true, "message": "All five rights verified"}

The five rights are the standard barrier against medication error. Nothing on this path read the patient record, the active MedicationRequest, the ordered dose or route, or the scheduled time. The handler bound db: Session = Depends(get_db) and never referenced it. It wrote nothing and audited nothing, so the attestation did not outlive the HTTP response.

WHY THIS IS A FINDING RATHER THAN A STYLE COMPLAINT. The same codebase contains the correct shape of this, in the same clinical domain: complete_surgical_safety_checklist in app/routes/hospital.py takes TEN caller booleans, including consent_verified and site_marked, and records them tenant-scoped, under an optimistic lock, with an idempotency key, through an audited command. It records attestations and never claims to have verified them — which is exactly what a WHO surgical checklist is. The five-rights endpoint took the same kind of input and claimed a different kind of output.

NOT CURRENTLY LOAD-BEARING, and that is stated as a measured fact rather than a mitigation: nothing consumes this endpoint (no frontend call site, no backend caller), and record_administration does not require a prior verification — it inserts and audits independently. The risk is forward-looking: if a medication administration screen is ever wired to this route, a nurse would be shown 'All five rights verified' by a call that checked nothing.

WHAT WAS APPLIED. The response no longer claims verification; it states that the clinician attested and carries verified_against_record: false explicitly, so a consumer cannot infer otherwise from the route name. The attestation is written to the hash-chained audit log attributed to the clinician and the lab, which is what gives the db parameter its purpose — an unattributed, unrecorded attestation protects nobody. A partial attestation is recorded too, because a clinician declining to attest two of the five rights is precisely the event worth keeping.

WHAT WAS NOT APPLIED. Real verification against the record. That is the open half and it is a clinical decision, not an engineering one.
findings.root_cause: The endpoint was named for the clinical ritual rather than for what the code does. 'Verify five rights' describes what a nurse does at the bedside; the code only ever received the nurse's answer. Nothing in the type system or the tests distinguishes an attestation from a verification, so the two collapsed.
findings.security_impact: None directly — nothing is bypassed and no authorization depends on the result. §7 nonetheless forbids fake verification, and this was one.
findings.legal_impact: An attestation that is neither attributed nor stored is not evidence. It now is both.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Previously nil — nothing was written. Now the attestation joins the audit chain.
findings.clinical_impact: The material risk. A screen showing 'All five rights verified' from a call that verified nothing would substitute a false assurance for the check it names. That is a medication-safety failure mode, and it is the reason this is not filed as cosmetic.
findings.operational_impact: One additional audit row per attestation. The endpoint has no current traffic.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED: stop claiming verification, state verified_against_record: false, and record the attestation to the audit chain attributed to the clinician.
findings.recommended_fix: Verify against the record: resolve the patient and the active MedicationRequest, compare the ordered drug, dose and route, and evaluate the scheduled time against an agreed tolerance. Decide first what a failed check must do — warn, block, or require an override with a recorded reason.
acceptance_criteria: No response from this endpoint claims the medication record was checked while it was not.
Every attestation, complete or partial, is recorded in the audit chain, attributed to the clinician and tenant.
No served endpoint whose request body is entirely caller-supplied booleans presents itself as a verification.
When real verification is built, the right-time tolerance and the failed-check behaviour are recorded decisions.
evidence: BEFORE, executed: a request of five trues returned {'passed': True, 'message': 'All five rights verified'}; the handler's db parameter was never referenced; log_action was called zero times on the path.

AFTER, executed: the same request returns attested=True, verified_against_record=False, and 'All five rights attested by the administering clinician. Attestation recorded; not verified against the medication record.'
AFTER, executed: the audit write is action='nursing.medication.five_rights_attested', user_id=77, lab_id=901, details={'checks': {...}, 'complete': True, 'verified_against_record': False}.
AFTER, executed: a partial attestation (right_drug and right_time withheld) returns attested=False, message 'Not attested: right_drug, right_time', and is still recorded.

MEASURED across all 2102 served routes: exactly ONE endpoint has a request body consisting entirely of caller-supplied booleans, and it is this one. It is pinned in a shrink-only ledger with a rot check.
CONTRAST, measured: complete_surgical_safety_checklist takes ten caller booleans and is tenant-scoped, version-locked, idempotent and audited, and claims only to record.
NO CONSUMER, measured: no frontend call site and no backend caller for /nursing/medication-admin/verify; record_administration does not consult any verification result.

Seven negative proofs, each failing with its intended message, every source restored byte-identical (md5): the old 'All five rights verified' claim restored; verified_against_record dropped from the response; the audit write removed; the clinician attribution removed; a partial attestation discarded; a new all-boolean verification endpoint added; a ledger entry left stale.
intersections: NR-096 — the same species: a clinical surface whose safety came from something other than a control. There it was a column-name typo; here it was the absence of any consumer.
NR-062 — audit coverage. This adds one mutating clinical event to the audited set.
app/routes/hospital.py complete_surgical_safety_checklist — the correct pattern, in the same domain, already in this codebase.
contradictions: The route is still named /medication-admin/verify while its summary and response now say it attests. Renaming the path is an API break and is left to the same decision that builds real verification.

findings.title: The self-healing Redis repair reported 'Redis ping OK' while Redis was down, because the in-memory fallback's ping() always returns True
findings.category: False green / Security control degradation / Session revocation
findings.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — the false success is gone and the degradation is now reportable; recovery without a restart is NOT implemented and is the open half
findings.blocker: Real recovery means rebuilding the `cache` singleton, and five modules bind it at import. Converting those to late lookups or a proxy changes the object behind rate limiting, sessions, MFA, the API firewall and idempotency platform-wide. That is a security-infrastructure change that needs review, not a side effect of fixing a log message.
findings.complexity: small for the honest reporting (applied); medium and review-gated for recovery
findings.regression_risk: Low for what was applied. The repair action's return value changed from True to False in exactly the case where it was lying; no control behaviour changed.
findings.evidence_strength: EXECUTED in all four states, including the positive one against a real Redis with two separate processes.
findings.verification_method: Ran the process with REDIS_URL pointing at a closed port, with REDIS_URL unset, and against a live redis-server on 6399; cross-process revocation checked by writing in one interpreter and reading in a second; 7 CI-gated guards with 7 negative proofs, sources restored byte-identical (md5).
findings.affected_users: Every authenticated user on a multi-worker deployment whose Redis was unavailable when a worker started.
findings.description:
app/security/redis_client.py binds `cache` once, at import:

    cache: _MemoryStore | _RedisWrapper = _build_cache()

_build_cache() falls back to _MemoryStore when REDIS_URL is unset OR when Redis is merely unreachable at that moment. The first path is gated -- config.py exits in production unless ALLOW_DEGRADED_REDIS=true -- and that gate is correct. The SECOND path needs no flag at all: a deployment that sets REDIS_URL properly, but whose Redis happens to be down when a worker boots, silently gets a per-worker store.

THE FALSE GREEN. _MemoryStore.ping() returns True unconditionally, documented 'Always return True for in-memory store as it's always available'. The auto-repair engine's _repair_redis_reconnect called cache.ping() and on True recorded ('redis_reconnect', 'Redis ping OK', True). So the self-healing layer reported a SUCCESSFUL Redis repair while Redis was down and nothing had been repaired. It is a liveness check on the object, not on Redis.

IT CANNOT RECONNECT. Nothing rebinds `cache` anywhere in the codebase -- one assignment, at line 152, at import. The docstring said 'Force Redis client to reconnect' and the comment in _build_cache said 'The self-healing system will attempt to recover it'. Neither was true. A worker that booted during an outage stays degraded for its entire lifetime, long after Redis returns, while monitoring says Redis is fine.

WHAT IT COSTS. Token revocation runs on this cache: security/auth.py blacklist_token and is_token_blacklisted. Executed: worker A revokes a jti, worker A sees it revoked, worker B does not. So logout -- and revoking a session known to be compromised -- becomes worker-local and the token stays valid elsewhere until it expires naturally. Sessions, rate limiting, MFA challenges, the API firewall and HTTP idempotency (NR-095) ride the same store.

WHY RECOVERY IS NOT ATTEMPTED HERE. Five modules bind `cache` at MODULE level: services/idempotency.py, security/session.py, security/rate_limit.py, routes/verification.py, firewall/api_firewall.py. They would keep the old store across any rebind, so a naive rebuild would recover revocation while leaving rate limiting and idempotency silently degraded -- partial recovery that looks total, which is worse than honest degradation. Those five are pinned in a shrink-only ledger so the cost of the real fix cannot grow unnoticed.
findings.root_cause: A generic store was given a Redis-shaped health method. _MemoryStore.ping() answers 'is this object usable', the repair asked 'is Redis healthy', and the two questions look identical at the call site. The singleton binding then made the condition permanent while the monitoring made it invisible.
findings.security_impact: Session revocation is not effective across workers while degraded. A token revoked on logout, or revoked because the session was compromised, continues to be accepted by every other worker until natural expiry. Rate limiting and the API firewall degrade with it.
findings.legal_impact: An audited logout that does not actually end the session elsewhere misrepresents what happened.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Indirect, through NR-095: idempotency claims are per-worker under the same degradation, so a retry can duplicate a clinical write.
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect and via NR-095 rather than direct.
findings.operational_impact: The material one. The health signal actively contradicted reality: an operator watching auto-repair saw 'Redis ping OK' successes during an outage. It now reports the failure and names the restart requirement.
findings.scalability_impact: Worsens with worker count: the more workers, the more of them a revoked token remains valid on.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED: is_shared() and degraded_reason() in redis_client, and _repair_redis_reconnect now reports failure with an operator-readable reason instead of success whenever the cache is not Redis-backed.
findings.recommended_fix: Make `cache` a thin proxy delegating to a swappable backend, so a rebuild reaches every call site including the five module-level binders, then let the repair action genuinely rebuild and verify. Alternatively require Redis and let the worker refuse to start, which trades availability for a guarantee. Either is a deliberate decision.
acceptance_criteria: No repair action reports success for a Redis reconnect while the process is on the in-memory store.
The degraded state is reportable by a function that does not rely on ping().
The operator-facing reason says the process cannot self-recover and needs a restart.
The set of modules binding `cache` at import does not grow.
When recovery is built, it reaches all call sites, proved by execution rather than by inspection.
evidence: EXECUTED, REDIS_URL set to a closed port: cache=_MemoryStore, is_shared()=False, cache.ping()=True. Before the fix _repair_redis_reconnect() returned True and recorded 'Redis ping OK'; after it returns False with the degraded reason.
EXECUTED, REDIS_URL unset: same verdict.
EXECUTED against a live redis-server on 6399 (positive proof): cache=_RedisWrapper, is_shared()=True, degraded_reason()='', _repair_redis_reconnect() returns True.

EXECUTED cross-process with that live Redis: a jti blacklisted in one interpreter is seen as revoked by a SECOND, independent interpreter. Under the memory store the same test shows worker A True, worker B False.
MEASURED: `cache` is assigned exactly once in the codebase (redis_client.py:152) and no code rebinds it.

MEASURED: 25 call sites import `cache` inside a function and would see a rebuild; 5 bind it at module level and would not — services/idempotency.py, security/session.py, security/rate_limit.py, routes/verification.py, firewall/api_firewall.py.

Seven negative proofs, each failing with its intended message, sources restored byte-identical (md5), including a positive-direction one (the repair must still report success when the cache really is shared) and a genuinely new sixth module added and removed to prove the binder ledger catches growth.
intersections: NR-095 — the same degradation reached through idempotency. That finding measured the store; this one found that the health layer reported it as healthy.
NR-097 — §32-D. idempotency_store already reports MEASURED_PASS/MEASURED_FAIL from is_shared(); this gives the cache the same honesty at its own layer.
NR-102 / NR-096 — the same species of defect: a mechanism reporting a result it did not compute.
contradictions: _build_cache()'s own comment says 'The self-healing system will attempt to recover it'. Nothing rebuilds the singleton, so that sentence was false when written. The repair's docstring now says so.

findings.title: FHIRTerminologyService.validate_code() returns True for every code, and lookup_code() echoes an unknown code back as its own display name
findings.category: Stub that would pass everything if wired / Unbuilt capability
findings.status: MEASURED — unreachable today; registered as a trap rather than repaired, because the repair is a BUILD decision
findings.blocker: The intended data source, ref_fhir_terminology, is declared as an ORM model but is NOT a built physical table. Implementing real validation means building that table and deciding what an unknown code must do — the same BUILD-vs-RETIRE question as NR-076.
findings.complexity: small once the terminology source exists
findings.regression_risk: None today: the method has no callers.
findings.evidence_strength: MEASURED — call-site census and built-table check, both executed.
findings.verification_method: grep for validate_code across backend/ excluding the definition (zero hits); import census for FHIRTerminologyService; built_tables() against PostgreSQL at head.
findings.affected_users: Nobody today. Anyone relying on code validation if it is ever wired.
findings.root_cause: A service interface was written before its data source existed, and the placeholder chose the permissive answer. A stub that returns False would have been equally untrue but would have failed loudly the moment it was wired.
findings.security_impact: None today.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None today. If wired, arbitrary strings would enter the record as valid coded concepts, which is a clinical data-quality failure rather than a security one.
findings.clinical_impact: None today; potentially significant if wired, since coded concepts drive decision support and reporting.
findings.operational_impact: None.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None applied. The honest interim would be to raise NotImplementedError rather than return True, so wiring it fails loudly instead of silently — but that changes an exported interface and is left with the BUILD decision.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide BUILD or RETIRE. If BUILD: create ref_fhir_terminology, back validate_code with it, and decide whether an unknown code is rejected or recorded as unvalidated. If RETIRE: remove the service and its two re-exports under §26.
acceptance_criteria: validate_code either consults a real terminology source or fails loudly; it never silently returns True.
lookup_code does not present an unknown code as its own display name.
evidence: AST sweep of app/: 13 functions named for a health or verification question whose body can only return True. Two are the redis ping()s addressed in NR-103 (_RedisWrapper.ping correctly raises on failure), ten are capability scaffolding, one is this.
MEASURED: grep for validate_code across backend/ excluding its definition returns ZERO call sites.
MEASURED: FHIRTerminologyService is exported by app/national/fhir/__init__.py and app/fhir/__init__.py and is never instantiated.
MEASURED: ref_fhir_terminology is NOT in built_tables() (422 physical tables at head), so the data source the real implementation needs does not exist.
intersections: NR-103 — this was found by generalising that finding's root cause into an AST sweep.
NR-102 — the same species (a validator that validates nothing), but that one was served and this one is unreachable, which is the whole difference in severity.
NR-050 / NR-053 — already cover the ten capability validate() stubs the same sweep found.

findings.status: RESOLVED — proven by execution against PostgreSQL
findings.title: A request body could hand one laboratory's donor to another laboratory
findings.description: BloodBankService._update_donor mass-assigned the request payload onto an existing donor row, excluding only 'id' and 'created_at'. lab_id was therefore assignable from the body. It is reached from POST /donors whenever the citizen already has a donor record in the caller's laboratory, so it is a live, client-reachable write path, not dead code. The same call also wrote no audit row, so a donor demographic change left no trail.
findings.root_cause: This is the inverse pattern the brief names: a correct control exists but is not applied to every reachable entry point. _owned() was added on the CREATE path for exactly this reason under NR-021 -- it drops lab_id and id from the payload and sets lab_id from the authenticated context -- but the UPDATE path hand-rolled its own exclusion list and omitted lab_id. Auditing control EXISTENCE would have found nothing; auditing control COVERAGE found this.
findings.evidence: Executed against PostgreSQL: register_donor with an existing citizen_id and {'lab_id': 990002, 'id': 'HIJACKED'} in the body. Before the fix the row's lab_id followed the body. After it, exactly one row remains, lab_id is still 990001 and the primary key is unchanged, while full_name -- a legitimate field -- does change, which is the positive control that proves the path still works rather than rejecting everything. A bloodbank.donor.update audit row is written and does not list lab_id among fields_changed.
findings.affected_users: Every laboratory sharing the deployment
findings.clinical_impact: A donor record -- including blood group and deferral status -- could be moved out of the laboratory responsible for it, where its deferral history would no longer be visible to the staff screening that donor.
findings.security_impact: Cross-tenant write through a client-supplied field. The brief's rule that client-provided tenant claims must not be trusted was violated on this path.
findings.data_integrity_impact: A tenant-owned clinical row could be reattributed with no record.
findings.operational_impact: A laboratory could silently lose a donor record it is accountable for.
findings.legal_impact: Tenant isolation is the basis of the per-laboratory data-custody claim.
findings.intersections: NR-021 (the control this path bypassed), NR-027 (same commit).
findings.recommended_fix: DONE. The exclusion set is now a module constant, _SERVER_OWNED_FIELDS = {'lab_id', 'id'}, shared by _owned() and by _DONOR_UPDATE_EXCLUDED, so the two entry points cannot drift apart again. The update also records which fields actually changed and audits them.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_blood_bank_mutations_are_audited.py::test_the_request_body_cannot_hand_a_donor_to_another_laboratory (PostgreSQL) plus a structural test asserting _SERVER_OWNED_FIELDS is a subset of the update path's exclusions.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met: no client-supplied field can change a row's lab_id or primary key.
findings.regression_risk: Low. The only behaviour removed is assignment of lab_id and id from the body, which no legitimate caller can want.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (PostgreSQL execution + negative proof + positive control)

findings.status: RESOLVED — proven by execution against PostgreSQL
findings.title: Donor deferral could never be recorded, so the deferral safety gate could never fire
findings.description: blood_bank_donor_deferrals.deferred_from is NOT NULL with no default in either the ORM or the physical schema. defer_donor was the only construction site for DonorDeferralModel and never set it, so POST /donors/{donor_id}/defer raised NotNullViolation on every call and returned 500. The route catches only DonorNotFoundError, so nothing softened it.
findings.root_cause: A NOT NULL column with no default and no assignment at its single write site. The endpoint had presumably never been executed against the real schema: on SQLite, which the unit suite uses, the same insert can succeed.
findings.evidence: Executed against PostgreSQL at revision 20260916_0001: 'null value in column "deferred_from" of relation "blood_bank_donor_deferrals" violates not-null constraint', with the full failing row. After setting deferred_from to the instant deferred_until is already measured from, the deferral row persists, is_active is true, and register_donation then raises DonorDeferredError for that donor -- which is the gate firing for the first time.
findings.affected_users: Every blood bank donor and the staff screening them
findings.clinical_impact: This is the consequence that makes it P1 rather than a broken endpoint. register_donation refuses a donation only when an ACTIVE deferral row exists. While no deferral row could be written, a donor deferred for low haemoglobin or infectious-disease risk was never actually blocked from donating: the deferral was requested, the write failed, and the next donation proceeded.
findings.security_impact: None directly.
findings.data_integrity_impact: defer_donor set donor.status to 'deferred' in the same transaction, so the status change was lost with the rollback too -- the donor was left active.
findings.operational_impact: A documented clinical decision left no trace anywhere.
findings.legal_impact: Donor deferral is a blood-safety requirement, not a convenience.
findings.intersections: NR-027 (found while proving the audit writes by execution).
findings.contradictions: The capability appeared present -- route, service method, model, table and the downstream gate that consumes it all existed. It was not safe merely because it was broken; it was unsafe BECAUSE it was broken.
findings.recommended_fix: DONE. deferred_from is set to the deferral's start instant.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_blood_bank_mutations_are_audited.py::test_a_deferred_donor_is_actually_refused_a_donation (PostgreSQL), plus a structural test that derives every NOT NULL, no-default column of DonorDeferralModel from the ORM metadata and asserts each is assigned at the construction site -- so the defect CLASS is gated, not just this instance.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met: a deferral persists and a deferred donor is refused a donation.
findings.regression_risk: Low. The endpoint could not succeed before, so nothing depended on its behaviour.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (PostgreSQL execution, both failing and passing, + negative proof)

findings.status: OPEN — measured and classified. The 7 permission-less class-A sites are closed under NR-108; the 29 master-admin sites still need the ownership decision.
findings.title: 101 write paths copy a request dict onto a tenant-scoped model without excluding lab_id
findings.description: Generalisation of NR-105, which was one instance of this in the blood bank. Two shapes recur across the platform: Model(**{k: v for k, v in data.items() if hasattr(Model, k)}) on create, and 'for k, v in data.items(): setattr(obj, k, v)' on update. Both copy a caller-supplied dictionary onto a model whose table carries lab_id, so lab_id is assignable from the request body unless something else re-asserts it.
findings.root_cause: There is no shared server-owned-fields helper. app/blood_bank grew _owned() under NR-021 and now _SERVER_OWNED_FIELDS under NR-105, but every other package hand-rolls its filter, and the hand-rolled filters are about field EXISTENCE (hasattr) rather than field OWNERSHIP.
findings.evidence:
AST scan of backend/app (194 model classes carrying lab_id, discovered from TenantEntity inheritance or a lab_id Column/Mapped declaration; the scan asserts the model count is non-trivial so it cannot report vacuously). 101 matching sites, classified four ways by tracing each site's enclosing function to the route handlers that pass a body parameter into it:
  A. 36 -- reachable with a RAW dict body and no lab_id re-assertion.
  B.  4 -- reachable, but the enclosing function re-asserts lab_id.
  C. 24 -- reachable only through a Pydantic schema body, so lab_id reaches the service only if that schema declares it.
  D. 37 -- no route path resolved. NOT proven safe; unclassified.
Of the 36 in class A, the router permission was then resolved and mapped through shared/rbac/permissions.py: 29 sit behind require_permission('system:admin'), which only master_admin holds -- a legitimately cross-tenant role, so those are an under-specified ownership model rather than a tenant breach. The remaining 7 resolved to NO require_permission at all: 4 in app/pilot_platform and 3 in app/identity (adaptive_auth, federation, trust). The identity three are mounted with dependencies=[Depends(get_current_niam_actor)] by identity/api/router.py, which an AST scan of the route module cannot see, so they are authenticated but ungated by permission. app/pilot_platform is mounted by factory.py:811 with no dependencies and its route module contains zero references to get_current_user, require_permission or require_role.
findings.affected_components: backend/app/ems, critical_care, command_center, biomedical, pilot_platform, public_health, national/*, identity/{adaptive_auth,federation,trust}, services/ehr_service.py, services/clinical_service.py, nhdw, nursing, pharmacy, radiology, routes/hospital.py, routes/care_continuum.py
findings.affected_users: Potentially every tenant, depending on which class a given site falls in
findings.clinical_impact: UNKNOWN per site and deliberately not asserted. The class-A sites include EMS incidents, ICU beds, fluid balance, critical alerts and immunisation records -- all clinical -- but 29 of the 36 are master-admin-only, and whether a master admin writing an arbitrary lab_id is a defect or the intended behaviour is an ownership-model question, not a code question.
findings.security_impact: The brief's rule that a client-provided tenant claim must not be trusted is structurally unenforced: it is enforced in one package by a local helper and nowhere else. This is a control-COVERAGE finding, not a control-EXISTENCE finding -- auditing whether the platform 'has' tenant scoping would report PASS.
findings.data_integrity_impact: A tenant-owned row can be created or moved into a tenant the caller does not act for.
findings.operational_impact: Rows can be attributed to the wrong laboratory with no error and no audit.
findings.legal_impact: Per-laboratory data custody is the basis of the tenancy claim.
findings.dependencies: The class-A count cannot be reduced to a fix list until the master_admin ownership question is settled: if a master admin may legitimately write any lab_id, 29 of the 36 are not defects.
findings.intersections: NR-021 (the blood bank instance, fixed), NR-105 (the blood bank update-path instance, fixed), NR-101 (whether public_health should be tenant-scoped at all -- that decision changes this finding's scope for that package), NR-065 (national orchestration tenancy).
findings.contradictions: app/blood_bank now enforces this and is the only package that does, so the platform simultaneously demonstrates the correct pattern and does not apply it.
findings.recommended_fix: A single canonical helper -- server_owned(payload, model) -- that drops lab_id and id and sets lab_id from the authenticated context, applied at every write path, with a CI-gated shrink-only ledger of the sites not yet converted. Do NOT start by converting the 29 master-admin sites: settle the ownership question first, because the correct behaviour there may be to keep an explicit, audited lab_id parameter rather than to override it.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: DONE for the permission-less subset. app/pilot_platform (4 sites) and app/identity adaptive_auth/federation/trust (3 sites) were the seven class-A sites with no resolvable permission. NR-108 gated pilot_platform with require_permission('system:admin') and confirmed the identity three are mounted with _AUTH_REQUIRED, so all seven now require a credential before the mass-assign is reached. The mass-assign itself is unchanged: a master_admin can still supply lab_id in the body on those paths, which is the ownership question below.
findings.verification_method: A CI-gated scan asserting the site count cannot grow, plus per-package execution proof that a body-supplied lab_id does not reach the row. Neither exists yet. This entry is DISCOVERY.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every write path to a tenant-scoped model derives lab_id from the authenticated context, or is explicitly and audibly a cross-tenant administrative path.
findings.regression_risk: Medium. Overriding lab_id on a path where a cross-tenant administrator legitimately sets it would break that administrator's workflow, which is why the ownership question is a precondition rather than a detail.
findings.evidence_strength: MEDIUM-STRONG for the measurement (AST scan with a guard-the-guard floor, route tracing, RBAC resolution). NO execution proof per site yet, so no site outside NR-105 is claimed exploitable.

findings.status: RESOLVED for every gap found — proven by execution against the served application
findings.title: Twenty-seven mutating endpoints answered an unauthenticated request, including NIAM session termination and device trust
findings.description:
Measured by sending an unauthenticated request to every mutating operation in the application's own OpenAPI contract: 1089 operations, 1031 answered 401, and 58 reached their handler. Of those 58, 31 are the authentication surface itself or otherwise legitimately reachable. Twenty-seven were genuine gaps, in six groups:
  app/identity  6 -- POST /niam/sessions/{session_uuid}/terminate, /niam/sessions/account/{account_id}/terminate-all, /niam/devices/{device_uuid}/trust, /niam/devices/{device_uuid}/revoke, /niam/devices/register, POST /niam/persons/ (and with them the GET twins GET /niam/sessions/account/{account_id} and GET /niam/persons/{person_uuid})
  app/governance 4 -- POST /governance/audit-events and /governance/workers/{worker_id}/{competencies,trainings,productivity}
  app/pilot_platform 6, app/lifecycle_platform 7, app/certification 3, app/contracts 1 (POST /contracts/export)
findings.root_cause:
THREE DISTINCT OMISSIONS OF AN EXISTING CONTROL, not a missing control.
(1) identity/api/router.py defines _AUTH_REQUIRED = [Depends(get_current_niam_actor)] and applies it to ten of its twenty-two include_router calls. persons, sessions and devices were mounted with no dependency and had no actor dependency of their own either.
(2) governance_routes.py defines admin_dep and elevated_dep at module level and puts them in the DECORATOR of most routes. Four routes simply omit it, with gated siblings on the lines immediately above and below.
(3) pilot_platform, lifecycle_platform, certification and contracts contain no reference to get_current_user, require_permission or require_role anywhere in their route modules, and were mounted with no dependency, while their peer platform-operations routers (ems, command_center, critical_care, biomedical) all declare dependencies=[Depends(require_permission('system:admin'))].
findings.evidence:
Execution against the served FastAPI application, not a source scan -- reading is unreliable in both directions here because include_router(dependencies=[...]) never appears in a route's own dependant. Three earlier measurement errors were found and corrected before any conclusion was drawn:
  (a) A walk over app.routes that descended into _IncludedRouter.original_router double counted every included route at its PRE-prefix path, producing 167 phantom '404 Not Found' rows that looked like reached handlers. Enumerating from app.openapi() instead removed all 167. The 404 bodies -- all Starlette's uniform 'Not Found' -- are what exposed it.
  (b) A 422 can mean FastAPI rejected the request shape BEFORE a security dependency ran. Re-probing with every required parameter filled from the OpenAPI schema turned three governance 422s into 500s -- the handler ran and hit the database -- while /niam/auth/refresh turned into a 401, so it was guarded all along.
  (c) A static AST scan of governance_routes.py reported 43 of 70 handlers as ungated. That was wrong: it searched for admin_dep, require_role and get_current_user and missed elevated_dep, a third dependency name. The runtime probe found 4, not 43, and the runtime probe was right.
Counts after the fix: 1058 refused, 31 reached. 1058 - 1031 = 27, exactly the operations gated. The /api/ai/* group answers 503 with its feature flag off, which is not evidence of authorization, so it was proven separately: with ENABLE_AI_DATASET=true and ENABLE_AI_FEEDBACK=true all four answer 401 AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED.
findings.affected_users: Every account on the platform
findings.clinical_impact: POST /governance/workers/{worker_id}/competencies let an anonymous caller set a named clinician's competency LEVEL, and /trainings assert a completed training. Those are the records a laboratory relies on to decide who may perform which test.
findings.security_impact: The three worst, in order. POST /niam/devices/{device_uuid}/trust -- a trusted device is an input to the adaptive-authentication decision, so an unauthenticated caller could elevate a device and weaken the MFA outcome for it: an authentication bypass ENABLER, not merely an open endpoint. POST /niam/sessions/account/{account_id}/terminate-all -- unauthenticated, targeted, repeatable logout of any account. POST /governance/audit-events -- the parameters include actor_id, so an anonymous caller could write national audit events attributed to anyone. That FORGES the trail rather than merely bypassing it, which is worse than the gap CLAUDE.md's 'never reduce audit-log coverage' rule contemplates.
findings.data_integrity_impact: POST /niam/persons/ wrote the canonical identity registry -- demographics, national_id_hash and health_id, all as QUERY parameters -- with no credential, and GET /niam/persons/{person_uuid} read it back.
findings.operational_impact: POST /contracts/export answered 200 and wrote files to the server's filesystem. The path was already safe (output_dir is pattern-constrained to one directory name under a configured root), so this was unauthenticated disk consumption rather than traversal.
findings.scalability_impact: Unauthenticated write endpoints are a free amplification target.
findings.legal_impact: An audit trail that an anonymous party can write entries into is not an audit trail, and transfusion and credentialing traceability rest on it.
findings.intersections: NR-046 (the same control-coverage pattern in the same dependency), NR-107 (four of its seven permission-less class-A sites are these), NR-013 (audit coverage), NR-099 (route reachability).
findings.contradictions: Every one of the three omissions sits beside a correct application of the same control, in the same file, often on the adjacent line. Auditing whether the platform HAS authentication would have reported PASS at 1031 of 1089.
findings.recommended_fix: DONE, fail-closed, and each fix matches what its own neighbours already do rather than inventing a policy: _AUTH_REQUIRED on the persons, sessions and devices includes; elevated_dep on the three worker-credentialing routes and admin_dep on the audit-event write, matching their siblings; require_permission('system:admin') on the pilot_platform, lifecycle_platform and certification routers, matching ems and command_center; the same on POST /contracts/export only, leaving the GET contract-publication routes public, which is what that router is for.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied in full. Nothing could have depended on the previous behaviour: the pilot_platform, lifecycle and certification routes all returned 500 on any call because their tables are not built, and the rest were never intended to be anonymous.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_unauthenticated_mutations_are_declared.py -- 7 tests that probe the served application once per mutating operation and require every operation reaching a handler to be declared with a reason in one of four ledgers (PUBLIC 21, SECRET_AUTHENTICATED 3, RETIRED 3, FLAG_GATED 4). DECLARED_GAP is EMPTY and _GAP_CEILING is 0, so a new unauthenticated mutating endpoint cannot be admitted to the ledger at all -- it has to be fixed. Guarded in both directions: a floor of 1000 operations, an assertion that most refuse (a probe whose requests never arrive would look like a platform-wide finding), an assertion that NOT everything refuses (login must be reachable or the whole file measures nothing), and a concrete pair -- POST /login must reach, POST /patients must refuse.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met: every mutating operation either refuses an unauthenticated request or is declared, with a reason, in a ledger that cannot grow.
findings.regression_risk: Low, and asymmetric: the change only ADDS credential requirements. The risk is an internal caller that relied on anonymous access; none was found, and the affected endpoints could not succeed anyway.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (1089 executed requests against the served app, before and after; three measurement errors found and corrected; 7 CI-gated tests; 7 negative proofs with every source restored byte-identical)

findings.status: RESOLVED — proven by execution against PostgreSQL, before and after
findings.title: The governance repository audited into a table no migration builds, so every governance write failed at flush
findings.description:
GovernanceRepository._write_audit ran on every create, update and delete of every governance entity and wrote a HealthNumberAudit row. It was wrong four ways at once, which is why it survived a detector, a reviewer and a green test suite:
  1. WRONG TABLE, AND THE TABLE DOES NOT EXIST. gov_health_number_audit is mapped by the ORM and built by no migration, so the write raised ProgrammingError inside the caller's transaction and took the clinical effect with it.
  2. WRONG RESOURCE. The entity's id went into the `health_number` column, so a break-glass grant, an identity merge and a guardian record were all recorded as health-number events, indistinguishable in the one trail an auditor would query for a health number's history.
  3. WRONG ACTOR. changed_by was the literal "system" for every caller.
  4. NOT TAMPER-EVIDENT. Not the SHA-256 chained audit_logs.
Seven repositories route through it: identity records, QR codes, recovery requests, guardians, BREAK-GLASS ACCESS GRANTS, merge proposals and merged identity records.
findings.root_cause: GovernanceRepository.__init__ accepts `audit_resource`, stores it, and _write_audit never reads it -- confirmed at runtime, not by eye, via GovernanceRepository._write_audit.__code__.co_names. The subclasses were already supplying it correctly: BreakGlassAccessRepository passes 'gov_break_glass'. The intent was recorded in the code and then discarded by the implementation.\nThe class also had no actor parameter at all, so there was nothing to attribute a row to, and "system" filled the hole with a false claim.
findings.evidence:
Executed against PostgreSQL at 20260916_0001.
BEFORE: gov_break_glass_accesses, gov_identity_records, gov_qr_codes, gov_recovery_requests, gov_guardians and gov_merge_proposals are all built; gov_health_number_audit is NOT. Adding a break-glass record and flushing raised: ProgrammingError (psycopg2.errors.UndefinedTable) relation "gov_health_number_audit" does not exist.
AFTER: the same record persists, and exactly one audit_logs row is written with action='governance.gov_break_glass.create', resource_type='gov_break_glass' (the DECLARED resource, previously ignored), a chain_hash, and the full UUID preserved in details['resource_id'] because audit_logs.resource_id is INTEGER. user_id is NULL, which is honest: no caller supplies an actor yet, and a visible NULL is not the false claim "system" was. Zero fixture rows left.
WHY THE SUITE WAS GREEN, and this is the part worth keeping: backend/tests/test_persisted_identity_governance.py builds its schema with GovernanceBase.metadata.create_all, so it CREATED gov_health_number_audit and tested against a table production does not have. 35 tests passed against a database that could not exist. That is NR-036 demonstrated in one file -- a schema built from ORM metadata certifies the ORM, not the database. The fixture now also creates audit_logs, which is the table the code under test actually writes.
findings.affected_users: Every governance and identity operator
