findings.clinical_impact: Break-glass is the emergency override of access control. A grant that cannot be persisted either blocks emergency care or, had any caller swallowed the error, would have granted access with no record at all. PersistedBreakGlassService.request_access does not catch it, so it failed closed -- but it failed.
findings.security_impact: The most consequential audit record on the platform could not be written, and the mechanism that appeared to write it produced a false record in the wrong trail with a false actor. CLAUDE.md Security Invariant #2 was unmet on every one of these paths while looking met.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Identity merges and guardian relationships could not be recorded either. Had gov_health_number_audit ever been built, the health-number audit trail would have been polluted with rows whose health_number is actually another entity's primary key.
findings.operational_impact: Seven repositories could not write at all.
findings.legal_impact: Break-glass and identity-merge traceability are regulatory expectations.
findings.intersections: NR-036 (the test schema is built from ORM metadata -- this is its clearest consequence), NR-027 (the same actor-threading and resource-id normalisation), NR-105 (duplicate logic drifting apart), NR-108 (POST /governance/audit-events, now authenticated, still cannot write because gov_national_audit_events is unbuilt), NR-062, NR-066.
findings.contradictions: The package satisfied a package-level 'does this audit?' detector, and a 35-test suite, while none of its writes could reach a database.
findings.recommended_fix: DONE. _write_audit now calls the canonical log_action with resource_type=self._audit_resource, the actor threaded through new optional actor_user_id/actor_lab_id parameters, and the unabridged identifier in details. audit_logs IS built, so the seven repositories can write again -- the fix repairs four defects and one outage with one change.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: Applied. Also consolidated: the varchar-to-INTEGER resource-id normalise existed independently in ClinicalCommandGuard and in the blood bank service, which is exactly the duplication that let the blood bank create and update paths disagree under NR-105. There is now one implementation, audit_service.normalize_resource_id, with three callers, and a test that fails if a fourth copy appears.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_governance_mutations_reach_the_audit_chain.py -- 7 tests, 6 structural in the unit job and 1 against PostgreSQL in the migration job. It asserts on the AST node rather than on a substring: a substring check for 'self._audit_resource' PASSED a perturbation that replaced resource_type with a literal, because the identifier also appeared in the action string one line above. The guard would have reported green while the defect was back. It now reads the resource_type keyword of the log_action call specifically.\nIt also generalises the defect: no audit-writing function anywhere in app/ may construct a model whose table is absent from built_tables(). That scan immediately found two more, declared in a shrink-only ledger rather than guessed at.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Met: every governance mutation reaches the hash-chained audit log, under the resource type its own repository declares.
findings.regression_risk: Low, and measurable. The 35 tests in test_persisted_identity_governance.py went 33-failed/2-passed to 35-passed once the fixture built audit_logs; the failures were the fixture missing the table, not the change.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (PostgreSQL execution before and after, 7 CI-gated tests, 6 negative proofs, and one weak guard caught by its own negative proof and replaced)

findings.status: OPEN — measured and ledgered. The fix is a MIGRATION, which CLAUDE.md reserves.
findings.title: Two correct, rich audit writers target tables no migration builds
findings.description: Found by generalising NR-109 into a scan: no audit-writing function may construct a model whose table is absent from built_tables(). Two survive beyond NR-109's own:\n  app/services/mpi/resolver.py::_write_audit -> national_merge_audit. Master Patient Index merge decisions.\n  app/governance/services/security_governance_service.py::log_audit_event -> gov_national_audit_events. National security audit events.
findings.root_cause: Neither is NR-109's defect. Both writers are CORRECT and rich. The MPI one is itself SHA-256 hash-chained -- prev_hash plus canonical JSON -- and records decided_by_user_id, a real actor. The governance one carries actor_id, actor_role, resource_type, resource_id, action, status, ip_address, details, severity and node_id. What is missing is the table.
findings.evidence: built_tables(), derived from the migration chain rather than a snapshot, contains neither. The scan that found them asserts built_tables() returns more than 300 tables first, so a broken migration scan cannot make it accuse every writer.
findings.affected_users: Identity stewards and national security operators
findings.clinical_impact: An MPI merge joins two patient records. Its decision trail cannot be written, so a wrong merge cannot be reconstructed.
findings.security_impact: POST /governance/audit-events writes gov_national_audit_events. NR-108 authenticated that endpoint; it still cannot succeed, so the national security audit trail has no writer that works.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Both writes raise inside the caller's transaction.
findings.operational_impact: Every caller of either writer fails at flush.
findings.legal_impact: Identity-merge and security-event traceability are regulatory expectations.
findings.dependencies: A migration must create both tables.
findings.intersections: NR-109 (the scan that found them), NR-059, NR-067, NR-108.
findings.contradictions: The platform has two well-designed audit mechanisms that have never been able to write a row.
findings.recommended_fix: Create both tables in a new migration, from the existing ORM definitions. Do NOT rewrite either writer onto log_action: that would LOSE evidence -- the MPI chain, the match score and features, the severity and node_id -- in exchange for a generic row. This is a DB schema change, which CLAUDE.md reserves for human approval, so it is declared rather than applied.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None available without the migration. Declared in DECLARED_UNBUILT_AUDIT_TARGETS in backend/tests/test_governance_mutations_reach_the_audit_chain.py, which is shrink-only with a ceiling of 2 and a rot check that forces each entry out the moment its migration lands.
findings.verification_method: Two CI-gated tests: the ledger cannot grow, and an entry must be removed once built_tables() contains it. Both negative-proven -- removing an entry makes the class scan name that exact table, and adding a third entry fails the ceiling.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Both tables exist and both ledger entries are gone.
findings.regression_risk: Creating a table breaks nothing; both writers already expect it.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (migration-chain derivation + a guarded scan + 2 negative proofs)

findings.title: A fresh deployment could not be administered at all
findings.description:
/login refuses any account whose role is in PRIVILEGED_ROLES (master_admin, ministry_admin, province_admin) until that account has an active MFA device (app/routes/login.py:143-161). The only enrolment endpoint, POST /mfa/totp/setup, is itself behind get_current_user (app/routes/mfa.py:55). The bootstrap creates exactly one account -- the master admin -- and it is privileged. On a clean database nobody can log in, nobody can enrol, and therefore no lab can ever be approved.
OBSERVED on a live server against a freshly migrated PostgreSQL database: POST /login -> 403 'MFA enrollment required for privileged accounts', with audit row action=login_denied_mfa_required. No out-of-band enrolment path existed anywhere in scripts/ or the bootstrap.
FIX: scripts/enroll_mfa.py enrols TOTP through MFAService.setup_totp using database credentials rather than a session -- a strictly stronger authority than the one it substitutes for. The login gate is untouched; enrolling ADDS a factor and never bypasses one. The enrolment writes action=mfa_enrolled_out_of_band to the audit chain.
PROVEN: enrol -> login 200; --verify with a live TOTP code -> OK (exit 0); --verify with 000000 -> FAILED (exit 2); re-enrol without --force -> refused.
findings.evidence: live HTTP against uvicorn + PostgreSQL; audit_logs rows 2 and 3

findings.title: Twenty-six SQL filters compiled to WHERE false and could never return a row
findings.description:
db.query(Lab).filter(not Lab.is_active) is not a SQL negation. Python evaluates `not` eagerly, an InstrumentedAttribute is truthy, so the argument is the literal False. COMPILED AND CONFIRMED: 'SELECT labs.id FROM labs WHERE false'. It matches nothing, ever, and raises nothing.
26 sites across 5 modules. Measured consequences:
  GET /admin/labs/pending returned total:0 with two labs waiting for approval. The onboarding approval queue was empty by construction, so no registered lab could be approved through the intended workflow. After the fix the same request returns total:2 and names both labs.
  PACSService.revoke_share filtered `not ImageShare.is_revoked`, never found the share, and always returned False -- a shared radiology study could not be revoked.
  20 LIMS list endpoints filtered `not X.is_deleted` and returned zero rows regardless of the data (instruments, specimens, orders, panels, results, reagents, consumables, lots, reference ranges, auto-validation rules, reports, QC programs, suppliers, storage, delta-check rules, departments, manufacturers).
  HospitalService._get_entity and the pharmacy _get_or_404 helper raised 404 for every row they were asked for.
FIX: ~Model.flag for the NOT NULL soft-delete flags (the idiom already in use three lines above one of the defects, app/services/hospital_service.py:127); ImageShare.is_revoked.is_(False) for the nullable security flag (fail-closed on NULL); Lab.is_active.is_not(True) for the pending queue (a lab that is not definitely active belongs in front of a reviewer).
findings.evidence: compiled SQL before/after; live GET /admin/labs/pending 0 -> 2; AST scan 26 -> 0

findings.title: MFA is enforced as an enrolment checkbox, never as a challenge
findings.description:
app/routes/login.py checks mfa.has_mfa_enabled(user.id) and, if a device exists, proceeds straight to create_token(). No TOTP code, no WebAuthn assertion, and no MFA session is ever demanded. OBSERVED: after enrolling TOTP out of band, POST /login with email and password alone returned 200 with a full access token and refresh token -- the second factor was never presented.

The pieces for the real flow are already present and unused: MFASession, MFA_SESSION_TTL_MINUTES = 10, MFAService.verify_totp, and the /mfa/webauthn/authenticate/{begin,complete} pair.
NOT FIXED TODAY: the fix changes /login's response shape (a partial mfa_session_token instead of an access token) for privileged accounts, which CLAUDE.md lists under 'requires human approval' as an API response-shape change that breaks mobile clients. Registered rather than guessed at.

findings.status: CLOSED — logout now revokes the session an API client actually holds; proven live.
findings.title: Logout was a no-op for every non-browser client
findings.description: POST /logout read the access token from request.cookies only. Every client using the documented `Authorization: Bearer` contract -- the mobile app, the device bridge, any API consumer -- sends no cookie, so the read returned None: no JTI was blacklisted, user_id stayed None, and therefore the perm_version bump (the documented 'safety net if Redis is wiped') never ran either. Both revocation layers were dead for bearer sessions.\nMEASURED on a live server: POST /logout -> 200 'Logged out successfully', then GET /session with the SAME bearer token -> 200. The session survived its own logout and stayed valid until natural expiry.\nFIX: the handler falls back to the Authorization header for the access token and to X-Refresh-Token for the refresh token. Both existing revocation layers then run unchanged. After the fix the same sequence returns 401.
findings.evidence: runtime_gates.py gate 3b, 4/4 PASS on a clean database

findings.title: POST /patients answered 500 for every request on PostgreSQL
findings.description:
Creating a patient -- the most basic clinical operation on the platform -- could not succeed against a migration-built schema. Two independent overflows, found one after the other by executing the request:
  1. health_id. The generator emitted 'GULA-' + secrets.token_hex(8).upper(),      21 characters, into patients.health_id which is varchar(20) in the      immutable base schema. psycopg2.errors.StringDataRightTruncation.
  2. gender. PatientCreate.validate_gender explicitly ACCEPTED 'male' and      'female' and passed them through to patients.gender, which is varchar(1).      The API's own contract therefore guaranteed a 500. PatientUpdate had no      gender validator at all, so PUT /patients/{id} had the same defect.
WHY THE TESTS MISSED BOTH: SQLite does not enforce varchar length. The suite runs on SQLite; the product runs on PostgreSQL.
FIX: the health id generator reads its width from the column (Patient.__table__.c.health_id.type.length) so the two cannot drift again; gender is folded to the single character the column stores by a shared normaliser used by both the create and the update model. The set of accepted inputs is unchanged, so no client contract moves.
A sweep of the other generated identifiers (invoice_number, reference, sale_number) against their column widths across every declarative base found no further overflow.
findings.evidence: live POST /patients 500 -> 201; runtime_gates gate 5 fixture now creates patient id 1

findings.status: CLOSED — root cause found (NR-126). 87 -> 0 failures, 3021 -> 3126 passes.
findings.title: 87 unit tests fail only when the suite runs together
findings.description:
MEASURED both ways, on the same machine, same interpreter, same flags (pytest tests/ -q -p no:randomly -m 'not integration'):
  at HEAD (1dbca8f0), unmodified:   87 failed, 3021 passed
  with this session's changes:      87 failed, 3031 passed  (+10 new tests)
Identical count, identical files. Re-running exactly those 87 with --lf: 87 passed in 42s. So every one of them passes alone and fails in company -- shared state, not broken code.
Concentrated in: test_tenant_isolation_matrix (45), test_tiers_privilege (14), test_system_improvements (12), test_wearable_measurements (8), test_user_preferences (5), test_startup_guard (2), test_capability_import_roots (1).
This matters beyond tidiness: a suite that is red for reasons unrelated to the diff trains everyone to ignore it, and it makes a real regression indistinguishable from the background noise. Recorded here with the exact before/after numbers so the next pass starts from measurement rather than from a guess about whose change did it.
FIRST CAUSE ATTRIBUTED (NR-124): tests/notifications/test_ntfy_connector.py imported `from backend.app.integration.connectors.ntfy import NtfyConnector`. That loads a second copy of the module tree under a root that does not exist on a deployed backend, and it stays in sys.modules for the rest of the session, so test_capability_import_roots::test_a_real_application_start_loads_no_stateful_second_copy failed in company and passed alone. Corrected to `app.…`; the full suite went 87 -> 86 failures and 3031 -> 3039 passes. Each remaining cluster still needs its own cause found rather than assumed.
ROOT CAUSE FOUND — see NR-126. Of the 87, exactly one (NR-124, the shadow `backend.` import) was independent. The other 86 had a single cause: tests/test_staging_config_guard.py evicting app.config from sys.modules and never restoring it. Full suite after the fix: 0 failed, 3126 passed.

findings.title: Four clinical endpoints 500 because national_patients is built by no migration
findings.description:

findings.title: Twenty-one frontend calls request a path with an empty segment, and the contract guard skipped exactly those
findings.description:
frontend-v3 calls 434 distinct backend paths; 367 are served after NR-122. 21 of the remainder contain an empty path segment where an id belongs:

    api.get("/national/documents//versions")

findings.title: A test imported through the shadow package root that two earlier findings exist to prevent
findings.description:
tests/notifications/test_ntfy_connector.py line 7:
    from backend.app.integration.connectors.ntfy import NtfyConnector
`backend/` is not a package -- it has no __init__.py, and backend/pyproject.toml publishes include = ["app*"] -- so this only resolves when the repository root is on sys.path, which is the test environment and not a deployed one. When it does resolve it loads a SECOND copy of that module and everything it imports, each with its own state. That is exactly the defect class NR-056 and NR-058 were opened for.
In a test suite it is worse than elsewhere: the import stays in sys.modules for the whole session, so it becomes a cross-test failure. It is the attributed cause of test_capability_import_roots::test_a_real_application_start_loads_no_stateful_second_copy failing in the full run and passing alone -- one of the 87 order-dependent failures of NR-118. Full suite after the fix: 86 failed / 3039 passed, against 87 / 3031 before.
WHY IT CAME BACK: the NR-056 guard scanned app/engineering/ only, because that is where the defect was found. 'Where it was found' is a weaker boundary than 'everywhere the root is importable from', so the scan now covers every Python file under backend/, tests included, with a positive control asserting it reaches tests/.
findings.evidence: 87 -> 86 failures on the full suite; 26 guard tests green

findings.status: CORRECTED — this was a SYMPTOM of NR-126, not an independent cause. The code change is retained as hardening; the diagnosis was wrong.
findings.title: Two startup-guard tests set an environment variable the code had already frozen
findings.description:
TestTestModeBypass set os.environ["RUNTIME_MODE"] = "test" and expected run_startup_guard() to take the test-mode bypass. It does not. The function reads `from ..config import RUNTIME_MODE`, a module constant bound the first time app.config is imported.
Run alone, that import happens inside the call and picks the freshly set variable up, so the test passes. Run after anything that has already touched app.config -- which is nearly the whole suite -- the constant is already "api", the bypass never fires, run_startup_guard() attempts real validation against an in-memory SQLite with no alembic_version table, and system_ready stays False.
So the failure was the test's assumption about import timing, not the guard. Both now monkeypatch app.config.RUNTIME_MODE, which is the faithful analogue of production, where the value is fixed at process start and the constant IS the truth.
Full suite: 86 -> 84 failures. Attributed causes of NR-118 so far: NR-124 (1), NR-125 (2). The three remaining clusters -- test_tenant_isolation_matrix (45), test_tiers_privilege (14), test_system_improvements (12), test_wearable_measurements (8), test_user_preferences (5) -- each still need their own cause found rather than assumed from these two.
DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED. This attributed the failure to import timing -- that app.config had already been imported with RUNTIME_MODE="api" so a later os.environ write could not affect the constant. MEASURED AFTERWARDS: with NR-126 fixed, both tests pass with the ORIGINAL os.environ form restored (window 229-260: 526 passed, 0 failed). So the constant was not stale because of import ordering; it had been REWRITTEN to 'migration' by the staging-config helper evicting the module. These two failures were part of the same 86 that NR-126 explains, and this finding did not fix two independent failures as first recorded.
The change itself stays: monkeypatching the attribute the function actually reads is a more faithful analogue of production than setting an environment variable that config reads once at import. But it is hardening, not a fix.
findings.evidence: both tests pass alone and after test_system_improvements; full suite 86 -> 84

findings.status: CLOSED — smallest-boundary fix in the helper that caused it, 4/4 negative proofs held, full suite 84 -> 0.
findings.title: A config-isolation helper evicted app.config from sys.modules and never put it back, and 86 tests failed 503
findings.description:
SINGLE ROOT CAUSE of 86 of the 87 order-dependent failures recorded as NR-118.

MINIMAL REPRODUCER, three files, found by delta debugging after plain bisection failed (the two halves of the window each reproduced NOTHING, because the two halves of the interaction are in different halves of the file order):
    tests/test_reference_side_door_stays_closed.py   (order index 230)
    tests/test_staging_config_guard.py               (order index 253)
    tests/test_tenant_isolation_matrix.py            (order index 261)
  -> 45 failed, 8 passed.   Any two of the three: all pass.

THE CHAIN, each link measured rather than inferred:
  1. migrations/env.py line 16 runs `os.environ["RUNTIME_MODE"] = "migration"` at import, unconditionally and without restoring it. (Lines 17-21 beside it use setdefault; line 16 does not.) test_reference_side_door_stays_closed.py imports that module, so the process environment is poisoned from then on. Harmless alone: app.config was already imported with RUNTIME_MODE="test" and a module attribute does not follow os.environ.
  2. tests/test_staging_config_guard.py::_load_config does `sys.modules.pop("app.config", None)` so it can import a second copy under a staging environment -- and leaves it evicted. Harmless alone: the next import rebuilds it from an environment that still says "test".
  3. Together: after the eviction, the next `from ..config import RUNTIME_MODE` anywhere re-imports app.config against the poisoned environment and binds RUNTIME_MODE="migration". Instrumented and captured:
       tests/test_staging_config_guard.py::test_staging_uses_hardened_production_guards
           ('test', False) -> ('migration', False)
  4. app/core/startup_guard.py:793 imports RUNTIME_MODE INSIDE run_startup_guard(), so it reads the name at call time. Line 796's `if RUNTIME_MODE == "test"` bypass stops firing.
  5. The guard then runs full production validation against the conftest's in-memory SQLite, fails at check_migrations() with 'alembic_version table not found', and leaves the module global system_ready = False.
  6. ReadinessMiddleware answers 503 to every non-whitelisted path for the rest of the session. The observed assertion was literally `assert 503 in (401, 403)`.
All five failing clusters sit AFTER index 253 and use the `client` fixture, which is exactly the predicted blast radius.

CLASSIFICATION: test-isolation defect, with a latent production-side contributor. The fix is in the test helper only -- the smallest boundary that closes it -- because migrations/env.py forcing migration mode is CORRECT for Alembic, and changing line 16 to setdefault would alter production migration semantics. That half is recorded here rather than changed.

THE FIX NEEDED TWO PARTS, and the first alone was not enough. Restoring sys.modules left RUNTIME_MODE at "api" instead of "migration" -- still not "test" -- because importlib.import_module ALSO rebinds the attribute on the parent package, and `import app.config as cfg` reads that attribute before it consults sys.modules. Measured: window 229-260 went 13 failures -> 7 -> 0 as each half of the restore was added.

BEFORE/AFTER, same command (pytest tests/ -q -m "not integration"):
    HEAD 1dbca8f0   87 failed / 3021 passed
    after NR-124    86 failed / 3039 passed
    after NR-125    84 failed / 3041 passed   (masking, not fixing -- see NR-125)
    after NR-126     0 failed / 3126 passed
findings.evidence: three-file minimal reproducer; instrumented RUNTIME_MODE transition; 4/4 negative proofs; full suite 84 -> 0

findings.status: CONTAINED — 2026-09-19. The header trust boundary is removed. nhop-platform/app/core/trusted_context.py is now the only source of caller identity in the service and it fails closed: require_trusted_context raises 503 because no identity provider is federated with NHOP. It is attached once, to api_router in app/api/v1/__init__.py, so it covers all 14 served /v1 operations including the ones that read no actor. All 6 header reads across citizens.py, doctor.py, notifications.py, outbreak.py, test_results.py and core/rbac.py now read current_context(request); zero Header() reads remain under app/. There is deliberately no env var or header that can switch the context on -- tests supply one through app.dependency_overrides. NOT CLOSED: the 21 endpoints are unavailable until GULA identity is federated, which replaces only the body of require_trusted_context. Regression: nhop-platform/tests/test_trust_boundary.py (32 tests).
findings.title: nhop-platform has no authentication: every authority decision reads a client-supplied header
findings.description:
MEASURED, whole-repository scan. The X-Actor-Id / X-Role trust-boundary defect is NOT in backend/. backend/ has zero occurrences outside one unrelated docstring, and backend/tests/test_security_regression.py:177 already asserts that X-Role / X-Lab-Id / X-User-Id confer no authority there. The entire defect lives in nhop-platform/.

nhop-platform has NO authentication stack at all. app/core/ contains exactly database.py and rbac.py -- no JWT, no login, no session, no token, no current-user dependency anywhere in the tree. rbac.py says so itself:
    "The production auth stack (JWT-backed) lives in the GULA platform.
     Until NHOP shares that identity surface, routes that need
     authorisation read the caller's role from the X-Role request header."

So the complete authority model is: whatever the client puts in a header.
  app/core/rbac.py:33   role taken from the X-Role header. Any caller may
                        send X-Role: MINISTRY and pass require_roles().
  citizens.py:47, doctor.py:60, notifications.py:36, outbreak.py:40,
  test_results.py:60    actor identity taken from X-Actor-Id. Any caller
                        may act as any actor, and the value is PERSISTED
                        as the recorded actor.
  doctor.py:76-86       the doctor gate requires X-Actor-Role == DOCTOR
                        and a non-empty X-Actor-Id. Both are client input.
21 routes across five modules; only 2 of them even call require_roles.

DEPLOYMENT STATUS, stated precisely because it changes the urgency and I do not want it overstated either way: nhop-platform is INDEPENDENTLY DEPLOYABLE -- it ships its own Dockerfile and its own docker-compose.yml -- but it is NOT wired into the platform deployment. Zero references in the root docker-compose.yml / .full.yml / .scale.yml, and nothing matching nhop under k8s/, helm/, terraform/ or digitalocean/. The two CI workflows that name it use it for an import-walk and a dependency scan only. So it is not exposed by the current stack, and it is one `docker compose up` away from being exposed.

WHY THIS IS NOT FIXED HERE. Closing it requires a trusted server-derived context, and nhop-platform has none to derive from. The only routes to one are (a) build an identity stack inside nhop-platform, or (b) federate GULA's. Both create or move canonical identity semantics across a service boundary, which is an explicit stop condition and is reserved. Patching the 21 endpoints individually is also explicitly out of bounds, and would leave the same header as the root of authority.
findings.evidence: repo-wide grep: 27 header occurrences, all under nhop-platform/ and its tests; app/core/ has no auth module; 0 deployment references

findings.status: CONTAINED — 2026-09-19 by NR-127's fix. POST /v1/test-results/ now answers 503 before the handler runs, so a result can no longer be filed against a lab named in the request body. This route is exactly why the dependency was attached to api_router rather than to each handler that reads an actor: create_test_result reads no actor at all, so per-handler wiring would have missed the worst route. NOT CLOSED: the body's lab_id must still be compared against the caller's own lab when federation lands -- containment removes the reachability, not the missing ownership check.
findings.title: A clinical test result can be filed against any lab, for any citizen, by anyone
findings.description:
nhop-platform/app/api/v1/test_results.py:184, in create_test_result:
    lab = db.query(Lab).filter(Lab.id == payload.lab_id).first()
    if lab is None: 404
    if not lab.is_active: 400
The lab is taken from the REQUEST BODY and the only checks are that it exists and is active. Nothing establishes that the caller is that lab, because nothing establishes who the caller is -- the route has no authentication and does not even call require_roles (see NR-127).

Consequence: an unauthenticated caller can file a fabricated clinical test result, attributed to a real named laboratory, against any citizen identified by health_id. The result is validated for plausibility (validate_result checks unit and reference range) and persisted with lab_id=lab.id, so it is indistinguishable downstream from a genuine result from that lab.

This is the classic BOLA shape -- a client-supplied object id used as authority -- but it cannot be fixed in the usual way (compare the body's lab_id to the caller's own) until a caller identity exists. It is therefore blocked on the same decision as NR-127 and recorded with it rather than patched at this one endpoint.
findings.evidence: nhop-platform/app/api/v1/test_results.py:184; route has 0 require_roles and no auth dependency

findings.status: CLOSED — 2026-09-19. All 18 imports now come from the standard library; the service imports its own app on the container's path. Regression: backend/tests/test_engineering_tooling_imports.py::test_nothing_under_nhop_imports_the_shadow_root.
findings.title: The nhop-platform container cannot start: 15 modules import the backend shadow root
findings.description:
MEASURED. 15 modules under nhop-platform/app/ do `from backend.app._compat import UTC`, among them app/models/citizen.py and app/models/lab.py, which app/main.py reaches transitively at import time.

nhop-platform/Dockerfile copies only `app/`, `alembic/` and `alembic.ini` into /app and runs `uvicorn app.main:app`. There is no `backend/` anywhere in that image, so the import raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'backend' before the app object is built. The service as packaged cannot boot. Reproduced directly: running pytest from nhop-platform/ without PYTHONPATH=<repo root> fails collection at app/models/lab.py:17 with that exact error; the suite only passes because the repo root happens to be on sys.path when run from the monorepo.

This is the NR-124 shadow-root class (`backend/` is not a package -- it has no __init__.py, and pyproject publishes include=["app*"]), but the existing guard in backend/tests/test_engineering_tooling_imports.py scans backend/app and backend/tests only, so nhop-platform is outside its reach.

Blast radius is bounded: nhop-platform is not referenced by the root docker-compose.yml, k8s/, helm, terraform/ or digitalocean/ -- it ships its own compose file and is not part of the primary deployment. That is why this is P1 and not P0.

Fix shape: nhop needs its own UTC compat shim (the symbol is a one-line datetime.timezone.utc alias) and the import guard should be widened to cover nhop-platform/. Not done here because it touches 15 modules across a service outside the P0 trust boundary.

FIXED 2026-09-19. The 15 app modules and 3 test modules now do `from datetime import UTC` directly. A compat shim was written first and then deleted: nhop's Dockerfile is FROM python:3.14-slim and the code already uses enum.StrEnum unguarded, which is 3.11+, so the sub-3.11 branch the shim existed for was dead code and the shim was pure indirection. Importing the symbol from the standard library is what the rest of the tree already does for StrEnum.

PROOF, replicating the container rather than describing it: with only nhop-platform on sys.path and no monorepo root, `import app.main` raised ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'backend' before; it now builds the app and serves 14 paths. The suite gives identical results with and without the repo root on the path (39 passed / 21 pre-existing errors either way), which is itself the evidence that nhop no longer depends on the monorepo layout.

GUARD: the NR-124 shadow-import scan now covers nhop-platform/app and nhop-platform/tests as well as backend/, with its own positive control on the module count. CI compiles nhop-platform but never imports it, so a syntax gate could not have caught this and did not. Negative proof: restoring one shadow import fails the guard AND breaks the container import again.
findings.evidence: nhop-platform/app/models/lab.py:17 and 14 sibling modules; nhop-platform/Dockerfile:19-21 (COPY app/ alembic/ alembic.ini only), Dockerfile:27 CMD uvicorn app.main:app

findings.status: CLOSED — 2026-09-19. All 21 now run and pass; the nhop suite is 60 passed / 0 errors, from 5 passed / 21 errors. Fixed without the sys.modules purge.
findings.title: 21 nhop-platform tests had never run: two broken fixtures, two different causes
findings.description:
CORRECTION. This finding first recorded that 'every one of the 21 is the same cause'. That was wrong, and measuring properly before fixing showed two:
  10 in tests/test_doctor_api.py — NameError: name 'sys' is not defined, from conftest.py:25 using sys in the app_client fixture without importing it.
  11 in tests/test_outbreak_detection.py — fixture 'db_session' not found. It was never written. No amount of repairing app_client would have reached these.
Baseline at HEAD, confirmed by git stash: 5 passed / 21 errors.

NOT FIXED BY ADDING `import sys`. The line it would have enabled purges every `app.*` entry from sys.modules mid-suite to rebind the app to a test database. That is the NR-126 state-leak class just closed in backend/: modules imported earlier keep stale references while later imports get fresh ones, and the suite becomes order-dependent. FastAPI already has the mechanism — override the get_db dependency — so app_client now swaps the database without touching the import system at all, and db_session was written.

A SECOND DEFECT THE TESTS HID. test_doctor_api drove the production app and asserted 403/201 on /v1/doctor/*, but doctor_router is not included in api_router: the deployed service does not serve those paths, so every request would have answered 404. Had the fixture merely been repaired, all ten would have failed on a 404 that says nothing about the router's logic. The router is now mounted in the test's own app, exactly as production mounts a /v1 router, which exercises its logic without changing what the service exposes — the same thing test_outbreak_api.py does for the equally dormant outbreak router.

They also authenticated with X-Actor-Role and X-Actor-Id headers, which NR-127 removed. They now supply a caller by overriding require_trusted_context, and the auth test asserts the new contract end to end: no context -> 503, forged identity headers -> 503, a real non-doctor caller -> 403, a doctor with no actor id -> 401. The dead doctor_headers fixture was deleted rather than left to describe a contract that no longer exists.

NEGATIVE PROOF: removing the router-level containment fails all 10; making the role gate accept anyone fails exactly the auth test. Both byte-restored.

The 11 outbreak-detection tests were already correct and needed only the missing fixture; they now cover outbreak ratio thresholds, noise suppression, alert ordering, the province heatmap and the resistance report — logic that had no coverage at all.
findings.evidence: nhop-platform/tests/conftest.py:25 (sys used, never imported); nhop-platform/tests/conftest.py:130 doctor_headers; baseline `pytest tests/` = 5 passed / 21 errors, confirmed via git stash

findings.status: CLOSED — 2026-09-19. Fixed and proven end to end. Regression: frontend-v3/src/api/devProxyContract.test.ts.
findings.title: The documented `npm run dev` workflow could not reach the backend at all
findings.description:
MEASURED against a real backend. The API client's base URL is /api (frontend-v3/src/api/client.ts:7). In production the gateway serves that prefix as `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://gula_backend/; }` (config/nginx/conf.d/api.conf:159-161), and the trailing slash on proxy_pass STRIPS /api before the request reaches the backend. The dev proxy in frontend-v3/vite.config.ts forwarded /api to http://localhost:8000 with changeOrigin but NO rewrite, so the prefix survived and the backend, which does not serve it, answered 404.

Probed through `npm run dev` against a running backend:
    POST /api/login            -> 404      POST /login            -> 422
    POST /api/patients         -> 404      POST /patients         -> 401
    POST /api/admin/labs       -> 404      POST /admin/labs       -> 401
    POST /api/api/ai/providers -> 404      POST /api/ai/providers -> 405
    POST /api/health/ready     -> 404      POST /health/ready     -> 405
5 of 5. Not login alone -- every live-mode call in development.

The backend serves 1794 paths, of which 66 sit under a genuine /api prefix (/api/ai/*). endpoints.ts declares both shapes, and both are correct in production: /admin/labs arrives as /api/admin/labs and is stripped to /admin/labs; /api/ai/chat arrives as /api/api/ai/chat and is stripped to /api/ai/chat. One prefix, not two. The fix is the same anchored strip the gateway performs, so a greedy replace would corrupt the second shape -- the regression test covers that case explicitly.

WHY IT SURVIVED: all 13 Playwright e2e specs mock the API with page.route (e2e/auth.spec.ts:8 mocks **/api/login outright), so the entire suite passes against a frontend that cannot talk to a backend. 53 e2e tests, 64 unit tests, typecheck, lint and build were all green over this defect.

PROOF OF THE FIX: scripts/runtime_gates.py was pointed at http://127.0.0.1:5173/api -- the frontend's dev server, at the API client's own base URL -- and all 62 gates passed: authentication, session, refresh, revocation, rate limiting, lockout, authorization, forged-header rejection, tenant isolation and the clinical path. The same 62 run directly against the backend give the same result, so the proxy is transparent. Before the fix the same run scored 0 reachable.
findings.evidence: frontend-v3/vite.config.ts server.proxy['/api']; config/nginx/conf.d/api.conf:159-161; frontend-v3/src/api/client.ts:7; frontend-v3/e2e/auth.spec.ts:8

findings.status: OPEN — registered 2026-09-19, deliberately NOT wired. See the description.
findings.title: Demo Mode cannot be exercised in development: /demo-api has no target
findings.description:
frontend-v3/src/api/client.ts:10 hardcodes DEMO_API_BASE_URL = '/demo-api', and vite.config.ts declares no proxy entry for it. Measured through `npm run dev`: POST /demo-api/login and /demo-api/patients both return 404 with no content-type. Demo Mode is unreachable locally.

NOT fixed by adding a proxy entry. .env.example states that the demo base URL 'must target a separate API deployment using DEMO_MODE=true, DEMO_DATA_ISOLATION_ACK=true, and synthetic data only'. Pointing /demo-api at the live backend on :8000 -- the only backend a developer has running -- would serve REAL patient data through the surface whose entire contract is that it serves synthetic data. That is a data isolation violation dressed as a convenience, and a 404 is the safer failure.

Correct fix: run a second backend with DEMO_MODE=true and point the proxy at it, or document that Demo Mode requires that deployment. Either way it is a deployment decision, not a config line.
findings.evidence: frontend-v3/src/api/client.ts:10; frontend-v3/vite.config.ts server.proxy; .env.example

findings.status: CLOSED — 2026-09-19. Fixed in scripts/runtime_gates.py; proven by running the suite twice against one database.
findings.title: The runtime gate suite could only be run once, and its second run lied about tenant isolation
findings.description:
scripts/runtime_gates.py created its gate 5 patient fixtures with fixed phone numbers (07701000001, 07701000099). Against a fresh database the suite scored 62/62. Run a second time against the SAME database, the create collided with the uniqueness constraint and returned 409, so the fixture guard returned early: 36/38, with gate 5 reported as failing and gate 6 never executed at all.

The reported failure was 'a forged lab_id in the body is refused outright' -- which reads as a tenant-isolation regression and is nothing of the kind. A verification suite whose second run reports a security failure it did not observe is worse than one that does not run: it is a false negative aimed at the highest-severity gate it owns.

Caught because the same 36/38 appeared BOTH through the frontend dev proxy and directly against the backend. Identical results on both paths ruled out the proxy and pointed at shared state.

Fixed with a per-run RUN_TAG applied to the fixture phone numbers and names, and to the search assertion that looks for those names -- so a row left by an earlier run can no longer collide with, or be mistaken for, this run's. Proven by two consecutive runs against one persistent database: 62/62 then 62/62.
findings.evidence: scripts/runtime_gates.py gate5 fixtures; two consecutive runs 62/62 on one database

findings.status: CLOSED — 2026-09-19. One allowlist in backend/app/security/origins.py, both layers read it. Regression: backend/tests/test_dev_origin_allowlist.py (15 tests).
findings.title: Two copies of the origin allowlist, both missing the loopback spelling the repo's own tooling uses
findings.description:
MEASURED. A browser write must pass TWO independent origin checks:
  backend/app/factory.py  — the CORS middleware allowlist
  backend/app/security/csrf.py::_allowed_origins — the origin check on cookie-authenticated mutations
Each read CORS_ORIGINS itself and each carried its own hardcoded development fallback. Two copies of one policy, and they had drifted identically: both listed http://localhost:{3000,4173,5173,8000} and NEITHER listed the 127.0.0.1 spelling.

The repository uses both spellings. frontend-v3/vite.config.ts sets allowedHosts: ['localhost', '127.0.0.1']; frontend-v3/playwright.config.ts drives the browser from http://127.0.0.1:4173 and starts its web server on --host 127.0.0.1. To a browser those are different origins. So every browser-originated write from a Playwright run against a real backend was answered 403 {"detail": "Cross-origin request rejected"} -- which reads as a defect in the page and is a gap in a list.

HOW THE SECOND COPY WAS FOUND: fixing factory.py alone changed nothing. POST /api/register still returned the same 403, because the rejection came from the other layer. That is the whole argument for one list: a request has to satisfy both, so repairing either in isolation is invisible.

FIX: backend/app/security/origins.py is now the only place the allowlist is computed, and both layers call it. It decides WHAT is allowed; factory.py keeps its own production validation on top (no wildcard with credentials, HTTPS-only in production). The development fallback now carries both spellings of the loopback host, and only when ENV is development or test -- production behaviour is unchanged and is asserted as such.

Separately, CORS_ORIGINS and TRUSTED_HOSTS are named in config.py under required_network_settings but were absent from .env.example, so a developer copying the template got an empty allowlist with no indication why writes were refused. Both are now documented there.
findings.evidence: backend/app/factory.py CORS block; backend/app/security/csrf.py::_allowed_origins; frontend-v3/playwright.config.ts:13,33-35; frontend-v3/vite.config.ts allowedHosts; POST /api/register -> 403 Cross-origin request rejected, reproduced before and after the factory-only fix

findings.status: AUTHENTICATION HALF CLOSED — 2026-09-19. NIAM is now the canonical identity a legacy login produces: the token carries account_uuid, a niam_sessions row is bound to that token's own jti, and logout terminates it. 12/12 runtime proofs. The clinical READ remains BLOCKED one step further on, at missing_workspace (NR-137) — organizational context provisioning, not authentication.
findings.title: No user who logs in through the frontend can read patients or orders through the frontend
findings.description:
MEASURED end to end against a running backend and a real session.

frontend-v3 reads clinical data through exactly one sanctioned path. src/api/workspaceScopedReads.ts sets DIRECT_REST_SCOPED_READS_BLOCKED = true and states that the legacy /patients and /lims/orders surfaces are 'blocked forever for frontend-v3'; reads may use only /api/v1/clinical/patients and /api/v1/clinical/orders.

Those two routes ARE served (confirmed in the OpenAPI document) and correctly answer 401 unauthenticated. But they are guarded by get_current_niam_actor_sync (app/clinical_gateway/routes.py:187,218), which requires a NIAM token: a payload carrying account_uuid and jti, matched against a niam_sessions row joined to niam_accounts (app/identity/api/workspaces.py:35-80).

POST /login mints a LEGACY token. Decoded, a real one carries exactly:
    act, exp, iat, jti, lab_id, perm_ver, role, type, user_id
It fails the gateway on BOTH counts, independently:
  1. account_uuid is absent from the claims entirely.
  2. niam_sessions rows matching that token's jti: 0. Logging in does not      create a NIAM session row, so even a token carrying the claim would      find nothing to join to.
Result, reproduced with a freshly registered and activated tenant:
    GET /api/v1/clinical/patients -> 401 'Invalid NIAM access token'
    GET /api/v1/clinical/orders   -> 401 'Invalid NIAM access token'

So the platform's primary clinical read surface is unreachable by any session the platform's only login path can mint. The workspace cannot show a patient or an order to a real user, ever.

WHY THIS LOOKS LIKE SOMETHING ELSE. workspaceScopedReads.ts maps 401 to the reason 'missing_workspace' and the message 'لا تملك جلسة أو صلاحية قراءة'. The page renders 'قراءة المرضى غير متاحة لهذه الجلسة' -- 'patient reading is not available for this session' -- and e2e/patients.spec.ts asserts that text under the name 'blocks direct patient reads until server enforcement is proven'. That reads as a deliberate governance gate awaiting a server-side control. It is not. The control exists and is sound; the session simply cannot authenticate to it. A capability gap is wearing the costume of a safety decision, which is why it has survived: every test that touches it asserts the blocked state is present.

NOT A SECURITY DEFECT. It fails closed with 401 and no data is exposed. The gateway's envelope contract is well built -- it pins contract_version, requires a workspace context, and explicitly rejects phone, national_id and lab_id from patient records. Nothing here should be weakened to make the read work.

WHY IT IS NOT FIXED HERE. Any repair picks a canonical identity: mint NIAM claims from /login, create a niam_sessions row at login, bridge legacy tokens to NIAM accounts, or move the gateway onto the legacy actor. Each is a different answer to 'which identity system is canonical', each has migration and audit consequences for existing sessions, and AUTH-002 already analysed the options. Choosing one autonomously is precisely the change this work is not authorised to make.

RESOLVED 2026-09-19 for the authentication half, after the identity decision was made: NIAM is canonical, legacy auth is a compatibility boundary.

app/identity/services/legacy_session_bridge.py resolves the canonical account from the ALREADY-AUTHENTICATED legacy row through niam_legacy_account_links -- the bridge primitive that already existed -- and binds a niam_sessions row to the jti of the token /login just minted. One login, one jti, one session. The client supplies a credential and nothing else: account_uuid, identity_id, person_id, lab_id and role are never read from the request on this path.

It creates no accounts. LegacyMappingService states it 'never creates canonical accounts ... those actions require separate approved waves', and direct account creation is fail-closed at 410 behind a review-gated intake. Auto-provisioning would cross both boundaries, so it is NR-137.

MEASURED, 12/12 over real HTTP against PostgreSQL: login succeeds; the token carries the canonical account_uuid; a niam_sessions row exists for that exact jti and is bound to the right account; the NIAM-protected surface no longer answers 401; forged identity headers change nothing; a client-supplied account_uuid, lab_id or role in the login body changes neither identity, tenant nor privilege; two logins yield two live sessions and no corrupt state; logout terminates the canonical session and the surface then refuses the token.

ONE DEFECT INTRODUCED AND FIXED DURING THIS WORK, kept as a regression test: wiring the lookup into /login made every login query niam_legacy_account_links, so against a database without the NIAM tables the OperationalError propagated and LOGIN ITSELF FAILED -- test_auth_infrastructure.py went from 30 passed to 6 passed / 24 errors. The lookup now runs in a SAVEPOINT and treats a database error as 'no canonical account': a failure withholds authority and can never grant it, and a missing table is not an outage.

findings.title: Every GitHub Actions run in this repository fails in seconds, and has since 2026-08-21
findings.description:
MEASURED across the 40 most recent workflow runs, repository-wide, all branches and all triggers:
    conclusions: 39 failure, 1 startup_failure, 0 success
Durations: 4-7 seconds. Every workflow, not one: IAM Hardening Gate, Frontend Bundle Budget, CodeQL Advanced, CodeQL Analysis, Dependency Review, Formatting Check, Constitution Compliance, Opt-in PR Auto-Merge.

On the BASE BRANCH too: the last five IAM Hardening Gate runs on main all failed, the oldest on 2026-08-21, several completing in 5-7 seconds. So this predates every branch currently in flight and is not any PR's failure.

RULED OUT, each by direct check rather than inference:
  - Workflow syntax. .github/workflows/iam-hardening.yml parses; jobs are     backend-identity, migration, frontend-v3, security-regression.
  - Runner label. All four jobs are runs-on: ubuntu-latest.
  - Gated jobs. No job-level `environment:`, no `secrets.` reference, no     job-level `if:`; permissions is contents: read.
  - The code. The entire 'Frontend v3 contract, type and build gates' job was     run locally on the same head: typecheck clean, lint clean at     --max-warnings 0, 69 unit tests, build succeeds, bundle budget 0     violations. The backend suite is 3180 passed / 0 failed. The red is not     the code.
  - Log retrieval. Downloading job logs returns HTTP 404 -- not truncated     logs, no logs. No step ever executed.

WHAT IT POINTS TO. Jobs that fail in seconds with no logs at all, across every workflow and every branch, while a non-Actions check on the same commits succeeds (the Vercel GitHub App deploys normally, Building -> Ready), is the signature of an ACCOUNT-LEVEL Actions block rather than anything in the repository: included minutes exhausted with no payment method or a spending limit reached, or Actions disabled by repository/organisation policy. The one run whose conclusion is `startup_failure` is GitHub reporting that it could not start the workflow at all.

REMEDY, for the repository owner: GitHub billing -> Actions minutes and spending limit for the account, and Settings -> Actions -> General for the repository's Actions permissions. Nothing in this tree can change it.

CONSEQUENCE WHILE IT HOLDS: there is no CI signal on any commit. Every gate claimed in this register has been proven locally instead, and that is stated as such rather than being called a CI pass. A standing-down comment is on PR #258. Re-running is not available to this session (403 on rerun-failed-jobs), and would not help: the account, not the run, is blocked.

findings.title: A canonically-authenticated account still has no organizational context, so the clinical read stops at missing_workspace
findings.description:
With NR-135 in place a legacy login now produces a real NIAM session and the clinical gateway authenticates it -- 401 became 403. Measured in-process, the gateway then blocks with reason_code `missing_workspace` (app/clinical_gateway/context.py:66).

The context resolver requires a chain this account does not have: workspace -> membership -> legacy identity resolution -> facility mapping, with `cross_tenant_scope` and `facility_mismatch` as its tenant-isolation controls. Those controls are already canonical and correct; nothing parallel should be built beside them.

TWO THINGS ARE MISSING, and both are provisioning rather than code:
  1. Canonical ACCOUNTS for legacy users. LegacyMappingService 'never creates canonical accounts ... those actions require separate approved waves and an explicit feature-flagged cohort', and POST on the account-creation route is fail-closed at 410 behind a review-gated intake. The NR-135 runtime proof provisions one out of band, as a fixture, precisely because the product has no sanctioned path.
  2. Organizational CONTEXT for those accounts: workspace, membership and facility mapping.

WHY NOT GUESSED. AuthenticationService._create_session calls WorkspaceService.ensure_citizen_workspace, so the NIAM-native login does create a workspace -- a CITIZEN one. Giving a laboratory administrator a citizen workspace to make the read succeed would be inventing identity semantics and could widen scope. The decision needed is which workspace and membership a bridged legacy lab_user is entitled to, and by whose approval.

GULA_CLINICAL_GATEWAY_MODE also gates the surface (default off; the proof runs with it ON in the test environment only, production default untouched). That is a rollout control working as designed, not a defect.
